f615783b8ed4.text: By — Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press By — Anne D'Innocenzio, Associated Press Anne D'Innocenzio, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/consumer-concerns-grow-as-retailers-adopt-ai-assisted-pricing-tools Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Consumer concerns grow as retailers adopt AI-assisted pricing tools Economy Oct 19, 2026 2:35 PM EDT U.S. consumers aren't just frustrated with high prices. They're angry and confused about the increasingly high-tech ways that restaurant chains and major retailers are setting those prices. Digital price tags are rapidly replacing paper ones in grocery aisles. Artificial intelligence tools help businesses decide what to charge by predicting how customers might respond. Terms like "dynamic pricing" and "surveillance pricing" are stirring anxiety on social media, where users wonder if different people are getting different prices for the same product. Americans have grown accustomed to changing prices when booking flights, hotel rooms and rides, but the prospect of everyday spending shaped by algorithms they don't understand and personal data they may not realize they're sharing has touched a nerve. "There are major tensions happening right now between who's really going to have the power with some of these algorithms and usage of bots and AI: the companies or the shopper," said Katie Thomas, who leads an internal consumer behavior think tank at the management consulting firm Kearney. Companies using the technology say some concerns stem from misconceptions about how their pricing tools work. Walmart CEO John Furner said in a blog post last month that digital price tags save workers' time and keep prices up to date. He said the labels aren't used to raise prices based on the weather, time of day or individual shopper. "We price the product, not the person," Furner wrote. But companies aren't always transparent about the customer data they collect and how it's used, which has made consumers suspicious and led to speculation. For example, social media posts falsely imply that electronic shelf labels Walmart plans to put in all its U.S. stores scan shoppers' faces or cellphones to set individualized prices, Thomas said. Lawmakers and regulators are taking action. Legislators in at least 30 states have considered pricing bills this year, including measures addressing algorithmic and personalized pricing, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. The Federal Trade Commission has proposed an enforcement policy warning businesses that failing to disclose their use of personal data to set individualized prices could violate consumer protection law. Here are some of the pricing practices and technologies drawing scrutiny. Dynamic pricing can raise and lower prices What it is: Dynamic pricing means adjusting prices in response to changing market conditions, including supply and demand. An airline that adjusts ticket prices as departures approach is using dynamic pricing. Uber's practice of lifting fares when demand outstrips the supply of available drivers, such as during rush hour, is a type of dynamic pricing known as surge pricing. Why it matters: Frequent price changes extend well beyond food. Decodo, a web data company, tracked price changes in 2025 across products ranging from electronics to clothing and home improvement supplies. About half the U.S. changes it recorded were decreases, contrary to consumers' assumptions that dynamic pricing only raises prices, said Gabriele Vitke, a senior product marketing manager. Digital price labels are coming to more US stores What they are: Digital displays that let stores update shelf prices electronically instead of replacing paper tags. Why it matters: Digital price labels, long used in Europe and Asia, are drawing more attention as they spread to major U.S. retailers like Walmart and Whole Foods. Consumer advocates have argued that digital labels could eventually be used for surge pricing or personalized pricing. Labor unions also have opposed the technology. READ MORE: Inflation worsened last month to 3.7% as midterm elections near The electronic shelf labels make frequent changes easier but don't necessarily lead to higher prices during periods of strong demand. Retailers typically update electronic shelf prices on a regular schedule, often weekly, because shoppers value consistency, said Asa Farquhar of Relex Solutions, a retail technology company. Researchers who tracked prices at an unnamed grocery chain found "virtually no surge pricing" after the labels were introduced. "Changing prices throughout the day, the way airlines or rideshare apps do, is exceedingly rare in grocery and general merchandise today," Farquhar said. Personalized pricing, also called surveillance pricing, draws on customer data What it is: Personalized pricing means offering customers different prices and discounts based on their locations, incomes, web-browsing habits and other information about individuals or groups of shoppers. Some advocacy groups and regulators use the term "surveillance pricing" for the same practice. Why it matters: It's unclear how widely businesses use personal information to customize prices. An FTC staff report released in January 2025 found that intermediaries offering tools that can tailor prices and promotions worked with at least 250 clients, including grocery and clothing retailers. Lawmakers in Maryland, New Jersey and Connecticut recently enacted restrictions on using shoppers' personal data to determine what they pay. The Maryland and New Jersey laws focus on groceries, with exceptions for certain loyalty discounts and other promotional offers. Connecticut's legislation covers a broader range of retail purchases. The US has ordered all artificial intelligence (AI) technology from the Chinese firm DeepSeek to be removed from most government systems.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has banned all use of DeepSeek within civilian government agencies, and any technology built with the aid of its AI models.
As a powerful AI model that is open source - meaning it is free to access and less expensive to use - DeepSeek has been seen as a disruptive force in the ongoing AI technology race.
While the DHS notice did not detail the exact security concerns surrounding DeepSeek, the White House has this year criticised AI firms from China.
The DHS, DeepSeek, and the Chinese embassy in Washington DC have been contacted for comment.
The DHS made the order public on Monday, but the ban took effect from the end of July.
The order is specific to civilian agencies, including the Department of the Treasury, the Department of State and the Department of Justice. However, agencies within the Department of Defense are excluded.
The ban follows criticism of Chinese AI from the Trump administration, and from American firms.
White House tech lead Michael Kratsios wrote earlier this year in an internal memo that "malicious exploitation" of American AI firms had been occurring, mainly by rival firms in China.
Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which are poised to list on the public stock market in the coming months, have also claimed to have had their AI models essentially copied by some Chinese AI firms, including DeepSeek.
US president Donald Trump has made clear that he sees China as the key US rival when it comes to development of AI, something he sees as crucial to the future of the country.
DeepSeek has grown in popularity since its initial public release in 2025, with models being in such demand that the company's servers have gone down at times.
While DeepSeek's free chatbot app is one of the most downloaded apps in the Apple App Store rankings, its AI models are also used by US tech companies. Companies like Snowflake, Vercel and OpenRouter all incorporate DeepSeek in their offerings to customers.
Startups have flocked to open source models like DeepSeek.
For a technology or AI developer, using DeepSeek in their work costs a fraction of what a closed model like Google's Google's Gemini, Anthropic's Claude or OpenAI's Codex would.
Similarly, the expense borne by DeepSeek to develop its models has been astronomically less than what it has cost US AI firms to develop their own.
Last year, DeepSeek said it took about $6m (Â£4.5m) to train the debut version of its model, while the costs associated with OpenAI's GPT-4 were roughly $100m. Such revelations sent tech stocks tumbling.
The most recent version of DeepSeek was released last week. Users of the model have praised it online, saying it beats even the most advanced AI tools out of OpenAI on common tasks for AI tools like computer software coding.

88e595b18aee.text: By — Steven Sloan, Associated Press Steven Sloan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/iowa-is-testing-whether-democrats-can-win-rural-voters Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Iowa is testing whether Democrats can win rural voters Politics Oct 19, 2026 2:12 PM EDT NEW HAMPTON, Iowa (AP) — Standing in the doorway of his home near the corn and soybean fields that blanket this stretch of northeast Iowa, Dave Roethler doesn't know what happened to the Donald Trump he supported during his first presidency. Trump did a "heck of a good job" back then, the 70-year-old school custodian said. But now Roethler laments an economy in which "it's the middle-class families that are taking the big hit" while Trump is "going to come out way ahead." He scoffs at the Republican president's effort to win accolades such as the Nobel Peace Prize or a spot on Mount Rushmore. "I think he has delusions of grandeur," said Roethler, who plans to support Democrats next month in a state that has become a midterm battleground after Trump carried it by 13 percentage points two years ago. The president will return to Iowa twice before the election to rally supporters. Democrats face a steep challenge in winning rural communities like this one in Chickasaw County, a onetime party stronghold that swung sharply to the right in the Trump era as a broader realignment swept through much of the agricultural Midwest. But by simply narrowing their losses with appeals to voters such as Roethler, Democrats hope to become newly competitive from Iowa and Kansas to Nebraska and Ohio. Josh Turek, the Democrat running for a U.S. Senate seat in Iowa, said his party has "looked at this math problem incorrectly." "You've got to go out there in these rural counties and trim the margins," he said in an interview. Competitive races in states that usually aren't Republicans know they are on defense in these states. Trump recently held a rally in Nebraska to boost U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts and will do the same for U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas on Monday. Republicans are pumping money into both states before the Nov. 3 election. Few places represent the party's challenge like Iowa, where Democrats are mounting spirited campaigns for governor, U.S. Senate and several U.S. House seats, including the 2nd Congressional District, which encompasses much of the state's northeast and was considered reliably Republican until recently. With tariffs disrupting the agricultural economy and the war in Iran driving up gas prices — diesel surpasses $6 a gallon in Iowa — U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., swung through the district to ask voters to keep his fragile majority in place. WATCH: As cancer rates fall nationally, Iowa sees a troubling rise in diagnoses "This state is so important to us," Johnson said in Cedar Falls. The Republican erosion was evident about 45 miles north in New Hampton. A few houses away from Roethler, 69-year-old Bill Stonecypher voted for Trump in 2016, expecting him to apply his business acumen to governing. Now Stonecypher plans to vote for every Democrat on the ballot for the first time in his life. "I just know it's a mess and it's going to take years to fix," he said. Another neighbor, 70-year-old Deb Thorne backed Trump in 2024 but said he hasn't followed through on his pledge to lower costs. "He lied to us," she said. "I'm looking more at Democrats for everything." How a candidate for governor is reaching beyond the party base Democrats in Iowa are buoyed by Rob Sand, the state auditor whose campaign for governor is built on explicit overtures to independents and disaffected Republicans. A few dozen people gathered recently in an American Legion hall in St. Ansgar, a square-mile town near the Minnesota border. Sand opened by describing a "pretty standard upbringing" centered on hunting, fishing and church. He distanced himself from the fighting over cultural issues that has bogged down the national party. A few heads in the room nodded as he spoke of opposition to transgender girls playing on female sports teams. "All that stuff was stuff that nobody was talking about back when we were in high school," said Sand, whose opponent is Republican Zach Lahn, a political newcomer. The only reason he was a Democrat at all, Sand said, was that he had to pick a party to participate in primaries and he thought Democrats were stronger on issues like clean water and protecting public land. Jim Wherry, a Republican member of the Mitchell County Board of Supervisors, attended the event and said Sand "has a pretty good chance." "My big thing is sometimes things get focused on urban areas," he said. "So I like that he's actually incorporating rural Iowa." Sand, who has won two statewide elections as state auditor, said he's received support from voters who also backed Trump. "One of the things that people who vote for both of us find in common is that we say what we think and we're dissatisfied with the political system," he said. Democrats are boosting rural investments Democrats are stepping up their rural investments. The Democratic Governors Association has directed $10 million each to campaigns in Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Wisconsin and could spend elsewhere ahead of the election. "What I see is a map that has grown and grown and grown and that is good for Democrats," Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who leads the DGA, said in an interview. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which is focused on retaking the House, launched a rural engagement program for the first time this election cycle, including polling, paid media and staff. The group has made a six-figure investment in television advertising in Iowa's 2nd Congressional District alone. Democratic candidate Lindsay James, a chaplain who often speaks of her faith to connect with voters, could see a boost because the district includes Sand's hometown of Decorah. ad1512785fcf.text: By — Rob Gillies, Associated Press Rob Gillies, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/carney-fights-to-keep-canada-united-as-albertans-consider-path-to-independence Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Carney fights to keep Canada united as Albertans consider path to independence World Oct 19, 2026 2:01 PM EDT EDMONTON, Alberta (AP) — Voters in Canada's oil-rich Alberta province were deciding on Monday whether to begin a process that could lead to independence, testing national unity as Canadians rally against U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war and threats to claim Canada as the 51st U.S. state. Monday's vote is not a direct referendum on independence. Alberta, home to most of Canada's proven oil reserves — the fourth largest in the world — will decide whether to remain a province or begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation. More than 1.35 million Albertans, or 43% of eligible voters, cast advance or special ballots ahead of Monday's referendum, an unusually high level of early participation that underscores the intense interest in the province's future. Polls close at 8 p.m. local time, with results expected in the hours afterward. Alberta is Canada's oil heartland and cowboy country, a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment toward Ottawa runs deep, but has not traditionally translated into widespread support for independence. But even if Albertans reject the proposal, separatist leaders say the movement has transformed a fringe cause into a force in provincial politics and is not going away. Prime Minister Mark Carney urged Albertans to deliver a decisive vote for unity. "Vote like Canada's future depends on it because it does," he told a rally Friday in Edmonton, where he grew up. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who called the referendum despite opposing independence, cited a poll showing just 22% support for separation, a figure she said was still too high. The vote also comes as Alberta reels from a grass fire that suddenly shifted into a military training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, killing four service members and injuring 39, including 19 critically. Crowds erupt when Carney talks about the US The biggest cheers at Carney's rallies in Calgary and Edmonton came when he spoke about diversifying Canada's trade away from the United States. The applause showed how Trump's trade war and annexation threats have fueled Canadian nationalism even in traditionally conservative Alberta. Liberal prime ministers have long faced resentment from Albertans over federal energy policies, but Carney has emerged as an unusually popular figure by backing policies more friendly to fossil fuels, such as a proposed oil pipeline to the Pacific Coast. READ MORE: How Alberta separatism went from fringe cause to referendum Joining Smith in a show of unity against independence, Carney warned that the referendum comes at the "worst possible time" and urged Albertans not to use their votes merely to send Ottawa a message. Smith, who frequently clashed with Justin Trudeau, praised Carney for improving relations. "I think what we can agree on is that we have had some real change in the last 18 months," she said Friday. Smith opposes separation By calling a referendum she opposes, Smith acknowledged pressure from separatist activists within her governing United Conservative Party who helped bring her to power. Some of those activists helped oust former Premier Jason Kenney in 2022. Kenney said separatism had traditionally been a fringe cause, with independence parties typically attracting only 1% or 2% of the vote. He said the pandemic mobilized activists angry over public health restrictions and government authority. Separatist leader Jeff Rath said federal COVID-19 vaccine mandates drove him toward independence, while Tanya Clemens, co-chair of Let Alberta Decide, said pandemic restrictions spurred political organizing. Keith Wilson, the group's other co-chair, was a lead lawyer for the 2022 trucker convoy that paralyzed downtown Ottawa for weeks in a protest against vaccine mandates and other COVID-19 restrictions. Alberta's longstanding grievances with Ottawa Wilson argues that Alberta's grievances go deeper. With much of Canada's population concentrated in Ontario and Quebec, he said Liberal governments can win elections without significant support in Alberta, leaving the province vulnerable to federal policies opposed by its energy industry. Wilson argues that Carney's proposed Pacific Link pipeline illustrates the dysfunction, saying federal restrictions have discouraged private investment and could leave taxpayers financing the project. At the same time, Wilson rejects Alberta becoming an American state. "I have no interest in substituting a master that rules over my children's future, who's in Ottawa, with a new one who's in Washington," he said. Other separatist leaders have sought contact with the Trump administration. Rath and fellow independence advocates met three times with U.S. State Department officials in Washington to discuss Alberta's future. Chief Sheldon Sunshine of Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation condemned those meetings, calling them "absolutely treasonous to the people of Canada, people of Alberta." Sunshine said Alberta cannot leave Canada without First Nations' consent, citing treaties that predate the province — and said his nation would remain part of Canada even if Albertans vote for independence. Separatists see success even without victory No matter the outcome, the referendum campaign has generated unprecedented discussion about Alberta's place in Canada, Wilson said. "I think we've already hit success when you look at the voter turnout," he said. "People are engaged and people are talking about this topic at a level that's unprecedented historically." ff97606f4ef5.text: By — Dánica Coto, Associated Press Dánica Coto, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/haitian-gangs-target-foreign-troops-in-biggest-attack-since-force-began-operations Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Haitian gangs target foreign troops in biggest attack since force began operations World Oct 19, 2026 1:45 PM EDT SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico (AP) — Gangs in Haiti opened fire on an armored vehicle over the weekend, leaving four soldiers from El Salvador unaccounted for in the first major attack since an international gang suppression force began operations in the violence-wracked Caribbean country. The attack occurred Sunday in Croix-des-Bouquets, a once-peaceful community in Haiti's capital, Port-au-Prince, that is now controlled by violent gangs. The armed forces of El Salvador said in a statement Monday that the four aviation technicians were returning to camp when their armored vehicle was attacked with explosives and set on fire. The military noted that the four men managed to flee the burning vehicle and it is working with international forces to "establish contact and determine the location of our military personnel." Salvadoran authorities said that helicopters were dispatched to the area but they, too, came under fire as they dispersed armed men in the area. "Multiple attempts to approach by land and air have been made, but these have been hampered by the intensity of the fighting," the Salvadoran military said. The weapons and ammunition gangs are using are not made in Haiti and will continue to find ways to enter the country, Wien-Weibert Arthus, Haiti's deputy permanent representative to the U.N., told the U.N. Security Council Monday. "This latest episode is a reminder, as if we really needed one, of the fact that the security challenges in Haiti are complex and complicated," he said. "We hope that those who are missing will be able to go back to their families unscathed." Gang violence has displaced nearly 1.5 million people, a record, across Haiti in recent years, with more than 5,700 people killed or injured from January to mid-September, and more than 230 others kidnapped, according to the U.N. A warning from the U.S. Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the U.N., condemned the attack during the U.N. Security Council meeting on Haiti. "We believe the four men survived, but they do remain unaccounted for," he said. "We will bring you home." Waltz said that gangs attacked the armored vehicle with "hundreds of bullets and explosives." "To the gangs and gang leaders who carried out this cowardly attack, if you think you're going to intimidate this coalition into retreat, you have made a terrible mistake," he said. The gang suppression force said in a statement that it's assessing the situation and has advised residents where the attack occurred to remain indoors. READ MORE: Hundreds attend funeral in Haiti for 4 victims of brutal gang attack that killed 47 "Gangs are testing the gang suppression force," Jack Christofides, the force's special representative, said at the U.N. Monday as he noted that attacks against the force have recently increased. He warned that gangs have carried out reprisal killings in some areas following operations by Haitian and international forces, and that they have pushed deeper into places including the community of Kenscoff and the Artibonite region. "The reality is that we cannot be everywhere at once," Christofides said. Haiti prepares for an election despite violence The area where the armored vehicle was targeted is controlled by gangs including Chèn Méchan; Kraze Barye, led by Vitelhomme Innocent; and 400 Mawozo, led by Lanmo Sanjou. Both gang leaders have been sanctioned by the U.N. and the U.S. Romain Le Cour, head of the Haiti Observatory at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, said that while some gangs have been under pressure since the suppression force was deployed, "others want to show that they can strike back." "If these soldiers are indeed being held, the groups gain (an) edge to negotiate and to pressure the security forces," he said. In September 2025, the U.N. Security Council authorized the 5,550-member force to replace a former Kenya-led multinational force that struggled with a lack of funds and resources as it tried to help Haiti's National Police quell gang violence. The gang suppression force has more than 2,000 troops on the ground in Haiti, including soldiers from Chad, Jamaica and Guatemala. "The force is making a difference with what it has," Christofides said, adding that authorities have started to see early signs of reduced gang influence and control in certain areas. No one has claimed responsibility for the attack on the Salvadoran troops. It comes as Haiti prepares for its first general election in more than a decade and showcases the power of the gangs that control an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince. Carlos Ruiz Massieu, the U.N. special envoy to Haiti, said at Monday's meeting that electoral preparations "have reached an unprecedented level of progress." He said that more than 35 parties and political groups have registered, along with 3,500 candidates. Among them is former Haitian President Michel Martelly, who was sanctioned in November 2022 by Canada and in August 2024 by the U.S., which accused him of facilitating drug trafficking and sponsoring multiple gangs. 8113b3ad5a88.text: By — Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/justice-department-charges-more-than-2-dozen-foreign-nationals-in-california-sweep-targeting-noncitizen-voters Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Justice Department charges more than 2 dozen foreign nationals in California sweep targeting noncitizen voters Politics Oct 19, 2026 12:53 PM EDT LOS ANGELES (AP) — Federal authorities have arrested more than two dozen foreign nationals Monday in California, who authorities said have illegally registered and voted in U.S. elections. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The statewide sweep is part of a Trump administration effort to root out noncitizen voting ahead of next month's midterm elections, even though data shows that the problem is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races. The arrests also reflect a further escalation in a simmering voter roll fight between the federal government and California that came into focus last week when the Justice Department sued the state and later warned that local election workers who knowingly process or tabulate ballots submitted by noncitizen voters are at risk of investigation and potential prosecution. The Justice Department said all of those arrested as part of a sweep dubbed Operation Protect the Vote are lawful permanent residents — but not U.S. citizens who are permitted to legally vote. They are charged with crimes including making false statements on a naturalization application and submitting fraudulent voter registrations. California emerges as a flashpoint for voting dispute The federal government has made noncitizen voting a priority this year, demanding detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states. Before Monday, the Justice Department had charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election. A flurry of activity has unfolded in heavily Democratic California, which is not typically regarded as a key battleground state but does have a handful of competitive congressional races that could help determine which party controls the U.S. House for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term. Over 23 million people are registered statewide. READ MORE: DOJ says California officials who process ballots from suspected noncitizens risk prosecution The administration last week sued California to prevent it from counting mail ballots from people the federal government has identified as "likely" noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed. The complaint was filed after California officials were given, and did not meet, a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contained a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters. A warning for poll workers On Friday, the Justice Department followed up with a letter warning that state election officials who knowingly process ballots cast by noncitizen voters are at risk of investigation. "The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring a federal crime are significant. Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful," warns the letter from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general at the Justice Department. It adds: "If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime." The letter is addressed to the Los Angeles County Counsel's office and also is copied to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan, effectively putting the entire state on notice. In response to the letter, Logan said his office is focused on conducting a fair and secure election while noting that Election Day is a mere 18 days away. "The U.S. Department of Justice has chosen to litigate their unverified assertions of voting eligibility. At this point, it is best for this to be addressed in court," he said. CNN's chief international anchor, Christiane Amanpour, has announced she will leave the organisation next year after more than four decades.
"After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!" Amanpour said in a statement., external
The 68-year-old said she "looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral".
CNN chairman Mark Thompson described her as "one of the most trusted and beloved journalists anywhere" and said the network will take time to celebrate her "before she departs next year".
Amanpour began working for CNN in 1983 as an assistant on the international news desk, and went on to become one of the network's best-known correspondents, often reporting on conflicts and wars.
She has presented her own nightly interview program on CNN International since 2009.
In a memo to staff on Monday, Thompson wrote: "Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months.
"Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I'm very sorry to see her go, but I've come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.
"In the meantime, on behalf of the entire CNN leadership team, I want to thank Christiane for 43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship," he added.
In her own statement, Amanpour said she wanted to thank "all the amazingly talented people I've worked with throughout this incredible journey. Especially my beloved show teams and field crews."
Amanpour reflected on her "very first big exciting assignment covering the First Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between".
"It's the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much," she continued, "as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favour."

As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory feeling: that attacks like that could not happen here, and that it was only a matter of time until they did.
Australians will tell you this is a largely peaceful society with a comparatively civil public discourse. Violence targeting politicians has been rare, the bungled assassination of Labor leader Arthur Calwell in 1966 now a distant and fleeting memory.
But MPs and public figures â backed by experts â have been warning of a volcano of threats against them as social cohesion cracks, polarisation intensifies and the tone of debate grows hotter.
And on Monday, their worst fears appear to have been realised.
Independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car and severely injured outside her office in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta.
Police say a 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene, and a knife seized, but they have not said Haines was hit deliberately.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, however, swiftly described the incident as an apparent attack.
He was briefed by federal police â whose counter terror squad is helping state officers investigate â and told the national broadcaster: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."
Though he stressed no motive had been confirmed, Albanese earlier got emotional as he talked about the growing fear amongst MPs that they would end up targets.
Earlier this year Albanese himself was evacuated from his official residence over a bomb threat. As of August, about 20 cases in which people were accused of making violent threats against him were winding their way through courts around the country.
In recent years, politicians here have been mailed bullets. Female MPs â and in some cases their children â have been threatened with sexual violence. A Jewish MP's office has been firebombed, a Sydney mayor's car has been torched and countless other politicians have had their workplaces vandalised.
Just last week Small Business Minister Anne Aly said she had received a wave of death threats after a politician from the opposition said she should be "shamed and stoned in the square" over a tax policy.
According to government statistics, there were 1,067 reports of "harassing and threatening behaviour" against "high office holders" in the year to June: an increase on last year.
"We tend to bury our head in the sand and say, 'Not here', but this has been happening now for well over a decade," Josh Roose, a Deakin University Professor on violent extremism, tells the BBC.
Socioeconomic strain, growing mental health problems in the community, "grifters" who benefit politically or financially from whipping up further discontent, and a "carcinogenic" online environment are drivers of the trend, he says, which has dramatically escalated since the pandemic.
But the political class must also take responsibility for their role, he adds.
"We've seen a willingness to cross previously sacred terrain - you know, not targeting individuals, not targeting their families - but we now see that this is part and parcel of Australian political life.
"This is occurring at both ends of the political spectrum."
And experts like him warn it is not just politicians who are vulnerable: it is members of the media, academics, court officials and other public figures too.
Mike Burgess, the head of Australia's spy agency, has warned for years that the spectre of political violence is looming in Australia.
"Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack," he said in his annual threat assessment for 2026.
And the Federal Police have said it is not just ideology motivating cases in recent times. "Grievance" is radicalising people.
"They're feeling distanced, they're feeling alone, they're looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose," Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC earlier this month.
There have been frustrated rumblings in Canberra from some MPs who say security arrangements have not changed with the climate and â if a political motivation for this incident is confirmed â one of the greatest tenets of the nation's political culture could now be at risk.
It is not abnormal for you to run into your local member at the shops, or chat to them at the footy, and many open up their offices for constituents who want to raise concerns or share ideas.
Haines is particularly renowned and respected for that, Albanese said on Monday night.
"Here in Australia, it is a good thing that politicians are able to go about their community and engage with people," he said.
"I don't want to see a political system in which you can't have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the street, at street meetings, public forums â that's an important part of our democracy."

A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing, external in California.
US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the AI firm, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and say a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest.
It was argued the 35-year-old engineer therefore posed a flight risk and should be detained, pending trial.
The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.
Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder.
The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.
A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted.
He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated.
The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed.
It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son.
Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same.
On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official.
"Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued.
The FBI investigation is ongoing.
Alfozan is scheduled to âappear â in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (Â£188,000) fine.

More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local authorities say.
A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city, which was being used as a training centre for recruits to the security forces and police.
The head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, condemned what he called the "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response".
The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations".
Yemen's devastating civil war has flared up in recent months.
At the start of October, pro-government forces launched a major offensive that aims to retake territory in western Yemen that is controlled by the Houthis.
With air support from a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states, they managed to regain control of territory on the Red Sea coast that overlooks the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, which the Houthis captured in a surprise assault in September.
However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib and al-Jawf provinces.
The Houthis have also responded to the Saudi air strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
Monday's attack in Shabwa is one of the deadliest reported since the start of the escalation.
Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces. According to a preliminary assessment, 53 were killed and more than 200 injured, it added.
A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground.
Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based. Some of them were in a critical condition, he said.
Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target.
He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes".
The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.
In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children.
According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks.
The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August.
In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donald Trump.
"The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president," the former US president wrote on X, calling the probe "so appalling".
The White House defended the inquiry, saying the justice department was "focused on restoring law and order".
Last week, homeland security agents searched the Minnesota Democrat's Washington DC home as part of an investigation into her immigration status. Born in Somalia, Omar moved to the US with her family as a child.
US media outlets have reported that the probe is tied to her American citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995.
Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date.
Obama said in his X post on Sunday that her father became a naturalised citizen when she was 17, and not yet legally an adult, which then gave her citizenship.
"Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen," he wrote.
"If this becomes the new normal," he added, "there's no reason to believe it will stop with her - or that future presidents, in either party, won't do the same."
According to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services, a child born outside of the US automatically becomes a citizen when he or she has at least one parent who is a citizen by birth or naturalisation, or he or she is under the age of 18, and is a lawful permanent resident living in the custody of a citizen parent.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis denied the investigation was politically motivated.
"Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes," she said in an emailed statement to the BBC.
"The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe."
Trump has often argued that federal criminal investigations against him as he campaigned for re-election were politically motivated.
The investigation into Omar could lead to the justice department seeking to "denaturalise" her, or revoke her citizenship. It would have to prove there were material lies in the naturalisation process.
In 2023, Republicans removed Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee for comments and tweets she made about Israel, which drew bipartisan criticism.
Omar has said that Trump has targeted her for years with "baseless lies and smear campaigns" and called the investigation "the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation".
But Trump has said the investigation had "nothing to do" with him, while describing Omar as a "terrible person" and a "complainer".
Federal agents reportedly seized her phone, computers, notebooks and passport in the raid a week ago.
Her lawyers have demanded the government return her belongings, CBS News, the BBC's US partner, has reported, arguing in a letter sent on Friday that the seizure of property had violated restrictions put in place by a judge to protect her work as a federal lawmaker.
The lawyers also alleged agents did not duly notify Omar or the House of Representatives general counsel that a search would be taking place and kept her from contacting her attorney for more than an hour, according to CBS.
Democrats characterised the raid as the president attempting to interfere with the legislative branch of government. Republicans, meanwhile, have said Omar should be treated the same as anyone else under the law.
When Obama first ran for president, and throughout his two terms in the White House, Trump repeatedly raised questions about his citizenship, asserting he was not born on American soil and was disqualified from serving in office. Obama released two records proving he had been born in Hawaii.
Obama did not mention that history in his X post on Sunday.

Curraghs Wildlife Park has experienced its busiest October weekend ever after the birth of eight capybara pups, which staff say have "delighted" people and boosted conservation funding.
The pups were born to two females within days of each other, on 26 September and 1 October.
Their arrival has sparked huge public interest, with the park's manager Kathleen Graham saying the reaction to this "overload of cuteness" had been extraordinary.
"The car park was full, it was like a bank holiday. Everybody coming to see the capybara babies," she said.
The arrival marks a milestone for the park, which last welcomed a single capybara pup four years ago.
Graham said the scale of this year's births has been "a super overload of cuteness really."
The animals, native to South America, are the world's largest rodent, and thrive in wet marshland environments.
Graham said the pups' appearance on social media immediately drew far more attention than expected, and the surge translated directly into visitor numbers
"They have been delighting people. Even grown men were like cooing," she laughed.
Although capybaras are not endangered, Graham said they play a vital role in helping visitors understand threatened wetland habitats
The park is part of the European Association of Zoos and Aquaria's Eaza Wetlands for Life campaign and sits on a Ramsarâdesignated wetland.
Graham said the pups helped highlight how wetlands supported both wildlife and people.
"We rely on wetlands to soak up excess rainwater. And they're management systems, really. So they need looking after and protecting," she said.
'A lot of joy'
The pups' popularity also directly supported conservation work, she explained, as each visitor contributed Â£1 to the park's conservation fund unless they opted out.
"Although themselves [capybaras] may not be endangered, they've actually created a lot of extra money this weekend for the conservation fund and spread a lot of joy and oohs and aahs," she said.
The fund supports projects locally with Manx Wildlife Trust and internationally, including work in the Pantanal, where wild capybaras live.
She said the pups arrival had lifted spirits at a time when many people were seeking moments of joy.
"I think when there's so many just awful things that happen in the world, sometimes these little things just give us a bit of light relief, don't they?," she added.

Please check your inbox to confirm. "Look at this beautiful guy," Trump said at a Saturday rally in Kentucky, referring to U.S. House candidate Ed Gallrein, a former U.S. Navy SEAL with an angular face who stood nearby the stage. "Central casting." That's a common refrain from Trump, who owned the Miss Universe beauty pageant and grew his clout on the reality television show "The Apprentice" before entering politics. Aesthetics have long been part of the president's measuring stick, either as a source of praise or target for ridicule. Now, Trump is deploying his handsomeness appraisals as he boosts Republican candidates in a midterm election which already includes debates over which candidates are more masculine. The outcome will determine whether Republicans keep control of Congress or Trump faces emboldened Democratic opposition in Washington. 9f90235753e9.text: The Supreme Court on Monday agreed to hear a challenge to the Reconstruction-era ban on distilling alcohol in private homes. Why it matters: Americans can legally brew beer or make wine at home, but making whiskey, vodka or other spirits can land them in federal prison. The Supreme Court could change that. Driving the booze: SCOTUS will review Department of Justice v. McNutt, an April ruling by the conservative 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that found the nearly 160-year-old home-distilling ban unconstitutional and an overreach of Congress' taxing power. Distilling in your home carries a penalty of up to five years in prison, a $10,000 fine or both. The 6th Circuit reached the opposite conclusion in a separate April ruling for Ream v. Department of the Treasury, arguing Congress can restrict distilling at home to protect federal alcohol tax collections. What they're saying: Advocates argue that Congress overstepped their powers by banning distilling in the home through a measure meant to prohibit fraud from commercial distillers, per the Associated Press . The government says Congress acted within its authority as the restriction was intended to stop producers from evading federal excise taxes, per AP. Lifting the ban, the government argues, could undermine Congress' authority to enforce federal tax laws. Friction point: Both appeals courts agreed Congress' taxing power alone doesn't authorize the ban. They split over whether it is a permissible way to collect liquor taxes under the Constitution's Necessary and Proper Clause. Reality check: You didn't hear this from us, but the practice of distilling hooch and moonshine still happens in the U.S. despite the federal prohibition . Some states, like West Virginia, allow some home distilling. But, much like marijuana, those state laws don't override federal law. Advocates hope the Supreme Court will strike down the federal ban and its associated criminal penalty. Why distilling drinks at home is banned Flashback: Congress banned distilling spirits in homes and connected properties in 1868, during the Reconstruction, as part of a crackdown on widespread tax evasion. The restrictions also cover certain premises where beer or wine is made. Yes, but: Federal law allows Americans to brew beer and make wine at home, but not distill spirits. Distilling spirits requires a process that gives people a more concentrated drink and can involve fire hazards and dangerous contamination risks. What happens if SCOTUS overturns the ban? What's next: Even if SCOTUS strikes down the ban, this doesn't mean people can start distilling automatically. Federal alcohol-production rules could limit what people could do at home. The government currently requires permits, registration and tax compliance for the production of distilled spirits. States could also impose their own bans, which would limit what people can make in their homes. The bottom line: SCOTUS could make it easier for Americans to produce their own liquor, but overturning the ban wouldn't necessarily mean anyone could legally set up a still in their backyard … yet.

President Donald Trump is expected to speak at a rally at 7 p.m. EDT. Watch live in our video player above. But this harvest season, they're doing it with diesel prices more than $2.50 per gallon higher than a year ago, adding to financial pressures from rising costs, unpredictable markets and shrinking profits. "I don't think it necessarily does that," Brunkow said. "But I think it dampens the enthusiasm for agriculture producers to get to the polls." "I am tired of being persuaded by charges that the boogeyman is going to get us," he said. "I am so fed up with the Republican Party and their willingness to play sycophant to our current commander in chief that I'm willing to consider alternatives." WATCH: Farmers warn of food price spike as war drives up fuel and fertilizer costs Debbie Geneva, 61, of Nortonville, Kansas, said she was impressed by Hamilton after he visited a local market to meet people, something she hasn't seen Marshall do. She's never voted for a Democrat, she said, but remains undecided about the Senate race. "I've never voted for a Democrat in my entire life, so that's a little scary for me to be undecided," said Geneva. "I told one of my friends that, and they can't believe it, but that's just the way I feel right now." Geneva said rising costs for healthcare and everyday expenses have added to her frustrations. "And then of course the trade agreements," she added. "The Republicans haven't done the Midwest any favors with that." Farmers face a financial squeeze Farmers have spent months feeling the squeeze as costs for inputs like diesel, fertilizer and seed have soared due to refinery constraints and supply disruptions tied to the Iran war. Diesel averaged $6.30 per gallon nationwide on Friday, more than 70% higher than a year ago, according to motor club AAA. The surge has been especially painful during harvest season, when farmers depend heavily on fuel to operate machinery and transport crops. READ MORE: 3 things to know about rising diesel prices and how they affect you "This is a time of year when we use a lot of fuel, and there just isn't much we can do," Brunkow said. "The margins are tight, and anything that cuts into that margin really hurts." The U.S. Department of Agriculture projects that net farm income will decline by 2.6% this year as production expenses rise by 4.5%. Local curfews may come into force in French towns following a weekend of disorder.
Most of the protesters were peaceful in expressing their opposition to rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
But others - dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas - set fire to cars, shops and buildings.
The scale of the destruction - including to some iconic landmarks - has shocked many in a country used to street protests.
The damage in the capital city is extensive. Shop fronts have been broken and stores looted.
The iconic Place de la Republique was vandalised, too.
A yellow vest - representative of the movement which helped co-ordinate the weekend protests - was draped around the body of the Statue of the Republic, erected in 1883.
Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, took over parts of the capital and wreaked havoc.
Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people but police struggled to contain smaller groups of people roving around the city attack businesses.
The full extent of the damage did not become clear until dawn broke on Sunday.
Further south in Marseille, protesters broke into the city hall by using a metal fence as a battering ram.
A bust of Marianne - symbol of the French Republic - was damaged and knocked to the floor in Marseille as people ransacked the building.
City Mayor BenoÃ®t Payan was furious with the "almost total lack of control" by the security forces.
"The world's sixth largest power does not deserve this. The world is watching us, this morning we are the shame of Europe," he said.
In the city of Lyon, Mayor GrÃ©gory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office, housed in a 19th Century building, was "a tragedy".
Fire crews also battled a fire at Limoges town hall, which caused part of the building to collapse. Local officials said the town hall was "largely lost".
"A wild horde" had "deliberately" set fire to the 143-year-old building, said Maurice Barate, the prefect for the Haute-Vienne department.
French authorities have admitted they lost control of cities to the protesters.
Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez offered his resignation - which has been rejected.
Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu has given local mayors the power to introduce partial curfews in some parts of the country, which he says is designed to protect people and businesses.
But the French are holding their breath - in anticipation of another chapter in this protest next Saturday.

The News
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said Monday that he would distribute to every American child a share in the AI-and-space-exploration company, a gift that, if realized, would dwarf a similar $6.25 billion gift from Michael Dell.
The gift could be worth roughly $10.8 billion, based on SpaceXâs current share price and the U.S. Censusâ estimate of under-18s living in the US. It would work out to roughly 1% of Muskâs current SpaceX holdings. Musk and the Trump administration originally discussed the share donations this summer when Trump accounts were first launched, Semafor scooped.
Musk made the announcement Monday in response to a social media post from Anthropic, which said it would commit 5% of its listed equities to a âpublic benefit fund.â President Donald Trump later tweeted a thank you to Musk: âThis is exactly what was envisioned when we created Trump Accounts.â
Musk and a Treasury spokesperson did not return a request for comment.
Rohanâs view
The pledge raises some questions about what kind of voting rights the shares would have; SpaceX is a dual-class stock and Musk enjoys supermajority control of the company. Recent regulatory changes allow individual equities to be held in Trump Accounts, the childhood savings program that has been a flagship initiative of this administration.
Musk has also not been a big philanthropist, relative to his wealth, and has argued before that the best way he can do good for humanity is by building great companies. Look at this through a strategic, rather than a philanthropic lens, however, and it makes a lot more sense.
Muskâs planned donation could generate goodwill from a skeptical public around him, his companies and his goals â space exploration, self-driving cars and AI, among others. If other businesses chose to do something similar, they could also benefit from a public-relations boost, or possibly amass a friendly shareholder block that helps protect against others that might disagree with their strategic direction.

US church on frontline of battle against drug known as 'tranq'
America has been fighting the War on Drugs for decades, but the drug cartels, the suppliers and the dealers appear to be always one step ahead of the authorities.
President Trump has declared the cartels, "terrorists" and labelled fentanyl, the powerful synthetic opioid, a "weapon of mass destruction".
But the drug supply is changing, with other deadly synthetics being added to the mix, including strong animal tranquillisers, known on the streets as "tranq".
While overdose deaths are falling, the potency of the new drugs has recovery workers worried. For some the answer might lie in reducing demand, giving users support and helping them end their addiction.
BBC international correspondent Quentin Sommerville and camera journalist Darren Conway travelled to Columbus, Ohio to find out more.
Read more on this story: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis.

The Islamic saying "a people who entrust their affairs to a woman will never succeed" has resurfaced in Morocco since King Mohammed VI named Fatima Zahra El Mansouri as the country's first female prime minister.
Mustafa Ramid, a former justice minister in an Islamist-led government, cited the saying earlier this month, in a lengthy Facebook post questioning whether a woman should hold the country's highest political office.
He argued that Morocco, a Muslim majority country, had found a balance between equality and the responsibilities of state leadership, as the highest office - that of the king - continued to be reserved for men.
Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy. Yet executive power remains in the hands of the 63-year-old monarch.
El Mansouri's Authenticity and Modernity Party (Pam) won the most seats in September's parliamentary election and has since announced a coalition with three other parties. Together, they hold 207 of the 395 seats in parliament.
El Mansouri's royal appointment was historic but it exposed persistent reservations about women in positions of power.
The day after her appointment, local broadcaster Chouf TV took to the streets to ask Moroccan men "what they thought" of a woman heading the government.
Several men, mostly middle-aged or older, hesitated before answering. Some said they accepted the decision because it was the king's choice.
One grey-haired man, who did not give his name or age, said: "It feels strange to have a woman as head of government. I'm not sure if it sits well with me."
Criticism of the monarchy carries legal risks in Morocco. The penal code criminalises certain forms of offence or insult against the king, the royal family and the monarchy.
Online, the appointment became fodder for political satire.
A video showing two women pulling each other's hair was widely shared, with captions suggesting that this is what parliamentary disagreements between El Mansouri and her colleagues might look like.
However many younger Moroccans, especially women, welcomed her appointment.
While attitudes are changing in Morocco, conservative, religious views still hold great weight.
Some of the country's most contentious debates over gender equality centre on family law, including inheritance, marriage and divorce.
Under existing inheritance rules, a daughter typically receives half the share of a son in comparable circumstances.
The Higher Council of Ulemas, the country's body of religious scholars, has resisted calls for equal inheritance, citing Islamic jurisprudence.
It has also rejected proposals to abolish taasib, a rule that can require female orphans without brothers to share their inheritance with male relatives, including distant ones.
In a 2022 report, Morocco's National Human Rights Council said unequal inheritance rules contributed to poverty among women.
Polygamy is also legal under certain conditions. Proposed changes to the family code have included allowing women to stipulate in their marriage contracts that their husbands cannot take another wife.
But exceptions remain, including provisions relating to a first wife's infertility or illness, which women's rights groups have criticised on grounds of privacy and medical confidentiality.
These issues are at the heart of proposals to reform the Moudawana, Morocco's family code, which governs marriage, divorce and child custody.
A package of changes was announced in 2024, but the reforms have yet to become law.
As well as family law, some young women hope the new prime minister will try to improve education for girls.
Morocco's High Commission for Planning, the country's official national statistics agency, found in 2025 that just 55% of girls aged 15â17 were going to school in rural areas, where poverty, early marriage and dropping out of school remain key barriers. In urban areas, it was 100%.
"Many girls in rural Morocco drop out of school early because schools are far away, transport is unsafe or unavailable, and families with limited means often keep their daughters at home," Chifae Laazouzi, a young Moroccan woman, tells the BBC.
She says one reason is that many girls in poor and rural areas cannot afford menstrual sanitary products.
"Menstrual health is still treated as a taboo... I would like to see free menstrual products in schools," Laazouzi says.
El Mansouri is no newcomer to politics. Over more than two decades in public life, she has served as mayor of Marrakech, held government posts and sat in parliament.
For the past five years, she served as minister for national territory planning, urban planning, housing and city policy under the previous Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.
After her appointment, El Mansouri presented the moment as a milestone for Moroccan women.
"Being the first female head of government is not just a source of pride for me, but for all the women of the kingdom," she said.
Since her appointment, she has not indicated whether she plans to try and push through the reforms to the family code.
In her political career so far, she has not made any prominent public statements about women's rights, even while changes to inheritance rules, polygamy and the family code were being widely debated.
Dr Irene Fernandez-Molina, an expert on the Global South at the University of Exeter in the UK, sees the appointment in the context of the monarchy's broader political interests.
"Two headlines have dominated coverage of [September's] parliamentary election in Morocco: a two-decade low turnout and King Mohammed VI's appointment of a woman as prime minister for the first time in this country's history," she tells the BBC.
"The latter cannot be understood without the former."
Official figures put turnout at just 38% of registered voters, while the proportion of all eligible voters who cast a ballot was even lower.

El NiÃ±o has been strengthening for several months now and is already having a significant impact on global weather patterns.
Countries including Indonesia, India and the United States have been experiencing droughts, floods and heatwaves in line with projections about how extreme weather events will be supercharged by the phenomenon.
The World Meteorological Agency says the record-breaking El NiÃ±o will strengthen further and persist until at least 2027.
Here are five ways its impact is already being felt around the world.
Indonesia battles worst wildfire season since 2015
Indonesia, which typically trends drier and hotter in El NiÃ±o years, is battling its worst wildfire season since 2015.
This year, since January, at least 895,657 hectares of land â nearly six times the size of Greater London â have been burned.
This is more than twice the area burned last year without the influence of El NiÃ±o.
The wildfires have led to school closures and an increase in hospital admissions across Indonesia.
Millions of people in Sumatra and Kalimantan have been exposed to toxic haze from the fires and around 175,000 people have suffered from respiratory illness.
More than 40,000 cases â which range from coughs to bronchitis and more serious conditions like pneumonia â involve toddlers.
East Pacific explodes with hurricane activity
In the eastern Pacific, where El NiÃ±o tends to strengthen hurricane activity, it has been a very active season so far.
There have been 22 named storms and 12 hurricanes, including 10 major hurricanes.
This is already above the number that would typically develop in the whole of an average season, with two months left to go until its end.
Here, El NiÃ±o provides the ingredients of higher ocean temperatures and weaker winds high in the atmosphere, making it easier for storms to gain strength.
Hurricane Polo is one such example of this.
The hurricane experienced rapid intensification, producing wind gusts of 180 mph (285 kmh), fueled by the very warm waters produced by El NiÃ±o.
Polo was also one of three hurricanes churning away in the same basin at the same time, along with Odalys and Nolo.
Moreover, it has happened twice now in the space of a month.
Earlier in September, the energy produced by exceptional ocean heat resulted in three simultaneous hurricanes in the central and eastern Pacific: Lowell, Karina and Marie.
Until this year, the last time there had been three Pacific hurricanes at the same time was 2015.
Atlantic hurricane season remains eerily quiet
In contrast, the Atlantic Ocean has remained eerily quiet.
El Nino has a tendency to increase wind shear in the north Atlantic, a factor which tears apart storms and limits formation.
There has only been one hurricane - Isaias - which made landfall in the Florida Panhandle and Alabama.
This was the latest forming hurricane on record in the satellite era (1960s onward).
Before this year, the record was 11 September, set in 2002 and 2013.
In an average season, there would have been 10 named storms, five hurricanes and two major hurricanes by this point.
This year, however, there have only been eight tropical storms: Arthur, Bertha, Cristobal, Dolly, Edouard, Fay, Gonzalo and Hanna.
Reduced monsoon rain threatens agriculture in India
The drier and warmer theme has also taken hold in India, where the essential monsoon rainfall has been 13% below average.
While the Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) would consider this still to be in the 'normal' range, the overall average doesn't reflect the variation in rainfall across India.
While Central India had around its normal expected rainfall, the east and north-east were around 26% drier than average and put into 'exceptional' drought. Southern states of India were 24% drier than average.
Even where rainfall was nearer to average, the rain did not fall continuously as is typical during the monsoon, instead flipping between long dry spells and extreme rainfall.
This adds more stress and vulnerability to agriculture yields.
India is influenced by a number of different weather patterns that can affect the monsoon season and so scientists suggest that El NiÃ±o may not have been the only factor.
Strong typhoons target east China and Japan
Further west in the Pacific, it's also been an active season in eastern China and Japan as storms including Maysak and Dujuan have brought recent widespread floods and landslides.
According to the Japanese Meteorological Agency, there have been 10 tropical cyclones forming in the western Pacific Ocean - the highest number in a season since 1966.
During El NiÃ±o the warmer Pacific brings changes to wind patterns, meaning cyclones tend to form further east, away from Japan and east China.
However, this means there is a bigger distance and more time where storms can feed off the warmer waters, gaining energy to become more intense typhoons before they hit land.
Scientists believe that additional typhoons are likely to develop this year with the potential for further impacts to Japan or east China.
