Ukrainian tennis star Elina Svitolina has announced the end of her marriage with French former tennis player GaÃ«l Monfils, citing the emotional impact of the war in her country.
The 32-year-old, who is ranked number six in the world, wrote in a heartfelt post on Instagram about the effect the conflict and "what the war has done to me inside".
"This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share," she wrote, saying "I need to find my way back to myself". Svitolina said she felt she could not do that within her marriage.
She said her husband Monfils, 40, "listened" and "respected what I need with a strength and grace I will never forget".
"Some battles happen deep inside you, and no amount of love from someone else can win them for you," the four-time Grand Slam semi-finalist wrote.
It was "the hardest thing I have ever had to tell the person I love", Svitolina said.
"Everyone knows how much Ukraine means to me," Svitolina, who grew up in Odesa, said.
Ukraine's Black Sea port city has been heavily bombed by Russia throughout the war.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"What you didn't see were the sleepless nights, the doubts, and the feeling of slowly losing myself."
The tennis power couple married in 2021 and have one child together - a four-year-old daughter called Skai.
Svitolina said her daughter "will always come first", adding "our marriage is ending, but our family is not".
Monfils, a former world number six, was expected to play the final tournament of his career at next month's Paris Masters in an emotional farewell.
However, the two-time Grand Slam semi-finalist's retirement was effectively confirmed last week when he appeared on the International Tennis Integrity Authority's list of retired players.
Once a player removes themselves from anti-doping protocols, they are not eligible to compete in professional tournaments.
Monfils, who won 13 titles on the ATP Tour, is preparing to start a new career in finance after joining a Swiss wealth management firm.

With growing concerns that red squirrels could soon become extinct in England, one Channel Island is a corner of the British Isles where they maintain a stronghold.
Jersey is home to a thriving red squirrel population, thanks to the complete absence of grey squirrels, which carry a virus deadly to their red cousins.
Red squirrels are endangered in the UK, with about 120,000 to 160,000 left in the wild and various projects are aiming to boost those numbers.
There have some strongholds in England, external, particularly islands, and 75% of the British population is in Scotland, external.
However, despite not being native to Jersey, Henry Glynn, an ecologist with the National Trust of Jersey, said they "really are iconic for Jersey".
He said: "When you speak to people who have come over to visit the island from the UK, a lot of them will say that one of the things they want to do whilst here is to see a red squirrel, because they're so rare and so difficult to see in large parts of the UK.
"That is actually really special for them."
Red squirrels are not native to Jersey, having been introduced in 1885.
However, Glynn described them as "naturalised", having become "assimilated into the natural environment" over many years.
The animals have previously featured in Visit Jersey, external tourism campaigns, including one fronted by conservationist Ben Fogle.
The National Trust of Jersey said the island was an "important refuge" for the red squirrel, where they were "fairly widespread, external".
It said the inland valleys and woodlands were the best places to spot them.
The species is legally protected, which means it would be a criminal offence to harm them.
Nina Powell, senior animal carer at the JSPCA [Jersey Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals], said Jersey has a "good population" of squirrels and that "you can see them almost anywhere".
While the primary reason for their success is the lack of grey squirrels, Powell said they also thrived "because people look out for them".
She said: "A lot of people do support them, put out feeders and stuff like that.
"Their habitats are decreasing everywhere... but we do have quite a lot of nature reserves.
"In some places, we've got rope bridges which really help them cross the roads, and our speed limits are quite low, so that helps them as well".
She said the JSPCA had handled 50 red squirrels so far this year, including hand-raising eight babies, called kits (kittens).
She said: "We want to keep all animals as wild as possible, so we try and be as hands-off as possible.
"Some of them don't like us... some of them are quite sweet. They really do vary in personality."
Glynn agreed that their success had come in part because of the efforts of islanders.
He said: "They're really beloved amongst the local community as well. A lot of people put out squirrel feeders or love to see them in the garden.
"We get lots of reports from people who just want to tell us they've seen them because they're so happy to have them around."

"Courage and leadership" are needed to ensure Northern Ireland catches up on tackling climate change.
The new chair of the Climate Change Committee, Nigel Topping, is spending two days on a fact-finding mission to hear the thoughts of people across different sectors.
He said Northern Ireland was a small nation that could be "agile and innovative" in tackling challenges like increasing renewable energy, improving waste management and reducing emissions.
But he warned that a failure to act would mean missing out on innovation opportunities, paying more for energy and damaging the health of children.
The Climate Change Committee is an independent body advising the UK and devolved governments on emissions targets.
Over the course of a two-day visit, Topping is meeting farmers, people from the business sector and politicians.
It is being described as a fact-finding mission, looking at "challenges and opportunities".
He acknowledged that politics in Northern Ireland was "complex" and that "when things flip-flop, it doesn't help", due to the impact on investment decisions and people's choices.
But he said there was "a real sense of collectively wanting to catch up" and avoid anyone being left behind on the road to net zero.
"You've had these lags where there's been no ministers sitting and so there hasn't been policy - there's been civil servants working but no policies," he said.
"It's going to take some real courage and leadership from all sectors of society to make sure that the just transition process is a conversation, that it doesn't just disappear into polarised views in different corners of different rooms."
Northern Ireland was the last part of these islands to adopt climate change legislation, which brought in legally-binding targets for reducing emissions.
Topping said people were experiencing climate change firsthand, with the effects of extreme weather being felt around the UK.
And he added that that would continue, until emissions reached net zero.
"But I see this as a race between our kind of obstinate, greedy selves and our brilliant, innovative selves," he said.
"And all of us have a bit of both of those extremes and we have those as societies, and I think if we can really tap into backing ourselves as innovators, then we can take this as an opportunity.
"The most important thing for me is that we're going to do this and we're going to have to do this because this is a collective chance for humanity.
"So we can either see it as a burden and complain all of our way and be laggards, or we can see it as an opportunity and say, we're resilient, we're adaptive, we're innovative.
When asked what will be the consequences of not taking that "opportunity", he is blunt.
"There's two ways of answering that question. One would be, oh, if Northern Ireland doesn't do anything, it doesn't make much difference to the world," he said.
"The other would be, if Northern Ireland doesn't do anything, it misses out on all the innovation opportunities, because other people take those.
"It continues to poison its children's lungs because it doesn't fix the air quality, and it continues to pay more for energy than it needs to.
"So that's like, dumb, dumb, dumb - why would you do that?
"So don't get stuck in the we're only small, what difference do we make?
"But see it as an opportunity as a small nation to be agile and innovative and derive benefit in all those different areas."

President Donald Trump has been boasting about the performance of the US economy ahead of the midterm congressional elections, claiming he has boosted incomes, reduced inflation and created jobs.
Trump has repeatedly said: "We have the hottest country anywhere in the world."
While the overall US economy is faring better than many expected after Trump launched his sweeping "Liberation Day" tariffs in 2025, there's evidence those import taxes and the impact of the US-Israel war with Iran have pushed up inflation, with the harmful effects felt by most American households.
The US economy is also being helped by an AI investment boom, and could falter if that spending were to dry up.
So how does all this feel for the average American? BBC Verify has looked at whether the evidence supports the president's claims.
1. US economy growing
The overall US economy is growing at a respectable clip by the country's recent historic standards.
The latest data shows US GDP, external - which is how economists measure the size of the US economy - currently expanding at an annualised rate of 2.2%.
And it has increased by around 3.2% overall since the end of 2024, just before Trump took office for his second term.
That is more growth than any other member of the G7 group of leading economies over that period.
The US growth rate has been faster than was forecast by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), external in the immediate wake of Trump's announcement of a swathe of new tariffs on goods coming into the US on 2 April 2025.
It downgraded its forecasts at the time, citing the negative impact of Trump's import duties on investment and consumer spending.
Though it is important to note that Trump eased the tariffs considerably in the months that followed, reducing the impact that had initially been expected on the economy.
The US economy has also been heavily supported in recent years by American technology companies making massive investments in AI, including by constructing data centres around the country.
Spending on building data centres, external (excluding the IT hardware to go in them) by US businesses in August 2026 was $5bn, almost double the monthly rate when Trump returned to office.
2. Inflation picked up
Many American voters wanted to punish Joe Biden in the 2024 presidential election, holding him responsible for the pain caused by a significant spike in prices in the wake of the pandemic.
The current rate of US inflation, external is 3.7%.
That's still well down on the recent peak rate of 9% under Biden in 2022, but higher than the 3% rate that Donald Trump inherited in January 2025.
Economists estimate, external US inflation would have been lower without the new tariffs imposed by Trump since he returned to office.
While the impact of the Iran war on global energy prices, with the significant disruption to oil and fuel supplies from the Middle East, has also helped push up US domestic inflation.
The price of a gallon of diesel in the US, external - a fuel used not only by drivers but also widely in agriculture and industry - hit a record high of $6.52 in September.
The price of some grocery staples , externallike beef and coffee have risen since Trump returned to office, though the price of eggs has fallen.
And some US retailers have warned, external that rising energy prices caused by the Iran war will make producing food more expensive and raise prices at the till.
3. Household income growth held back
Average US household incomes are still rising under Trump.
The median income - after adjusting for inflation - rose 2.6% in 2025 to $87,460, the highest on record, external.
However, the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP) think tank has estimated the combined effects of the following, external on US households:
- Trump's tax cuts
- The expiry of extra government subsidies that had made health insurance cheaper for millions of Americans
- Higher-than-expected price rises during Trump's second term, including those linked to tariffs and the Iran war
ITEP's conclusion is that the middle fifth of households are, on average, around $1,700 worse off in 2026 than they would have been, while the poorest fifth are around $750 worse off.
The richest 1%, by contrast, are estimated to be an average of $12,560 better off than they woud have been, primarily because of Trump's tax cuts.
ITEP's estimates about the impact of tariffs on American households of different income levels are broadly similar to those of the Tax Foundation think tank, external.
4. Job creation slowed down
Trump predicted his tariffs would result in America being "flooded with jobs", external as manufacturing firms set up new factories on US soil to avoid their products being taxed at the border.
Since he returned to the White House, an average of 34,000 jobs have been added to the economy each month.
ââBut that is significantly down on the 122,000 jobs added each month in the final year of Biden's presidency, external.
And the number of Americans employed in manufacturing, external - 12.6 million in September 2026 - is slightly lower than it was when Trump's second term began.
However, the US unemployment rate remains relatively low, external at 4.2%, which is broadly where it was when Trump returned to the White House.
Part of the reason for this is Trump's immigration crackdown and deportation programme, which has reduced the size of the available US workforce, external and means a lower number of jobs need to be created each month to stop unemployment rising.
5. Borrowing costs rising
US government borrowing has increased in Trump's second term, partly driven up by his significant tax cuts.
The federal government deficit - the gap between its revenues from taxes and its spending - was $2 trillion in the year to September 2026, external. That's equivalent to around 6%, external of US GDP.
And the US deficit is projected to rise to above 8% of GDP by 2030, external.

A Canadian man has been found guilty of animal cruelty after he took a flamingo from its enclosure in Las Vegas and brought it back to his hotel room during an alcohol-fuelled bender.
Mitchell Fairbarn, who was visiting the US city, took the Chilean flamingo named Peachy from the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino in March.
Videos shown at his trial showed a smiling Fairbarn carrying the bird by the neck as he took a lift to his room. He testified that he had drunk 30 to 40 beers before the incident and said he never meant to harm the animal. He faces nearly five years in prison.
Animal experts testified the flamingo had feathers torn out and suffered blood loss due to Fairbarn's actions.
A lawyer for Fairbarn said his actions were intended as a harmless prank, and blamed alcohol for his "bad decisions".
"He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn't have touched a bird, shouldn't have taken Peachy inside," said his lawyer Josh Tomsheck, external.
"The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions."
His lawyer added he had received death threats since his arrest.
Testifying in his defence, Fairbarn, 34, said he thought it would be "funny" to take the bird.
He said he had been up drinking all night and had just gotten off a call with a colleague when he made the decision to abscond with the bird.
The Flamingo Las Vegas, located along the famous Las Vegas strip, features a wildlife habitat inside its hotel and casino that is free to walk through. It features a flock of Chilean flamingos, other birds, fish and turtles.
During the trial, the jury heard from 14 witnesses and reviewed more than 112 pieces of evidence, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner.
It took a jury around five hours to convict him on felony and misdemeanour animal abuse charges.
Fairbarn has been unable to leave the US since his arrest. He remains on house arrest in Las Vegas, with a sentencing hearing due to take place in December.
A veterinarian for the state said that Peachy has largely recovered since the event but has a now has a more anxious demeanour around humans.

b84faf1059a4.text:
- Published
Protesters in Albania have fought with riot police on the seventh consecutive day of violent clashes.
The protesters, many of them high school and university students, are trying to oust embattled Prime Minister Edi Rama. Official figures said 295 people have been injured, 186 of whom are police officers, before Monday's violence.
"The moment the state negotiates with this," Rama told grim-faced police chiefs, brandishing a rock hurled at police on Sunday, "the state has fallen".
A police station and government buildings in Tirana have been attacked during the protests, which are being driven by demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and calls for Rama's resignation.
The protesters included "young men and women who have been radicalised by dark forces in Europe and the US", Rama said. "Albania has become one of the targets of a well co-ordinated attack."
In brilliant October sunshine in Rinia Park, also known as Youth Park, I watched people prising loose cobble stones - like that brandished by the prime minister - as ammunition for later battles with police. They did not have long to wait.
A convoy of police vehicles advanced down a broad boulevard, led by an armoured truck firing water cannon and tear gas canisters among the fleeing protesters.
Squads of riot police chased the predominantly student crowd through the park. Protesters took refuge in a cafe where even the eyes of the waiters streamed from the teargas.
Under trees, volunteers in yellow reflector jackets stood their ground helping those overcome by the fumes. I watched a young man remonstrating with a policeman, who then fired pepper spray in his face at point-blank range.
"The police actions are often chaotic and stupid," human rights lawyer Gentian Sejrani told the BBC. He provides legal support to more than 100 people who have been arrested.
"In court, the police rarely present evidence," he said. His clients include a man arrested on his way to a bus stop â completely unrelated to the protests, he said.
"Those who are actually throwing stuff at the police rarely get caught, because they run the fastest," Serjani said.
Police appear as incensed by the violence against their colleagues as the protesters are by the strong-arm tactics of the police. The result is mayhem.
Outside the cafe in the park, when the gas has cleared, 27-year-old activist Sidorela Vatnikaj, a masters student, describes her typical day. In a movement without leaders she is one of the more experienced, with eight years in the forefront of anti-government protests behind her.
"In the morning, you try to co-ordinate with all the groups - where they are, and where the protest is taking place. If any lawyers are needed, if any first aid kit or any kind of equipment is needed. And you also have to make sure all your friends, your family members in the protest are OK."
The day is spent going from protest to protest, much of it running from police, she said.
She is uncomfortable with the violence towards the authorities from her fellow protesters, but blames the police for starting and fuelling it.
"When I see people throwing stones at the police, I understand their anger. I don't judge them. I'm not happy, but they have no other way to be listened to," Vatnikaj said.
"They come from families whose family members had no other choice than to leave the country - a million in the past decade. They have not only been robbed, they have been bullied, ignored and now they they have also been beaten up."
At the weekend, the prime minister asked rhetorically what would happen if he stepped down.
"We need a technocratic government for one year, to prepare the country for real, democratic elections," Vatnikaj replies. She has accused Rama of rigging previous elections, and of being hand in glove with rich foreign investors and organised crime groups.
Young people in Albania feel encouraged by their fellow Gen Z protesters around the world, Vatnikaj said.
"I have seen my mother and father's generation, working all their lives and dreaming of having a democratic society where they could live with dignity. That never happened," she said.
Rama has been in power for 13 years, and has been a dominant figure in Albanian politics since the turn of the century. He has promised EU membership by 2030, and said he is the only one who can deliver it.

ffac654a1bc9.text: White House envoy Steve Witkoff is traveling to Oslo for talks Tuesday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders, a U.S. official said. The big picture: The talks will bring together Ukraine, European allies and the U.S. as they seek to develop a peace proposal to present to Russia . The Oslo talks are expected to include Zelensky , Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, representatives of the E4 nations (the U.K., France, Germany and Poland) and officials from the EU and NATO. Driving the news: The U.S. official said that following Oslo, Witkoff is also planning to travel to Russia, where he hopes to meet with President Vladimir Putin and present ideas developed in close consultation with Ukraine and European partners. Trump adviser Jared Kushner has the flu and will not attend the Oslo meeting in person, but will participate virtually, the U.S. official said. The planned meetings in Oslo build on the discussions held at Witkoff's Miami-area Shell Bay club , where Zelensky committed to reviewing and advancing a series of proposals aimed at creating a pathway toward a comprehensive and durable peace agreement, the U.S. official added. Zoom in: The U.S. official said American, Ukrainian and European representatives worked together over the past week to develop the proposals. "Steve and Jared also spoke with President Zelensky on Sunday to review progress and discuss next steps," the U.S. official said. The trip is also expected to include efforts to secure the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired American teacher whom the U.S. says has been wrongfully detained in Russia. What's next: The U.S. official said the discussions are focused on two parallel tracks: Securing Ukraine's future: Establishing a sovereign, secure, and prosperous future for Ukraine, including credible security guarantees, European integration, and a comprehensive postwar economic framework that addresses Ukraine's financial needs and creates opportunities for long-term growth and investment. Creating the conditions for a durable peace: Developing a comprehensive proposal to Russia that addresses the issues necessary to end the war, establishes a new and enduring security architecture between Russia and Europe, and explores opportunities for postwar economic cooperation. "President Trump has directed an intensive process to develop a comprehensive peace proposal with Ukraine and Europe, and the next step is to test whether that work can form the basis for serious negotiations with Russia," the U.S. official said. "These discussions remain fluid, and substantial work remains. President Trump's objective is clear: to end the killing, bring the war to a close, and establish the conditions for a lasting peace that benefits Ukraine, Russia, Europe, and the United States."

- Published
Mississippi police used "justified" force when they shot at a car during a shoplifting investigation, killing a one-year-old boy inside, the state's attorney general has ruled.
Kohen Wiley was killed in June while sitting on his mother's lap in the passenger seat of a car that police say was being driven at officers in the city of Senatobia.
Authorities have said they were called about a report that nappies and baby clothes were allegedly stolen.
His mother has denied the allegations. Neither she nor the driver of the vehicle have been charged with a crime. A lawyer for the Wiley family denounced the attorney general's findings on Monday and called for the release of footage from the incident.
Police were called to a Walmart store on 14 June after a report of baby supplies being allegedly stolen. According to the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation, officers arrived to find two women and a child walking towards a car.
Officers tried to stop the vehicle but it was allegedly driven at one of them, nearly striking an officer. One officer opened fire, fatally striking the boy and critically injuring the driver, Latoya Ferrell.
Kohen's mother, Vellesiya Wiley, has denied she or Ferrell were stealing and said she lifted her son up from her lap to show officers he was there before he was hit by gunfire.
"In this incident, the Attorney General's Office found the use of force was justified," Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch wrote in a short statement on Monday.
Police have not released any footage from the shooting, including from officer-worn body cameras or CCTV recordings taken from the parking lot.
The Wiley family's lawyer Benjamin Crump objected to Fitch's finding, saying: "How can anyone accept that conclusion when Kohen's family and the public still have not been allowed to see the body-camera footage?"
"If the footage supports the state's decision, release it," he continued. "We will not stop fighting until this family gets the truth."
Martin Zummach, a lawyer for the officer who fired the shots, told the Associated Press the driver had "tried to kill" his client.
"He had no choice but to fire his weapon," Zummach said.
The death, which happened on the Juneteenth US holiday, which recognises the end of slavery in the US, triggered protests in Senatobia.
Protesters have alleged that race played a role in the investigation. Kohen and both women are black, while the officer that fired the shots is reportedly white.
Last month, the city fired its white police chief after newspapers unearthed text messages that found him repeatedly using racial slurs.

Trump appointees asked a federal cybersecurity agency to secretly hack a voting machine
The request shocked staffers, who feared they were being asked to take part in political interference.
A few months into President Donald Trump’s second term, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security made an unusual request of its agency focused on cybersecurity: Secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it.
The appointees wanted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure the machine, examine it and report back the findings so they could be given to the White House, according to two former administration officials with knowledge of the request.
The proposition was shocking to CISA’s career staffers, according to one of the former officials. CISA typically worked to thwart hackers. Moreover, the agency had been directed not to alert the voting machine company if it uncovered flaws, contrary to its standard practices. The request made the CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference.
“My thought was they could keep it in their back pocket to invalidate any [election] results they don’t like,” one of the former officials said. “This goes against everything CISA represents.”
The CISA employees repeatedly told the political appointees that their request was impossible, in part because the agents capable of pulling off such an operation had just been laid off by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency initiative. The appointees eventually stopped pressing CISA.
Though not acted on, the request shows how the Trump administration has tried to use the agency for its own ends while draining it of resources for one of its critical missions: protecting the nation’s voting systems.
In Trump’s second term, his administration has laid off or pushed out more than 1,000 CISA employees, shrinking the agency by about one-third. The president’s 2027 budget proposal would reduce funding for the agency by another $700 million, which could necessitate 900 additional layoffs.
In response, Democratic lawmakers have called for an investigation into CISA’s ability to do its job and demanded answers as to why federal funds are not being used to support election security as directed by Congress.
Since Trump signed the CISA Act in 2018, the agency has worked with state authorities and voting machine vendors to help protect election infrastructure from cyberattacks. During Trump’s second term, though, CISA has abandoned much of this work. Several state election authorities said the agency provided them no assistance — and no explanation for its absence — during the most critical planning stages for the upcoming midterms.
“There is a difference between deprioritizing and being nonexistent,” said Ryan Macias, an election technology and cybersecurity expert who has worked as a consultant for CISA. In 2025 and through mid-September 2026 — when the bulk of preparations for the election typically would have been completed — “they were nonexistent. Literally nonexistent.”
While Trump has repeatedly warned that America’s elections are vulnerable to hacking, in some cases repeating disproven claims, experts said his administration is undermining the federal government’s role in helping secure them.
Though CISA re-emerged in September with a last-minute security plan for the election, some state officials told ProPublica they fear that what is left of the agency has been compromised by a conspiracy-obsessed presidential administration. In recent months, in reviving debunked theories about the 2020 election, the Trump administration has declassified troves of records, including sensitive material that state officials provided to CISA. Some state authorities said they no longer trusted the administration enough to share information with CISA, a key to the agency’s success in past elections.
“They’ve violated the entire premise of that information-sharing relationship,” said one former high-ranking federal cybersecurity official who now advises state governments on national security. “There’s no fucking way they’re ever going to give any information to CISA. And it’s unclear if they ever will in the future.”
A spokesperson for the White House declined an interview request but defended Trump’s handling of election security in an emailed statement. “President Trump has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections,” said Lauren Bis.
Bis referred specific questions about CISA’s handling of elections to DHS. DHS and CISA did not respond to interview requests or to a detailed list of questions.
Current and former CISA employees and state election officials describe an agency that has become significantly less equipped to help states fight legitimate cyber threats. State leaders say they have used their own resources to shore up gaps left by CISA, such as paying for sensor technology that can detect unusual activity in election networks. But some services, like intel on foreign actors, can’t be replicated. Some people interviewed said they were worried that Trump and his allies continue to ratchet up rhetoric about voting security, particularly about threats to voting machines. Officials in one large voting jurisdiction said they have met privately with machine vendors to come up with a contingency plan if the federal government seizes their machines or declares them unusable.
“I don’t pay attention to what the president says. I pay attention to what his administration does,” Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said. “And what they’ve done is basically cut us off and left us on our own.”
Defending elections from hackers wasn’t always part of DHS’s remit.

84fb732145e9.text: Social media lets us share our lives with family, friends, and strangers. But how do people decide what to post, what to leave out, and what do those decisions say about them? On "Settle In," Geoff Bennett discusses that with Kathryn Jezer-Morton, author of "The Story of Your Life," a new book about how the incentives of social media platforms have narrowed the kinds of stories we tell. Geoff Bennett: Social media has become the main way we share our lives with family, friends, and strangers alike. In this week's episode of "Settle In," I spoke with Kathryn Jezer-Morton, author of the new book "The Story of Your Life" about how the incentives of social media platforms have narrowed the kinds of stories we tell and shapes how we see ourselves. You write about what you call the redemption narrative, the pressure to turn whatever difficulty one is going through into this story of personal growth or triumph. Why are we so drawn to that? Kathryn Jezer-Morton, Author, "The Story of Your Life: How Social Media Shapes the Way We Experience Everything": You know, I think that's something that is really at the core of American identity. I mean, I think that the project of the United States was sort of built on this idea of starting something in a new place and overcoming the odds in order to make it work. And I think that's the story of capitalism. It's the story of economic progress as we know it today. So, to me, this is just an extension of that. But it's just not the only story. And I do think it makes sense to tell a story about redemption when you're talking about a business, when you're talking about an enterprise. I think it makes less sense to lean on that narrative when you're talking about a family or an individual, just because a family's life is always going to have ups and downs. Geoff Bennett: There's something almost radical these days about saying, yes, this experience was difficult, and it didn't necessarily make me a better person. (LAUGHTER) Geoff Bennett: It was just something I had to go through. Kathryn Jezer-Morton: Yes, right. That's right. That's -- to kind of just let it land on that kind of unresolved note is really dissonant, I think, to the contemporary ear. People want to hear a resolution. They want to hear the takeaways, what I learned from. And this is really, I think, a product of this narrative orientation that we have towards redemption. Make it better. Learn something from your troubles. And I just don't believe that that's always the path that we take. And the people that I spoke to in this book really reinforced that idea for me that it's not always just better and better and better. Geoff Bennett: Well, say more about the people with whom you spoke for the book and how you determined who you would speak with and what stories you would include. Kathryn Jezer-Morton: Yes, I mean, it really just started leaving my bubble, trying to find strangers. I joined like Meetup.com groups, just any place where I could go where I would be able to talk to strangers without making people uncomfortable. I went on Facebook and community groups, and I asked if I could talk to people. I really just kind of tried everything. And I just spoke to a lot of different kinds of people, mostly millennials, I would say. And I heard a lot of stories. Basically, if someone told me a story that really stuck in my head, I would be like, I'm going to build a chapter around this, and then I would find other stories, and I would just kind of put them together. But I kind of let the data lead the way, and I was just looking for people to surprise me. And it was not hard to find people to surprise me, I have to say. It was a lot easier than I thought it was going to be. Geoff Bennett: One of the real paradoxes you identify in your book is that social media promises individuality and self-expression, but actually produces an enormous amount of conformity. What did you find when you were sort of researching and stitching together that part of your book? Kathryn Jezer-Morton: Yes, I call it like a small-C conservatism. People want to replicate ways of being that they have already seen, which is a fundamentally conservative orientation. Like, I want it to be the traditional way. And I think a lot of that is just because people -- not everyone is like a natural-born storyteller with a huge creative well of ideas, and they just figure, hey, that looked cool, I'm going to do it that way. So, I mean, that's just a basic human orientation. But I also just think that we -- this is now our version of success. When we see someone taking a cool-looking vacation, we're like, that's what success is. I want to do that. If I'm able to do that, I will have succeeded. And so, yes, it does sort of funnel us into these ways of telling our story that are really, really similar to each other. Geoff Bennett: And you can watch all episodes of "Settle In" on our YouTube page or wherever you get your podcasts.

76008f2e0c4c.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday lobbied a bipartisan group of senators to press the Trump administration to remove what he claimed are restrictions on intelligence sharing and weapons supplies. Why it matters: Ukrainian officials say the Trump administration has quietly imposed these limits without admitting it publicly in an attempt to press Zelensky to accept a deal to end the war that includes more concessions to Russia. Trump and White House officials have denied for days that they've imposed any restrictions on Ukraine. Driving the news: The crisis began 10 days ago when Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia during a round of negotiations between his envoys and Ukrainian officials in Miami. The Ukrainians claimed that Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner threatened that Trump could cut off Ukraine from U.S. intelligence and stop selling weapons if it continued to ignore requests not to target Russian oil refineries . U.S. officials denied such a threat. They said Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainians that the U.S. was a strong partner, providing munitions and intelligence. Ukraine therefore shouldn't take actions that hurt American consumers, Witkoff and Kushner said.​ Behind the scenes: During a virtual meeting with a bipartisan group of senators led by Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Zelensky laid out the various problems Ukraine has been experiencing since the Miami meeting. Axios obtained a transcript from Ukrainian officials. Elon Musk's Starlink and the U.S. military's Starshield satellite systems remain partially restricted — despite claims by the White House to the contrary. "We still have no explanation for this. Just different strange stories we're hearing, unfortunately," Zelensky told the senators. It's hampering Ukraine's ability to shoot down Russian attack drones, he added. On three occasions the past week, including on Sunday, Ukraine didn't receive early warnings from the U.S. about Russian ballistic missile attacks, Zelensky said, suggesting it was a sign that intelligence sharing has been curbed. "We have received no clear explanation from Washington – why this is happening," he added. Zelensky said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is not signing off on the delivery of Patriot interceptors and AIM-9x missiles for the NASAMS air-defense system, even though NATO countries have already paid for them. "We have almost no Patriot interceptors left from the U.S. partners," he said. "All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us," Zelensky said. ​"We want to understand what is happening, why it's happening, and where all of this is heading." What they're saying : Tillis said after the meeting that Congress "remains committed to standing with Ukraine and our European allies to end Russia's brutal aggression and secure lasting peace." Blumenthal said afterwards that "bipartisan support for Ukraine was clear and unequivocal, which we'll be expressing in upcoming action." "Appeasement won't work with Putin, a thug who understands only strength and force," he added. The other side: President Trump told reporters on Monday that the U.S. is still sharing intelligence with Ukraine and said he didn't know who ordered the throttling of the Starlink satellite system. "But I am gonna find out," he said. "Frankly Zelensky is not helping matters much. He doesn't want to stop the war. Zelensky doesn't know what he is talking about," the president said. "Maybe it's time for Zelensky to let somebody else negotiate on behalf of Ukraine. … We have given a lot to Ukraine. They have given nothing to us." State of play: Zelensky spoke with Witkoff and Kushner on Sunday. They asked Ukraine again to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, Ukrainian officials said. Zelensky told the senators that he proposed to the U.S. envoys that Ukraine halt strikes on refineries for 30 days. In return, the U.S. would supply Ukraine with Patriot interceptors so it could defend itself from Russian ballistic missiles during that 30-day period. Zelensky told the senators that Witkoff and Kushner haven't shown any openness to the idea. What to watch: Zelensky told the senators that he'll be in Oslo, Norway next week and could meet with Witkoff and Kushner on Tuesday or Wednesday. Kushner and Witkoff could then continue on from Oslo to Moscow to meet with Putin, a source familiar with the matter said.

US special envoy Steve Witkoff has arrived in Norway ahead of talks with Volodymyr Zelensky with relations on the slide between the Ukrainian leader and US President Donald Trump.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re said Zelensky had asked Oslo and neighbouring Finland to organise the meeting with the US and European allies "at a critical time for Ukraine".
Ahead of the meeting, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected as "scandalous" and "outrageous" accusations that Ukrainians were dying because the US was withholding intelligence from Kyiv.
He was speaking after Zelensky's military technical adviser, Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, told the BBC that the lack of reliable US warnings meant lives were being lost.
"This looks very strange," said Beskrestnov. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."
Relations between Kyiv and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".
StÃ¸re said the aim of the Oslo talks were to steer relations towards "a more constructive path". He told reporters at the parliament in Norway that they wanted to ensure that the war ended diplomatically with a lasting and just peace.
Zelensky said earlier he had had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about the need for US early warnings, missile interceptors and SpaceX's Starlink internet network.
Last week a bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into disruptions to the Starlink network in Ukraine, and unconfirmed reports on Tuesday said the transfer of more Patriot interceptors had not yet been approved.
The US secretary of state is currently on a visit to India and admitted to reporters that it may be true that Patriot interceptor missiles had not yet arrived in Ukraine, although nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally.
Witkoff is expected to be joined by video-link by Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, and by several European representatives, including Finnish President Alexander Stubb and officials from the UK, Poland, France and Germany, as well as the EU and Nato.
It is not yet clear whether Witkoff will travel on to Russia after his visit to Oslo, however the Kremlin spokeman said he hoped a meeting with Trump's special envoy could be organised in the near future. Dmitry Peskov said "we greatly appreciate the mediation efforts of the American negotiators".
Earlier this month Russia's Vladimir Putin discussed the war with Trump over the phone, and not long afterwards the US president announce that Moscow would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the US and other markets, bringing to an end American sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
European leaders have expressed concern about recent statements from the US towards Russia, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke on Monday of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war, adding that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly".
He pointed out that the US had not been paying for the defence of Ukraine since the start of 2025, and Europe and other countries were shouldering the burden.
"It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV.
Asked whether or not Ukraine was a US ally, Vice-President JD Vance has said in a TV interview that Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy".
"We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too."

- Published
A 43-year-old man has been charged after Australian MP Helen Haines was hit by a car in Victoria state on Monday.
The suspect will appear in court on Wednesday to face charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official.
Local media earlier named the alleged attacker as environmental activist Brendan Nugent. His father and his partner said they had been friends with Haines "for more than 20 years" and thanked residents and officers who helped her after the "shocking and horrific crime".
Haines remains in a critical condition after surgery and is reported to have lost one of her legs.
"Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community," Rod Nugent and his partner Christine Cunningham said in a statement.
"All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends."
They promised to assist Victoria Police "in any way we can".
Police say they will allege the incident was targeted.
Haines, 65, the independent member for Indi, is in a critical but stable condition after undergoing surgery at a Melbourne hospital.
She was airlifted there after bystanders rushed to help as the suspect allegedly struck her twice outside her office in Wangaratta.
The driver reportedly did a U-turn to get into position before hitting her, then reversed and hit her again, the home affairs minister told national broadcaster ABC.
She was pinned between two cars and later lost a leg, the ABC reports. The outlet also says doctors are fighting to save her other leg.
A local barber says he pulled the suspect out of his car and took a knife from him.
"I just wasn't comfortable with his movements so I took it out of his pocket and threw it away," Ricky Jefferies told reporters.
"I don't think I'm a hero. I think that I was just a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish way."
Others who helped "didn't even check for danger," Jefferies said. "The car was still on and they sat in front of a rolling car, that's not an exaggeration."
In their statement, Victoria Police say a highway patrol unit was nearby at the time of the incident and "on scene" within eight seconds of the call coming through.
As they announced the charges against the 43-year-old, they said they had searched a property in Tarawingee, nearly 60km (40 miles) from Wangaratta.
"At this stage it appears this is an isolated incident, and there are currently no other known threats connected to this matter," they said, adding officers would maintain a presence in Wangaratta.
Haines won the seat of Indi as an independent in 2019, and has since become a prominent member of the crossbench, building rapport across Australia's increasingly divided political spectrum.
Her office is on Wangaratta's main street, which reopened to traffic on Tuesday. Cars slowly filed past the growing number of bouquets being left for her on the pavement.
The community, and country, remain in shock.
At the vigil earlier on Tuesday, locals queued patiently in the cathedral aisle, waiting for their turn to light a candle. Priests hugged some of those who'd come to pay their respects.
On the pavement outside her office there were a growing number of bouquets being left for her.
One card read "may you recover quickly and continue to be a light in this world".

Nearly eight months of war in Iran have produced one of the most severe energy shocks in decades, exposing a sharp divide between the countries that absorbed it with surprising ease and those forced into painful tradeoffs. Resilience, it turns out, comes less from any single technology or policy than from systems-level thinking, long-term investment, and deliberate planning.
The countries that coped best were not always those with the most energy resources. They were the ones that had built flexibility, redundancy, and alternative pathways into their energy systems.
China drew on strategic reserves, alternative pipeline imports, and fuel switching. The US benefited from record domestic oil and gas production, regional storage and solar to improve summer grid stability, and secure North American supply chains. Highly electrified countries such as Norway relied on hydropower, heat pumps, EVs, and infrastructure located far from the conflict zone.
Emerging markets fared worse. Bangladesh and Pakistan imposed electricity restrictions and other demand-reduction measures. Wealthier economies across Europe and Asia largely avoided shortages only by paying sharply higher prices for LNG and other fuels. The dividing line ran not between producers and consumers, but between countries with options and countries without them.
Three lessons stand out for governments and investors:
- Domestic electrons are safer electrons. The principle is straightforward: The shorter and more secure the energy chain, the fewer vulnerabilities a country carries into a crisis. Energy that is produced, generated, or stored at home is often more reliable than energy that must travel through vulnerable supply chains and geopolitical chokepoints. Few countries can achieve outright energy independence, but all of them can reduce their exposure to single points of failure.
Solar and storage have scaled quickly in recent years on cost and technical readiness alone. Some producers will expand oil and gas output as demand shifts away from the Middle East to places with safer access to global trade routes. The Iran war is also unlocking public and private money for nuclear and geothermal energy. Nuclear deserves renewed attention as both an energy and national security asset, since reactors provide reliable electricity largely insulated from short-term geopolitical shocks. Small modular reactors could go further, supplying dependable power close to military installations, advanced manufacturing facilities, and AI data centers. Meanwhile, breakthroughs in deep drilling and new enhanced geothermal systems could vastly expand access to around-the-clock power beyond âtraditional geothermal regions.â
- Electrification is now as much a security strategy as a climate strategy. Every domestically produced electron reduces exposure to disruptions in global fuel markets. That shifts the burden onto the grid. The challenge is no longer simply generating enough power. It is building the systems required to deliver that power where and when it is needed.
The US electric grid is one of the largest on Earth, and it is aging rapidly. Some 70% of transmission lines are more than 25 years old, and the average large power transformer has been in service for nearly four decades. Demand for transformers has surged, yet the US has only one domestic producer of the specialized electrical steel needed for transformer cores. In 2025, 80% of power transformer supply and 50% of the distribution supply parts came from abroad.
The American workforce is thinning too. The power sector will need more than 500,000 additional workers by 2030, just as hundreds of thousands of existing energy sector employees retire.
Permitting compounds the problem: Major US infrastructure projects can take four to five years to secure approvals, delaying as much as $1.5 trillion in investment. As energy supply struggles to keep pace with demand, those delays have drawn political attention and, finally, action, including significant legislation passed at the state level and a new bipartisan permitting reform bill proposed in the Senate.
- The countries that cope best with the next crisis will not necessarily be those that build the most infrastructure. They will be the ones that make the best use of what they already have.
Not every energy security challenge can wait a decade for a new power plant, transmission corridor, or major industrial project. In the US, with its aging grid infrastructure and rapidly growing power demand, that constraint bites. But many of the answers already exist: Long-duration batteries can store electricity during periods of surplus and release it when shortages emerge. Grid-enhancing technologies can raise transmission capacity, ease congestion, and improve the efficiency of existing assets. Smart-grid software and demand-management tools can shift consumption away from periods of peak stress without new steel in the ground.
Every crisis is said to carry opportunity. The lesson from 2026 is that the most successful energy systems of the next decade will not merely generate more power. They will store it better, move it more efficiently, and protect it more successfully.
Dr Sarah Kapnick is global head of Climate Advisory, J.P. Morgan. Derek Chollet is head of the JPMorganChase Center for Geopolitics.

008e69ec8888.text:
- Published
Residents living near South Africa's capital, Pretoria, have been warned not to drink or cook with tap water after more than 400 people, mostly children under four, fell ill after drinking contaminated water.
The cases were detected in Tshwane, the area which includes Pretoria, after people reported to their local hospital with "stomach cramps and diarrhoea" over a two-week period, officials said.
No deaths have been reported but high levels of E. coli were found in the water.
Tshwane has faced numerous outbreaks from waterborne diseases in recent years. In 2023, 29 people were killed by a cholera outbreak in a township just outside Pretoria.
That outbreak, in Hammanskraal, was linked to substandard water purification practices.
In 2025, officials confirmed 48 cases of typhoid in the same area east of Pretoria. The source of the outbreak remains unclear.
No cholera bacteria has been found in the latest cases.
The departments of water and health, in a joint statement on Monday, said 408 cases had been detected between 7 and 18 October in about five townships.
They said that lab tests "indicate that the illness has been caused by residents being exposed to contaminated water" from a local water treatment facility supplying water to several communities east of Pretoria.
Samples tested found norovirus, campylobacter, shigella and "other pathogens that cause stomach cramps and diarrhoea", officials said.
The team's early investigations found that local authorities had failed to warn residents about the contaminated water.
The water supplied to the area has been declared unfit for human consumption and authorities urged residents to only use it to flush toilets. Tankers have been dispatched to supply clean drinking water.
"Previously stored water should be discarded, and water containers must be disinfected using household bleach," officials said.
Additional reporting by Pumza Fihlani

e208bb1c248b.text:
When people face losing the ability to talk, they need alternative ways to communicate. One way people preserve their voice is by banking it. The process has improved in recent years, but it still produces a voice that can sound unnatural. Jules Rodriguez did this as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, left his own voice diminished. But he wasn’t happy with the sound.
New technology that uses artificial intelligence allowed Jules to create a voice clone, one that sounds like his old voice. With breaths, intonations and even stutters, these voice clones capture the quirks of a human voice. Jules’ voice clone was so realistic that his wife cried the first time she heard it. 
In this episode, hear how AI-powered voice clones are changing the conversation around how people connect. That includes a musician named Patrick Darling who uses his voice clone to sing and perform songs.
Episode 3 transcript
Laura Sanders: Jules Rodriguez’s voice was disappearing.
Jules Rodriguez: For me, it felt like I was fading away, like when Marty McFly was seeing his family fade away in the picture he had in “Back to the Future.”
Sanders: Jules has ALS, and like many people with that disease, this fading felt inevitable. But there was something Jules could do about it. I’m Laura Sanders, and this is episode three of The Deep End: Talk To Me, a Science News podcast on the human voice and all it can hold.
[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? The voice is absolutely an integral part of your identity. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi.
Sanders: On today’s episode, we’re going to hear about the return of Jules’ voice.
[voice] Your voice is you.
We touched on this in the last episode, but as a reminder, there are a few traditional ways people preserve their ways to communicate when they’re faced with losing a voice. One is for people to record themselves saying common or special phrases if they can still talk. That’s called message banking. And then there’s a technique called voice banking. It requires a person to record themselves saying very specific words. And then these sounds get fed into a computer program that can stitch them together to make any word a person wants to say. Sounds good in theory, but in practice, the output didn’t sound very human. Jules banked his voice soon after his diagnosis. MA describes what that was like.
MA: I remember both of us looking at each other while he was recording, basically the old school way, and they still recommend to bank your voice this way, besides your cloned voice, but you’re sent all these phrases that you’re just recording, like 350 phrases, and that goes into, you know, a file, and then when you do need it, the company will pull it up and plug it into your device.
Sanders: I spoke with Richard Cave. He’s a speech therapist at University College London who works with people with ALS. That’s also called motor neuron disease, or MND.
Richard Cave: My role was to build out the voice banking initiative across the UK. This was back in 2017. And I remember… After the first, I don’t know, six months, nine months, being very proud that I managed to put through 100 people or so at an average duration to complete the voice banking, all 1,600 phrases in around three months each. Very proud of that. They weren’t awful, but they weren’t good. And they didn’t really represent the person. They represented kind of part, a little bit, of the person. But that was the best we had.
Having decoded the signals from some input device, such as the switch, one then has to broadcast it in a form people can understand. This could be visually, with text or diagrams on the screen. Sanders: The late physicist Stephen Hawking had one of perhaps the most iconic computerized voices. Here he is giving a talk in 1994 at MIT.
[Hawking audio] Computerized speech synthesizers have improved a great deal in recent years, and this is important. Not only does one want to be understood, but also one doesn’t want to sound like Mickey Mouse or a Dalek.

[Hawking audio] This voice of mine may be a bit tinny and Irish, but it is almost human.

Harder, better, faster, stronger.

These voices are so realistic that sometimes you can’t even hear the difference.

Sanders: I used ElevenLabs to clone my voice. That’s a company that uses AI technology to create lifelike, digital replicas of voices. To do it, I used the professional option, which required 30 minutes of audio to make. So for input, I recorded myself reading a few podcast scripts.

It’s a good thing Rachel Lynde got a calling down. She’s a meddlesome old gossip.
Sanders: After a few minutes, poof, there it was, my voice clone. It was spooky how much it sounded like me. I spent a fun afternoon playing with it. You can control so many different parts.

Andyâs view
The new Tesla Roadster is science fiction: It can zoom into the air, perform barrel rolls, and then plop down softly using cold-gas rocket thrusters.
Unveiled last week at a rocket facility in Texas, the Roadster is a triumph of engineering â an exquisite toy for the super-rich, if it ever reaches production (the disclaimers on the advance orders suggest CEO Elon Musk himself has doubts).
Yet, paradoxically, it also represents a defeat: The Roadster isnât a vehicle that will turn the tables on China, outcompeting the likes of BYD in the consumer market. Instead, it represents the future in another way, one in which China owns global mass manufacturing not just in cars but everything else â machine tools, pharmaceuticals, ships.
As low-priced Chinese exports swamp global markets, politicians from Washington to Brussels to Berlin diagnose the problem largely as one of Chinese overproduction, and are putting up trade barriers to protect their domestic industries. The EU and China, for example, recently agreed to set quotas with tariffs for Chinese hybrid cars, and are considering similar restrictions on other industrial categories.
But this misses the broader challenge. Chinaâs surging shipments are much more than just surplus production, the difference between what comes out of Chinese factories and what can be sold domestically in a sagging economy. They are a deliberate strategy, clearly stated in the countryâs five-year industrial plans and, ultimately, represent Chinaâs quest for national power.
The implication for Western industry leaders is existential: They can either climb the technological ladder into increasingly rarefied niches â like Tesla, with its Roadster â or risk being destroyed by Chinese rivals, as is currently happening to Volkswagen in China, still its largest single market.
In fact, influential Chinese strategists donât recognize the concept of overproduction at all. Lu Feng, a professor at Peking Universityâs School of Government, sees a showdown on the way between Chinaâs âindustrial socialismâ and the USâ âfinancial capitalismâ â and he warns that caving to foreign pressure to curb âoverproductionâ would be âtying our own hands.â In this way of thinking, since Chinaâs desire for power is limitless, there can be no question of producing too much. Kyle Chan, a researcher specializing in Chinaâs industrial policies at the Brookings Institution, labels Luâs brand of economic nationalism, âindustrial maximalism.â
Perhaps, then, we should call the Roadster a prime example of its opposite: âindustrial minimalism.â
Among leading global automakers, Tesla had the best chance of owning the future of mobility. Indeed, its Shanghai gigafactory, built in 2019, and the local supply chains it developed were a catalyst for the entire Chinese EV industry. But Musk is now clear-eyed about the competition he helped spawn. Without trade barriers, he warned in 2024, China would âpretty much demolish most other car companies in the world.â
Musk is now betting Teslaâs future on becoming a robot maker. But heâll run into the same issues in that sector, too. The challenge from China is systemic, not industry specific. The countryâs industrial machine is set up to commoditize products through overwhelming economies of scale, to bring down prices, and conquer global markets â regardless of financial return. This is not about profit maximization. Itâs about power maximization.
Writing in The Guardian, the tech reporter Chang Che, who recently visited 11 Chinese robot makers across five cities, sees a future where the US leverages its advanced research capabilities to try to build the ultimate robotic machine â one that can âmow your lawn, walk your dog, and babysit your childrenâ â while China cranks out functioning robots for each of those tasks at a fraction of the price. Already, China accounts for 60% of all the worldâs new factory robots.
It also has the capacity to supply 100% of global demand for EVs. Michael Dunne, the author of the forthcoming Car Wars, told The Wall Street Journal that what remains for Western carmakers âis to move up or get pushed out.â The Tesla Roadster is, quite literally, aiming for the skies. Other carmakers will have to make a similar vertical ascent, or bite the dust.
Notable
- Zeroing in on the term âscenario innovation,â a recent Sinocities article explained Chinaâs state-sponsored process of opening up real spaces, like roads and factories, so that companies can test new technologies in real-world settings.

The first named storm of the autumn - Storm Austen - is set to batter parts of the UK with severe gales and heavy rain beginning from Thursday night.
Ahead of the storm, the Met Office has issued a yellow severe weather warning for wind, which will come into force at midnight Friday.
Damage to buildings and transport disruption is likely, with the possibility for power cuts.
While Storm Austen will move away later on Friday, another deep area of low pressure will bring more wet and windy weather on Saturday.
Over the next few days there willl be heavy rain across the UK, along with strengthening winds on Wednesday around west Wales and southern England.
But, it is from late on Thursday where a rapidly deepening area of low pressure - named Storm Austen by the Met Office - starts to approach from the Atlantic.
Heavy rain will move in across England and Wales through Thursday night accompanied by strengthening winds.
A Met Office yellow wind warning will be in force from midnight on Friday to 12:00 BST and covers south Wales, south-west England and along southern coastal counties of England.
Wind gusts of up to 70mph are expected which will likely bring damage to buildings, travel disruption and the risk of power cuts.
More widely gusts of 50-60mph will be felt around west Wales and through southern England.
While the strongest winds will ease from the south-west later on Friday morning, the rest of England and Wales will stay blustery with heavy rain at times through the day.
Scotland and Northern Ireland will largely miss any of the impacts caused by Storm Austen.
Wet and windy weekend
Storm Austen will clear away into the North Sea later on Friday and while there will be a quiet spell with clear skies overnight into Saturday, another area of low pressure will move in for the start of the weekend.
This deep area of low pressure - not expected to be as severe as Austen and therefore unlikely to be named - will head towards Scotland.
Gusts of 70-80mph will affect western Scotland with delays or cancellations to ferries and restrictions on bridges.
It will turn windy elsewhere across the UK throughout Saturday with heavy rain spreading east for most of us.
Sunday will turn drier but it will remain very wind, particularly towards the north east of Scotland.

37712028616b.text:
The Scene
Pascal Lamy negotiated Chinaâs accession to the WTO in 2001 on behalf of the EU. A decade later, in a speech in Shanghai, Europeâs former trade commissioner lauded what he called a âwin-winâ outcome.
But like a growing number of current and former European leaders, heâs grown alarmed as Chinaâs trade surplus with the EU has ballooned. Lamy, now with the Jacques Delors Institute, was one of the authors of a recent policy paper that called for restrictions on Chinese exports using a quota system â an idea that the EU has now embraced.
Q&A
This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and brevity.
Andy Browne: Is the EU-China trade war now off?
Pascal Lamy: I interpret the recent deal on hybrid carsâ export restraints as a first step in the right direction. I think the European side will consider this as a down payment. In my view, we need further steps to seriously address this rocketing Chinese trade surplus with Europe.
So is this a tactical concession by China or a strategic shift?
Both interpretations are possible. But from the EU side, this will not be seen as sufficient.
Is the car deal a model for other sectors?
Yes, indeed, although voluntary export restraints raise a series of technical issues. Itâs certainly easier for hybrid cars than it is for chemicals or pharmaceuticals. And, of course, when you look at the numbers you need quite a lot more given the [EUâs] â¬350 billion annual trade deficit with China.
You once called Chinaâs WTO accession a âwin-win.â Recently, you said that âChina is killing open global trade.â What changed?
I changed my mind because China changed. None of us predicted the speed of economic growth in China. A lot of people now say âyou made a mistake by not forecasting that China would become an enormous elephant.â My usual answer is: Who said that at the time? Give me some evidence that we had a choice between those who said âbe carefulâ and those who said âthatâs a great idea.â [Former Chinese Premier] Zhu Rongji thought that the Chinese miracle was a clever mix of Chinese characteristics and good old Western liberal capitalist market recipes. This is not the view of Xi Jinping. He believes that the incredible economic success of the past 20 years is due to the fact that China is led by the Chinese Communist Party. Also, the state-owned sector is larger today than it was in 2010. Whatâs changed, too, is that China no longer plays the game of comparative advantage, which is the ideological basis of the World Trade Organization. If you are better â cost and quality wise â than I am at everything, whereâs the comparative advantage?
Isnât a big part of the problem that China now out-competes Europe?
Iâm not saying that all of Chinaâs comparative advantage is, letâs say, WTO illegitimate. There is their education system, their engineers, their planning system, and the size of their market. But thereâs another part which is not in line with an open rules-based trading system. By the way, whatâs also changed is that a lot of markets that were open to China â the US, Turkey, Japan â have taken protectionist measures. Chinaâs exports are now going to Europe, the only large and deep market that is still wide open.
Germany and France have proposed a âkill switchâ that could shut China out of European markets completely. Is that a good idea?
I disagree with that formula. Itâs like the US using Section 301 to determine whether a trade partner is playing fair or not. The Jacques Delors Institute has proposed a WTO compatible quota system with in-quota tariffs and out-of-quota tariffs. Thatâs a big difference â itâs predictable, rules-based, with benchmarks and numbers, and everyone understands clearly how the system works. There is no unilateral determination except for the size of the quota.
China also has a âkill switchâ â rare earths. Can Europe really afford to risk a trade war?
Chinaâs rare earth dominance is time-limited. The US, EU, and Japan have started working on alternatives. If you over-use market dominance, markets adjust, and thereâs a big price incentive to innovate.
Tariffs raise prices. Are European consumers ready to pay a premium?
Some prices will be higher, yes. Protection is costly. But whatâs the alternative? You have to choose between that and industry closures, social problems, and the growth of extremism on the right and left of European politics.
Can China be persuaded to compromise?
Iâve been trying to convince my Chinese friends that they should care about this. We have to convince them that if the people who will govern Europe are the products of industrial and social shocks that China is creating, they will be much tougher with China than we, traditional center left or center right, are.

6cba97ffa33c.text: Slowly but surely, the leading AI companies are creating a national self-governing structure to oversee their technology and its societal impact. With the federal government largely hands-off, Anthropic, OpenAI and others are self-regulating their technology and now setting up their own plans to redistribute their wealth. Why it matters: Not since the age of the robber barons have America's industrial titans wielded such sweeping power to shape society — and decide how their private fortunes should serve the public good. In the modern era, Washington has largely exercised those powers through regulation, taxation and public spending. The big picture: President Trump has no interest in new regulations. Instead, he has blessed a basic framework for the AI companies to regulate themselves — and potentially each other — outside of formal government monitoring. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Elon Musk's XSI, Meta and Nvidia are working on different versions of this. This is all voluntary and rests on the public trusting companies the size of industrialized nations to responsibly police themselves. These companies are in a frantic race to create human-surpassing superintelligence. All are pressing ahead, even as their leaders — particularly at Anthropic — warn of potentially catastrophic risks and profound economic disruption. At the same time, some AI leaders are promising to direct a portion of their vast wealth to benefit those outside their companies. Zoom in: At least three competing visions are emerging for sharing the spoils of the AI boom, each with a different answer to who should control the wealth. Anthropic: The company. On the eve of its blockbuster IPO, Anthropic pledged 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund that could grow into one of the largest philanthropic institutions in history. At a hypothetical $2 trillion valuation, its stake would be worth $100 billion — more than the Gates Foundation's current endowment. Including earlier founder and employee pledges, roughly 20% of Anthropic's shares are earmarked for the public good. Musk: The people. Musk responded to Anthropic's announcement by urging the company to give shares "directly to the public." On Monday, Musk pledged to give every American child a share of SpaceX next year — a staggering $10.5 billion giveaway at current prices. Musk called it the "first of many," though he offered no details on how the unprecedented distribution would work. OpenAI: The government. CEO Sam Altman has floated giving the U.S. government a 5% stake in OpenAI through a sovereign wealth fund — potentially handing Washington a multibillion-dollar interest in one of the world's most powerful AI companies. Altman envisions an Alaska-style fund that could distribute the industry's investment returns directly to Americans, though the plan remains preliminary and would likely require congressional approval. Reality check: The numbers are staggering. So are the assumptions about future wealth, billionaire follow-through and the public's willingness to trust its benefactors. Bill Gates and Warren Buffett launched the Giving Pledge in 2010, a voluntary promise by billionaires — including Musk — to give away most of their fortunes. Gates built a philanthropic empire, only to become a lightning rod for conspiracy theories. Anthropic's ambitions depend on extraordinary growth projections — its own employees envision 17% GDP growth in 2030 — while Musk has a history of making spectacular promises that fail to materialize. Anthropic's roots in effective altruism , a philosophy deeply distrusted by the Trump administration and its allies, also raise a more fundamental question: Who gets to define the public good? Between the lines: No industry requirements or consensus exist on how best to redistribute their expected wealth. But Trump Accounts — which allow families, businesses and individuals to invest in tax-advantaged funds for children — are emerging as a favorite vehicle for free-market AI leaders. Billionaire investor Brad Gerstner, a driving force behind the program, is championing a vision of broad-based ownership in which ordinary Americans share directly in the economic upside of the AI revolution. SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband in July pledged roughly $320 million in company shares to 2 million children through Trump Accounts — a potential blueprint for distributing an even larger slice of Musk's fortune. What to watch: The Trump administration hasn't fully relinquished its regulatory authority, potentially complicating the emerging experiment in AI self-governance. After Anthropic disclosed that its AI had submitted a false homicide tip to Philadelphia police and improperly interacted with government websites, the White House declared that AI companies must report security incidents and remedy any harm. "This notification and remediation process is not optional," Trump's Super Intelligence Force warned — a striking assertion of federal authority just weeks after the president blessed a voluntary system of industry oversight. Axios' Zachary Basu and Bradley Olson contributed reporting.
