People in Alberta have voted overwhelmingly to remain part of Canada, projected results suggest, after residents of the western province were asked in a public ballot whether or not they wanted a referendum at a later date on becoming independent.
With most votes counted, more than two-thirds of voters had chosen to remain part of the country rather than pursue the referendum, according to Elections Alberta, external.
The outcome was hailed by Prime Minister Mark Carney as "a clear choice" on the part of Albertans.
At a pro-separatist watch party in Edmonton, the hum of upbeat chatter quickly quieted as those present saw the projected results. However, one separatist leader insisted his campaign was not over.
The vote was called earlier this year by the province's leader, Danielle Smith, in response to a public petition. It was seen as a major test of national unity.
Smith herself opposed the separatist push but said the public will for a vote was undeniable. She welcomed the initial results, commenting: "Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada."
In making the case for independence from Canada, many of the separatists said the oil-rich province's economic growth had been stifled by the environmental policies of Canada's central government in Ottawa.
But those who opposed a breakup - including Carney - called for Canada to present a united front in the face of external pressures, including an ongoing trade war with the United States.
After overnight vote projections were published by Canadian broadcaster CBC and others, the mood soured among the separatist camp. A pro-independence watch party attended by the BBC packed up quickly, and people went home.
One of the separatist leaders, Jeffrey Rath, struck a defiant tone, however, vowing that "our movement isn't stopping and we're continuing to move forward".
Speaking to the BBC World Service's Newsday programme, Rath, a lawyer based in Calgary, said he saw Monday's vote as a "first step" which had taught the movement some "valuable lessons".
Asked whether his movement would push to keep holding votes on independence until it got the result it wanted, he responded "why not?", and insisted that "the math and the economics" all added up on his side of the argument.
Smith called the vote in response to a grassroots group gathering about 300,000 signatures on a petition that asked for a binding referendum on separation.
The petition was blocked by a judge, saying it failed to consult indigenous First Nations people - however, Smith opted to go ahead with the ballot.
Another group collected signatures for its own petition that opposed separation, which was signed by more than 400,000 people.
The key question on Monday's voting paper asked: "Should Alberta remain a province of Canada or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?"
Smith said before the vote that if voters chose the first option, a referendum on separation would not be held - at least, not while she was in power.
Despite the projected results, the conversation around Albertan sovereignty is not over.
Separatists leaders have indicated that they plan to push Smith out of power within her United Conservative Party, in the hope of installing a leader who is more sympathetic to their cause.
It is unclear if they have the numbers on their side to do that, but debate around the issue could dominate politics in Alberta for years to come.
Another separatist leader, Mitch Sylvestre, told the BBC on polling day that "a lot of work will have to be done" to curb the appetite for independence if his side did lose.
Canada has grappled with challenges to its unity before. The province of Quebec held two referendums on independence, in 1980 and 1995. Both were unsuccessful, but Alberta separatists believe Quebec used the threat of independence to gain significant political leverage over Canada's central government.
Although responses to the referendum question are being tallied as a priority, there were nine other questions on Monday's ballot paper.
Five of these dealt with immigration, while the other four focused on the Canadian constitution.

The News
YOUNGSTOWN, Ohio â John Boccieriâs tour through northeast Ohio politics is a microcosm of the Democratic Partyâs decline, especially in state legislatures.
In 2008, Boccieri left his seat in the Ohio state Senate to flip a Republican-held House seat. He lost it in the 2010 GOP wave, which gave the party control over redistricting and put his old district out of reach. Democrats appointed him to a safe state House seat in 2015, though he left it to run for state Senate in 2018. But he lost that race, and went back to work as a pilot.
This year, Boccieri decided to try again for a seat in the state house. He bet that Republicansâ winning streak couldnât survive a second Trump midterm, with Vivek Ramaswamy leading their Ohio ticket.
âThe seat that Iâm running in is still gerrymandered,â he told Semafor last week. âBut we need someone whoâs going to help Amy Acton, when sheâs the governor, to push back on unregulated, unchecked data centers, and make sure that the state house corruption ends.â
Boccieri now exemplifies a new trend in Democratic politics: In the final weeks before the midterms, the party is trying to convince its donors that a âblue waveâ could spread even farther â if their money isnât all spent on a handful of House and Senate races.
âDemocrats are always in this spot of this âcoulda, woulda, shouldaâ with state legislatures,â said Leslie Martes, the CEO of Forward Majority, a nonprofit that spends on Democratic state legislative campaigns. The group has warned donors that Republicans are still ahead in both partiesâ top target races at the state level.
âThereâs this idea that these top-of-the-ticket candidates are going to lift the whole ticket, but thatâs not the case,â Martes explained. âI worked in North Carolina in 2008, when Barack Obama was winning the state, and we didnât pick up a single seat in Raleigh. Thereâs a lot of work to increase the name ID of our candidates at the state legislative level.â
The fight to control state legislatures intensified last year, after President Donald Trump urged Republicans to draw new congressional maps in the states they control that eliminate as many Democratic House seats as possible.
Strategists in both parties said that this redistricting scramble has changed how donors are being approached for state legislative races â rarely the first places where the largest political funders send their cash. Mason Di Palma, a spokesman for the Republican State Leadership Committee, said that his group began warning donors that Democrats could force their own gerrymanders if they swept state-level races in 2026.
In practice, that meant that if Democrats could expand their control in Minnesota, capture Wisconsinâs Assembly, and flip Pennsylvaniaâs state Senate, they would gain the power to delete GOP districts in each state.
âIf Dems get trifectas, what will stop them from redrawing maps?â said Di Palma. âYour dollar goes further in state legislative races.â
Both parties have stepped up their recruiting for downballot races, with Democrats benefiting from an overall confidence that theyâd make gains in the midterms. In Wisconsin they spotted a chance for their first trifecta since 2010 thanks to new maps; in Pennsylvania, the popularity of Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro was already helping them inch toward Senate control.
Know More
Redistricting is reshaping the political outlook in many states, with the possibilities for partisan control divided into three categories.
First, there are states where neither party thinks that they can break the governing trifecta: Republicans are at no risk in Arkansas, Tennessee, or Indiana; Democrats are not worried about losing either the governorâs office or the state legislature in New York, Illinois, and California.
The dead zone includes places where state legislative elections are held in off-years: Louisiana, Mississippi, New Jersey, and Virginia.
The next crop of states with marquee legislative fights this cycle feature one party thatâs trying to break a governing trifecta, or at least end a supermajority that makes it easier for the party in power to force new maps through.
This group includes Nebraska, where Republicans in the âunicamâ have been a vote away from eliminating the presidential electoral vote for Omahaâs 2nd Congressional District. Ohio, where Democrats donât think they can flip the state legislature, is also in this batch â it could still make Acton governor and elect enough legislators to sustain her vetoes.
âIâm very excited that we may break the supermajority in this election,â Acton told Semafor last week.
Finally, there are states where one party could win a trifecta, sometimes in places where theyâd have the ability to draw new maps in 2027. Wisconsin and Pennsylvania top that list for Democrats. It also includes Arizona, where the party is a few seats away from control â and where Republicans have said theyâd use a trifecta of their own to revisit the stateâs redistricting commission.
The total money heading into state legislative campaigns pales in comparison to what Republicans have spent to hold Texasâ Senate seat. But the States Project â which, like Forward Majority, was created to help Democrats win more legislatures â announced a $100 million haul last month; the RSLC is looking at spending ânorth of $52 millionâ on its targets.
In key states, Democrats say that they remain outgunned; in Wisconsin, local GOP donors have helped swing-seat Republicans in the Assembly spend $11.3 million, compared with $7.6 million for Democrats.
âThe right wing has been at this for more than 50 years,â said Mandara Meyers, the States Projectâs executive director. âThey have entrenched advantages and GOP megadonors are still pouring millions into individual races.â

86a520f634a2.text: Data: PRRI, 2026 American Values Survey ; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios White evangelical Protestants are the only major religious group in which a majority says empathy can become dangerous when it leads people away from a society guided by God's truth, according to a new survey . Why it matters : The survey lands amid a quiet civil war within American Christianity over who deserves empathy. Conservatives ranging from evangelical pastors to Elon Musk have framed empathy as a vulnerability in debates over immigration , racial justice and LGBTQ+ rights . In a February 2025 interview with Joe Rogan, Musk called empathy "the fundamental weakness of Western civilization," while acknowledging its potential good and warning against its weaponization. By the numbers: The annual American Values Survey from the nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute (PRRI) released Tuesday found that 42% of white evangelical Protestants agreed that empathy is a foundational moral value that helps build a healthy society. Separately, 54% agreed that empathy can become dangerous when it leads people away from a society guided by God's truth. In every other religious group, PRRI found that at least 66% agreed with the foundational-value statement, including 73% of white mainline Protestants and Hispanic Catholics. Empathy's foundational value was endorsed by 83% of religiously unaffiliated Americans, 80% of respondents grouped under other non-Christian religions, 77% of Jewish Americans and 65% of Latter-day Saints. The intrigue: The survey found a 30-point partisan gap: 84% of Democrats agreed with the foundational-value statement, compared with 54% of Republicans. Independents were at 70%. White evangelicals stand out among religious groups, but PRRI reports religious and partisan results separately. The survey doesn't establish how much white evangelicals contribute to the Republican-Democratic gap. Zoom in: The divide also tracks with PRRI's Christian nationalism measure. Among people PRRI classifies as Christian nationalism adherents, 38% agreed that empathy is foundational, compared with 94% of rejecters. PRRI classifies respondents as Christian nationalist adherents or sympathizers based on support for a U.S. government and laws grounded in Christianity and the view that Christians should exercise dominion over society. Six in 10 adherents agreed that empathy can become dangerous, compared with 6% of rejecters. What they're saying: "As Christian nationalist leaders attack the sentiment of empathy, a disturbing 'empathy gap' has opened, separating Republicans and white evangelicals from most other Americans," PRRI President and Founder Robert P. Jones said in a statement. Jones said the findings raise questions about the moral foundations that let people from different backgrounds share a democracy. Methodology: PRRI conducted the American Values Survey online Aug. 20–Sept. 7, 2026, among 5,200 adults in Ipsos' KnowledgePanel and 339 additional adults recruited through opt-in panels to increase sample sizes in smaller states. The survey covered adults ages 18 and older in all 50 states and the District of Columbia. The margin of sampling error is ±1.6 percentage points at the 95% confidence level for results based on the entire sample.

f2885070c43f.text: House Republicans are quietly scaling back hopes for the 10-seat boost they sought from redistricting nationwide, amid a souring political climate and polls showing a collapse in GOP support among Latino voters in Texas and Florida . Why it matters: On their down days, Republicans privately worry that the great redistricting war of 2026 will net them only one seat nationwide, according to top GOP strategists. Zoom out: At the beginning of the cycle, Republicans viewed redistricting like an umbrella in a storm: It could keep their House majority dry in a light drizzle — but in a political hurricane, it wouldn't be enough. They're not second-guessing the redistricting strategy, even as they wince at the price tag. According to AdImpact, Republicans have spent $133 million on TV ads trying to win in 15 redrawn districts that were supposed to be easy pickings. Still, they no longer talk seriously about redistricting saving their House majority, as they did a year ago — before the Iran war helped boost inflation and sink President Trump's approval ratings. By the numbers: Early this summer, Republicans believed they had created 16 more GOP-friendly seats: five in Texas , four in Florida , two in Ohio and one each in Alabama , Louisiana , Missouri , North Carolina and Tennessee . But since then, courts tossed a Missouri map and the political environment has darkened, with Democrats holding an 8-percentage-point lead in new Washington Post-ABC polling . GOP support has eroded particularly among Latino voters , raising Republican fears of losing seats their mapmakers counted on after Trump nearly won the Hispanic vote outright in 2024. "Texas, I'd be surprised if we got all five," Rep. Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) told Axios this month. "Florida, I'd be shocked if we got all four." The other side: Then factor in California , where Gov. Gavin Newsom, eager to show his party he was willing to fight back, engineered a new map with four more solidly Democratic seats — and one slightly more competitive seat. Democrats are supremely confident they can win all five — and their main super PAC has already stopped super PAC spending in one. Zoom in: So, two weeks before the Nov. 3 election, Republicans are squinting at the map and expecting to win 7 to 12 of the 15 remaining seats they redistricted. The breakdown: GOP strategists privately think Republicans can still win 2 to 4 of the 5 seats that were redrawn in Texas, and 2 (maybe 3) of the 4 new seats in Florida. They could go 0 for 2 in the redrawn seats in Ohio. The revamped seat in North Carolina is a jump ball. They're banking on winning all three new seats in Tennessee, Alabama and Louisiana. Under their most pessimistic calculations, Republicans worry their mid-cycle redistricting wave could yield just 7 new seats in red states. But then factor in Newsom's countermove in California, which put Democrats in a strong position to flip 5 seats. And in Utah, a judge forced the state to redraw its districts, obliterating a GOP-friendly seat — and creating a Democratic-leaning one in the Salt Lake City area. So as it stands now, a worst-case scenario for the GOP's final score after all that redistricting: Republicans gain 7 seats and Democrats gain 6. A year of nationwide redistricting to net one Republican seat. The details: Republicans are confident about three pickups in Southern states, where the Supreme Court's Voting Rights Act decision allowed GOP legislatures to redraw maps. They have already conceded one redrawn seat in Ohio as part of their midterm triage . Then there's Texas. Republicans are truly confident about just two of the five seats they redrew: The 9th District in the Houston area and the 32nd District in the Dallas area. The main Republican House super PAC has pulled out of Texas' 28th District in South Texas, essentially conceding the seat held by Rep. Henry Cuellar (D). It was rejiggered from a district that Trump won by 7.3 points in 2024 to one he would have won by 10.4 points. In Texas' 34th District , which touches the Rio Grande Valley and was similarly redrawn to include more Republicans, parties are spending roughly $18 million on TV ads. Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez had a small lead over Republican Eric Flores in the latest NYT/Sienna poll . And in Texas' 35th District in Central Texas, which went from one that Kamala Harris won by 33.7 points to one that Trump would have won by 10.4 points, both parties have spent close to $6 million, according to AdImpact. It's too close to call. The bottom line: In a true blue wave, Republicans could lose seats Trump won by double digits. But in that scenario, Republicans would be unlikely to blame their losses on redistricting. They'd point the finger at Trump.

Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., is one of three House Democrats who have yet to pay their DCCC dues in full despite plans to return to top committee jobs next year, according to a draft of the DCCCâs September dues report seen by Semafor.
The document, which is not final, only reflects dues paid through last month; Waters has paid $450,000 in dues to date, or about two-thirds of her goal, rather than the reportâs $200,000, a person familiar told Semafor, which will be reflected in the DCCCâs October dues report.
Other committee ranking members lagging on the goal, according to the September draft: The top Democrats on the House Administration and Ethics committees â Reps. Joe Morelle of New York and Mark Desaulnier of California, respectively.
Outgoing ranking members Angie Craig of Minnesota and Nydia VelÃ¡zquez of New York are also behind, though retiring members and frontliners generally donât pay dues in full.
A person familiar with DeSaulnierâs thinking said he always paid his dues in full and intends to continue to do so.
House Democrats are considering rules changes to mandate dues payments to serve on committees like Appropriations and Financial Services. The clashes over dues are a perennial issue among House Democrats that has animated previous challenges to gavels, but theyâve taken on increased importance as Democrats try to flip the House. And with House races becoming more expensive, some in the party think the dues issue will resonate with the caucus.
Virginia Rep. Bobby Scott, the top Education and Workforce Committee Democrat who is facing a competitive race, has paid his dues in full.

20704f9eec50.text: Data: Office of Management and Budget via Fred , U.S. Treasury; Note: 2026 GDP estimated using extrapolated Q3 growth via CFRB; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios The U.S. budget deficit is ballooning, reaching $2 trillion this fiscal year, according to the latest figures. Why it matters: That's the largest deficit since 2021, when the U.S. was climbing out of the pandemic recession. The deficit is being driven in part by the cost of servicing the nation's enormous debt at a time when interest rates are rising due, in part, to the inflationary impact of the Iran war. By the numbers: The federal government paid out $1.052 trillion in net interest on its outstanding debt — all those Treasury notes and bonds we keep writing about — for the 2026 fiscal year, which ended Sept. 30, according to the Treasury data. That's more than what was spent on defense, and was the country's third-biggest outlay after Social Security ($1.67 trillion) and Medicare ($1.07 trillion). Stunning stat: Federal net interest costs in 2026 are estimated at 3.3% of GDP, which would be a record high, according to an estimate from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. Between the lines: This is the price tag for years of borrowing at much higher interest rates — a sort of new normal since inflation started rising in 2021. Rising interest costs add to the deficit, driving still more borrowing and putting additional pressure on the federal budget. The intrigue: The last time interest costs approached these levels was when President George H.W. Bush was in office. At the time, the administration negotiated a bipartisan deficit reduction package that raised taxes, breaking President Bush's infamous "Read my lips, no new taxes" pledge and arguably led to him losing re-election. Still, in the 1990s, the Clinton administration and Congress worked to balance the budget through tax increases and spending cuts. What to watch: There's little appetite for that kind of work from either party, but the so-called bond vigilantes might still press for it.

The US isnât the only country struggling with a slice of the electorate that lacks confidence in its domestic elections.
Ahead of an Oct. 27 vote that will decide Israelâs future leadership, Israelisâ confidence in their elections sits at an eight-year low, according to new Gallup polling that found 56% have faith in the integrity of the vote. Thatâs down from a high of 71% in 2023, following the Oct. 7 attacks by Hamas.
Thereâs a huge confidence chasm between those who approve of the countryâs leadership under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and those who donât â just 37% of the latter have faith in the vote.
President Donald Trump has endorsed Netanyahu in his reelection bid (though his vice president, notably, has not), but fewer Israelis are pleased with him: Sixty-two percent of Israelis now say they currently approve of US leadership, down 14 points from last year.

The News
The debate around the contours of an acceptable federal AI safety bill shifted again after a draft of a proposal Anthropic has been pitching to lawmakers on Capitol Hill leaked late last week.
Anthropic, long seen as the safety-promoting frontier lab, found itself on the defensive, with one of its top lobbyists posting about tweaks it plans to make to the draft that more accurately reflect the dizzying pace of AI progress and the companyâs stance on pre-empting state laws.
That draft bill is a legislative version of an AI safety framework the company has been pitching for months, a company spokesperson told Semafor. However, AI safety advocates are arguing it doesnât go nearly far enough, unfairly pre-empts state laws, and accepts too much possible risk.
OpenAI quickly saw an opportunity to distinguish itself from its rival, with Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane writing in a post Monday implicitly directed at Anthropic: âPolicy decisions must ultimately be made through our democratic processes with our elected officials leading. â¦ No one company (including OpenAI) should write the rules alone for a technology with such profound implications for our economy, society and national security.â
Ashleyâs view
Over the past few years, Anthropic has embraced regulation in a way that other AI companies havenât. As the frightening possibilities of its advanced AI have emerged â and as its fight with the US government has brewed â the company has started to seek regulation through methods that have promoted heated debate within the federal government (like pitching the terms that would allow officials to block the release of certain models).
OpenAI has generally been a savvier, subtler Washington player, wanting to be seen as ready to endorse compromise federal AI bills written by lawmakers, as it pursues a strategy across the states of encouraging similar frameworks it finds acceptable.

If Sherrod Brown wins his Senate race, Ohioâs delegation will be the most awkward in the chamber next Congress.
Brown would have to serve with Republican Bernie Moreno, who defeated Brown in 2024 â and would likely become the leading tactician in charge of toppling the Democrat again in 2028. Thatâs thanks to a quirk in the Senate cycle math: Brown would have to run again for his seat in two years, against a National Republican Senatorial Committee that Moreno is likely to take over for the 2028 campaign.
Moreno told Semafor that the theoretical matchup âwonât happen,â predicting that incumbent GOP Sen. Jon Husted will win. But he joked it would be âtemptingâ to defeat Brown again: âSherrod Brown should just get a job.â
Brown and Moreno never spoke after Morenoâs 2024 win, according to a person familiar with the matter. They also never debated.
The Brown campaign declined to comment. A Brown-Moreno delegation would be even more dramatic than the 2024 rivalry between then-Sen. Jon Tester, D-Mont., and then-NRSC Chair Steve Daines, who successfully unseated him.

8b782dac0909.text:
Democrats Demand Tougher Standards for Companies Running Medicaid Systems
A group of Democratic senators is demanding that the federal agency overseeing Medicaid — the health coverage program for people with low incomes or disabilities — institute tougher standards for government contractors running complex computer systems that millions of people rely on to get benefits.
Three Democratic senators issued recommendations a year after launching an inquiry into companies — Deloitte, General Dynamics Information Technology, Gainwell Technologies, and Conduent — that are paid billions in taxpayer dollars to build or run eligibility systems for safety net health coverage. Those benefits, provided to the poorest Americans, can mean the difference between having medical care or going without.
A handful of states directly operate their Medicaid eligibility systems, but most rely on contractors to build and run them. KFF Health News found that Deloitte dominates this slice of government business. Deloitte-run systems have been plagued by errors that can result in eligible people losing their health coverage, previous KFF Health News investigations have shown. Malfunctions can cost millions of taxpayer dollars and take years to fix.
“Administrative errors in this line of work are not like errors in other fields,” the senators wrote in a new report. “There are life-and-death consequences for sick Americans who seek care only to find that their Medicaid coverage has been terminated.”
President Donald Trump’s signature tax and domestic policy law has mandated Medicaid changes that are forcing states to adapt their computer systems on a compressed timeline. Medicaid policies under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act add red tape and restrictions that make it harder for people to stay enrolled.
Those include the first federally mandated work requirements in Medicaid’s history. Next year, to keep benefits, millions of adult Medicaid enrollees in more than 40 states must prove they’re working or doing a similar activity for at least 80 hours a month, unless they qualify for an exemption.
Democratic senators Ron Wyden of Oregon, Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, and Raphael Warnock of Georgia say the new restrictions — layered atop computer systems with histories of problems — will result in large numbers of people improperly losing health coverage.
State eligibility systems “have been built up, patched, and frankensteined for decades,” the senators said.
The senators sit on the powerful Senate Finance Committee, which oversees government health programs such as Medicare and Medicaid. Many of their recommendations target the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Their ideas face long odds at the moment. Republicans control executive branch agencies, and any potential legislation would need to advance in a Republican-controlled Congress.
That balance of power could shift if Democrats win a majority of Senate seats in November’s midterm elections. The three lawmakers called on CMS to establish mandatory standards in state contracts with companies so states can receive federal funds.
These companies sign contracts with state governments, but the federal government approves them and pays the bulk of the cost. The federal government covers 90% of state costs to develop and implement state Medicaid eligibility systems and 75% of ongoing maintenance and operations expenses, according to federal regulations.
The lawmakers also said CMS should publicize the contracts and contract amendments. Currently, those documents can be obtained from state governments, but accessibility varies significantly.
The senators also said CMS should publicly disclose companies’ performance data and change orders. Change orders are used to adjust computer systems, and states set aside millions of dollars for them. But systems may require fixes beyond the agreed-upon work.
“The millions of Medicaid enrollees who will be required to prove their eligibility every six months, to document every hour of work on a glitchy portal, to find a doctor willing to certify that their cancer or their chronic condition is bad enough to qualify for an exemption — deserve contractors who are accountable for what happens when the system fails them,” they wrote.
In October 2025, the three Democratic senators, as well as Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), sent letters to several companies that CMS identified as eligibility system contractors. At the time, they wrote that it is each company’s responsibility to build functioning eligibility systems, “rather than to prioritize their bottom line.”
As of June, 66 million people were enrolled in Medicaid, according to CMS.
The lawmakers had asked the companies about their contracts, lobbying expenditures, and protocols for making changes in light of system errors, among other issues. The companies provided the lawmakers with some details but often did not answer their questions.
The companies said states are responsible for making the final call on whether a person receives benefits. State workers approve or deny eligibility, Deloitte said in its response letter, “not a private contractor or an automated system acting alone.”
The companies did not provide the senators with specific details about documents or processes they use to help states make eligibility determinations.
The companies also denied they have any financial incentives to remove people from Medicaid. Conduent said it gets paid less if enrollment drops.
The companies did not say whether states are on the hook for paying to fix the companies’ errors.
Deloitte, Gainwell, GDIT, and Conduent said it’s common for states to require that they meet certain performance metrics.
Gainwell told lawmakers, “We take seriously the issues raised.” GDIT said it would answer additional questions from lawmakers.
Deloitte said in its response to the lawmakers: “We are proud of our work serving individuals and families across the U.S.”

99fe5837d642.text: Silicon Valley moves fast and breaks things, but the U.S. electrical grid moves slowly and requires permits. The explosive growth of AI is colliding with the glacial pace of building out new power infrastructure, prompting a new warning from Goldman Sachs that energy bottlenecks are set to stall the AI race. Why it matters : Amid a wave of anxiety from Wall Street about the debt-fueled AI buildout, Goldman points to power as the biggest risk to trillions in spending in a new report shared exclusively with Axios. Driving the news: Goldman expects global data center power demand to surge 170% between 2025 and 2030, with more than 60% of that growth coming from the U.S., according to the report . "Power is probably the forever bottleneck," Jason Tofsky, Goldman's global head of digital infrastructure investment banking, noted in the report. The bank estimates roughly $7.6 trillion in capital spending between 2026 and 2031 across computing, data centers and power infrastructure. Zoom in: The physical infrastructure needed to support AI is moving far more slowly than the technology itself. The U.S. has roughly 2,600 gigawatts of proposed power generation and storage projects awaiting grid connections, more than twice the grid's existing installed capacity, though many projects may never materialize. The median time from an application for a grid connection to commercial operation is roughly five years. Between the lines: The so-called AI race, which has long been defined by advances in frontier AI models, is really about who can get their hands on enough power, Goldman argues. That could mean a longer, less predictable buildout, delayed financial returns and greater risks for companies investing heavily before securing power. Follow the money: The massive expansion is being financed with debt, raising the stakes if construction timelines slip. Goldman projects $420 billion in global hyperscaler debt issuance in 2027, up more than 60% from its 2026 estimate. Debt is expected to finance roughly 35% of hyperscaler capital expenditures next year. And hyperscalers account for just 40% of AI ecosystem credit fundraising, underscoring how widely the borrowing extends. The intrigue: Since January, 86 projects have been canceled or significantly delayed, including 76 directly linked to local opposition, according to Goldman. Put together, this paints a picture of extended delays. Yes, but : Slower deployment could also help prevent over-investment by giving actual demand time to catch up with spending. Meanwhile: The boom is transforming utilities from traditionally slow-growing businesses into major beneficiaries of AI investment. Utility capital plans are expected to reach $1.3 trillion between 2026 and 2030. Tech giants are considering arrangements to directly fund the power generation, transmission lines and electrical infrastructure their data centers require. The bottom line: If you build AI systems, users will come, but they can only stay if there's enough power to go around.

df7a2b02644c.text: Let's call it the Battle of the Bots, part 1: I decided to put two of the newest personal AI agents, OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse , through their paces, with the WNBA Finals providing a natural testing ground. Why it matters: AI companies are racing to create the digital assistant we turn to for everything from shopping to travel planning. But there's still a gap between what these agents can do and what I'm comfortable letting them do. They also need to pass what we'll call "The Human Benchmark" : that is, can they do something as fast, or as well, as a human? The answer is ... not quite yet, but the capabilities are still impressive. The big picture: For the test, I asked each assistant to plan a fantasy trip to Atlanta to see my beloved Golden State Valkyries, organize a purple-themed brunch watch party and create souvenir programs. I also had them help me shop for Valkyries merch, which eventually turned into a side quest for WNBA basketball cards. The cost: Muse is free for most uses, with optional $20 and $100 monthly subscriptions. Dots requires a ChatGPT Pro subscription, starting at $100 monthly, or access through a business or enterprise plan. More on Dots . Where they shined: Both agents were surprisingly good at handling complicated, multistep assignments. When I asked them to find flights and tickets for Game 3 in Atlanta, both caught that the game had been moved up a day and that tickets weren't yet on sale to the general public. The available seats were being offered through the resale market, likely at inflated prices. Both found good flight options. Muse opened a browser and let me enter my information to try to sign up for a ticket presale. Dots, meanwhile, flagged a scheduling conflict with an enrollment fair, which it gleaned from my AI-assisted effort to keep tabs on the joys of finding the right high school in San Francisco. Where they were creative, but imperfect: Both agents could turn broad instructions into surprisingly elaborate finished products, though neither was quite ready to replace a human editor. For my purple-themed brunch, Muse designed a colorful 10-page recipe booklet featuring ube waffles and lavender-honey butter. Dots produced a more practical eight-page packet with detailed cooking instructions and attention to dietary preferences. Muse's shopping list called for 12 eggs, while its recipes required 13. Both agents also designed invitations that needed aesthetic and language edits before I'd send them to friends. Both menus were far more elaborate than anything I'd actually make for a basketball watch party. Left to my own devices, I'd probably just buy some purple-frosted donuts. Another creative test: I asked both agents to create a 1980s-style WNBA Finals souvenir program, then later to turn my photos from Game 1 into a keepsake. Dots' 38-page vintage program was more visually engaging, with player photos, graphics and extensive statistics. Muse's 35-page version was less attractive but had some fun touches, including a fictional computer ad and an advertisement for my imaginary brunch. Both programs contained questionable statistics. Muse later sent an unsolicited update correcting several factual errors. For the photo program, Dots delivered a 12-page version in just 47 seconds, while Muse took considerably longer. It did, however, suggest an interesting photo spread highlighting different generations of Valkyries fans. Where they struggled: Actually doing things. I asked both agents to help me buy Valkyries merchandise, eventually settling on WNBA trading cards. Both helped compare options and prices. I chose Target, where my store credit card offered a 5% discount and free shipping. Muse attempted to complete the purchase but got stuck at Target's sign-in page. Dots instead directed me to the Target app, where my account and payment information were already saved. Dots' less automated approach turned out to be faster, even though both services support purchases with user approval. The trust problem: Both agents could have done more if I'd been willing to give them greater access to my accounts and wallet. I'm not yet comfortable authorizing purchases of hundreds or thousands of dollars, or at a point of trusting them enough for consequential decisions. The bottom line: For me, the sweet spot for these agents is doing the research and legwork while leaving me to make the final decisions. P.S.: I couldn't actually make the Atlanta trip or host the brunch because of other commitments. But I did end up buying three boxes of WNBA basketball cards. You know, for research.

20f2dbda52e0.text:
For nearly three years, Jonathan Bledsoe of Reading, Pennsylvania, took one prescription to stabilize his mood and one to keep his cholesterol in check, among a handful of other medications.
“You wouldn’t think you would have to be your own advocate and look out for yourself as far as managing your medications,” the Marine veteran said. “But when you wake up one morning and what you pee comes out the color of fresh brewed coffee, there’s an issue.”
He took his concerning symptoms back to his multiple doctors and learned the interaction between his medications was starting to damage his liver. After he changed medications, his liver and kidney function returned to normal.
Adverse drug interactions are becoming a bigger health concern as more people take multiple medications, said Amanda Mixon, a hospitalist and associate professor of bioinformatics at Vanderbilt University.
The percentage of Americans over 65 taking five or more medications, known as polypharmacy, nearly doubled from 2000 to 2020, according to a study published in JAMA Internal Medicine. Now, more than a third of older adults are taking five or more medications a day.
Mixon said she sees older patients with an average of 16 medications, often from multiple prescribers and pharmacies.
“As you accumulate more and more medications, the chance of them interacting with each other and having bad interactions increases,” Mixon said. “As these medications get added sort of progressively, that can accumulate over time, and then people are having more side effects.”
The QTip:
If you’re taking medications and supplements, keep your own up-to-date list and have it with you.
If you’re concerned about your medications, here’s what to know:
There’s No ‘Unicorn Pharmacist’
Sometimes, a medication intended to treat one issue leads to many more, known as a “prescribing cascade”: A prescription for the initial symptom causes a side effect, then that side effect needs to be treated. Eventually, the combination of meds may cause other issues that require yet another medication.
For instance, Mixon said, heart failure patients take a water pill to reduce fluid retention. As a result, the constant need to urinate can lead to incontinence, which is treated by another medication.
“We do an amazing job of treating. We are great at diagnosing, and medicines have an amazing role in increasing our longevity as humans,” said pharmacist DeLon Canterbury. He’s the CEO of the North Carolina-based consulting company GeriatRx, which focuses on helping patients get off unnecessary medications. “It’s not the intent of our providers to overtreat. It’s just what we’ve been trained to do.”
When multiple prescribers are involved, they may not be aware of the patient’s other medications, he said, especially if the health providers are affiliated with different health systems that have separate patient records.
“Do not assume that someone is checking all of these things in the background. There isn’t this magical unicorn pharmacist just making sure everything is safe. Yes, even at the local pharmacy,” Canterbury said. “So make sure, if you notice something is off, that you advocate for yourself.”
A Shift Toward ‘Deprescribing’
“Deprescribing,” the process of intentionally tapering off medications, has gained more momentum in the past decade, alongside the corresponding rise of polypharmacy and the associated health risks.
The science on how to taper patients safely is newer and still not widely taught in medical schools, Canterbury said.
He said patients who are worried about taking multiple medications — especially people experiencing a new symptom or an unexpected side effect — should start a conversation about deprescribing with their specialists or primary care providers.
“I promise you, they don’t bite,” he said. “Because you’ll be surprised that the more you bring up stopping a medication, the more willing they are to actually have that dialogue and help you get off of it if you don’t need it.”
The goal isn’t kicking as many meds as possible, Canterbury said — it’s patient safety. With age, bodies metabolize medications differently, he said, increasing the likelihood of harmful side effects like constipation, diarrhea, falls, and memory loss.
Keep a Medication List
Many pharmacists and doctors agree on the value of keeping an updated medication list, including the vitamins and supplements you’re taking. While there are QR code bracelets and medication tracking apps, sometimes the easiest strategy is an old-fashioned piece of paper.
“Everyone needs a medication list in their pocket,” said pharmacist Jen Hammons, director of rural health advancement at the Appalachian College of Pharmacy in Virginia. “If you can’t commit it to memory, you need to have a list.”
People and Policy
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has championed weaning Americans off psychiatric medications that he says are overused, a stance that has polarized the medical community. This year, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services released guidance that clarifies how physicians and pharmacists can be paid for their work reviewing medications and helping patients taper off when appropriate. Previously, physicians reported uncertainty over whether they could get paid for deprescribing, which can be a time-intensive process.
Katherine Ruppelt and Emily Siner at Nashville Public Radio contributed to this report.
HealthQ is a health series from reporters Cara Anthony and Blake Farmer, approachable guides to an unapproachable healthcare system. It’s a collaboration between Nashville Public Radio and KFF Health News.

06bc9a9c9962.text:
As Politicians Argue About China, US Patients Find Cutting-Edge Treatment There
Until recently, a Manhattanite might venture no more than a few dozen blocks to find the world’s most sophisticated cancer treatment. Cutting-edge American medicines have helped reduce the U.S. cancer death rate by about a third since 1990, and New York City hospitals deliver some of the best care in the country.
But in January 2025, the city’s health systems had no good options for Debbie Doppelt, a 60-year-old jeweler with an unusual form of lung cancer that mostly afflicts nonsmokers like her. The Food and Drug Administration hadn’t yet approved sunvozertinib, a drug developed in China that targets the mutation driving Doppelt’s tumors. She had been through chemotherapy and surgery, but the cancer had now spread to her brain. And she didn’t qualify for the relevant clinical trials.
Then an option emerged, in an offhand remark.
“Too bad she’s not Chinese,” a doctor told her son Max Doppelt, who had organized his mother’s care since her 2023 diagnosis. “She could go to a pharmacy in China and buy it.”
Within hours, mother and son had reached out to friends and relatives, one of whom procured a small supply of sunvozertinib from a contact living in China. A few months later, Max flew to Shanghai to get a refill.
Other patients have followed. “No organization or doctor is guiding patients to China, but word gets out,” Max said. He said he knows of at least 30 Americans who’ve made the pilgrimage to obtain the drug, which the FDA licensed in July 2025 but wasn’t yet on the U.S. market as of mid-October of this year.
Sunvozertinib, made by Shanghai-based Dizal Pharmaceutical, isn’t the only treatment drawing patients to China. Americans, Europeans, and others are trekking there to enter clinical trials for CAR-T therapy, an area in which China is now a world leader.
China, until recently known more as a supplier of drug precursor chemicals and generic medicines, has become a biotech powerhouse, accounting for as much as 46% of new drugs tested around the world in 2025. U.S. pharmaceutical companies are testing new therapies there and signing billion-dollar contracts with Chinese firms to develop and market their drugs.
China’s progress has alarmed some politicians, who warn of lost jobs and U.S. dependency on Chinese medicines. The Trump administration in June kicked off Operation TrialBlazer, aimed at speeding up some FDA regulatory processes to lure back more clinical trials.
China’s poor showing in vaccine and drug development during the covid pandemic prompted the country to overhaul its biotech sector, dramatically altering the global industry, said Sam Rasty, a veteran of small biotech companies who now leads one called FynderBio. Venture capital now flows heavily to early-stage clinical work in China and Australia, where regulatory systems enable key first-in-human studies much more quickly than in the United States.
Chinese companies are so much faster at this process that U.S. biotechs, which used to share early advances at conferences or funding meetings, now routinely conceal their progress out of fear that competitors will take their ideas and speed them to market, said Steve Potts, CEO of Breakthru Medicine, a small biotech.
At a meeting he attended in May, nearly all the 60 biotech CEOs in the room planned to run phase 1 trials in Australia, Europe, or China, Potts said. Five or 10 years ago, most of those trials would have been carried out in the U.S.
“Slow and prohibitive” FDA requirements are driving investment to more-nimble Chinese companies, President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the agency, Heidi Overton, warned in her opening statement at her Sept. 24 confirmation hearing.
The movement of clinical trials overseas “should give pause to every American and those who serve on their behalf,” Overton said. “When we lose this advantage, we lose our health security. And when we lose our health security, we lose everything.”
Overton pledged to continue TrialBlazer, which mirrors Australian processes begun in 1991. It is aimed at accelerating clinical trials and approvals so patients do not feel compelled to seek treatment abroad, said Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson Emily Hilliard. It is sometimes legal to obtain medication abroad for personal use, but the FDA “cautions patients about potential safety and quality risks associated with treatments outside our regulatory system,” she added.
As the FDA moves to streamline drug development, members of Congress are trying to slow Chinese firms’ integration into U.S. biotech.
Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), who chairs the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, in June co-sponsored legislation with Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) requiring all U.S. pharmaceutical deals with Chinese companies to be cleared by the Treasury Department.
Others see biotech protectionism as misguided. China’s focus on improved medicines can only help us, said Peter Kolchinsky, managing partner of RA Capital Management, which has Chinese investments in its biotech portfolio.
“We may be adversaries in many areas, but we’re not competing with them to cure cancer. We are collaborating with them to cure cancer,” he said. “There are things that are bigger enemies than any other nation on Earth.”
Cancer Knows No Boundaries
A minor but persistent cough led to the diagnosis of Debbie Doppelt’s cancer in late 2023. Chemo, immunotherapy, and surgery kept it at bay for months, but in December 2024, scans showed the cancer had spread to her brain, with 10 tiny tumors.
The FDA earlier that year had approved amivantamab, a drug that targeted the mutation driving Doppelt’s tumor, but Max was concerned about its toxicity. Also, several doctors he consulted told him that amivantamab might not penetrate brain tissue to fight cancer there.
Doppelt tried to enter a clinical trial at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, where she was a patient, for zipalertinib,

Federal lawmakers want to ban imports of wild sloths to the United States, a move experts say could have global implications for the conservation of the tree-dwelling species.
Maxwell Alejandro Frost (D-Fla.) is set on Tuesday to introduce a bill, co-sponsored by Laurel Lee (R-Fla.), known as the “SLOTHS Act”—Stopping Legalized Organized Trafficking and Harm to Sloths. It’s a reaction to mass sloth deaths at a planned attraction in Orlando.
An Inside Climate News investigation in April revealed that 31 sloths imported from the forests of South America died between late 2024 and early 2025 at the now-shuttered Sloth World, which planned to offer a $49 animal encounter experience along a busy tourist strip.
Additional government records obtained by Inside Climate News show that more than 50 sloths ultimately died—primarily due to stress and illness—at Sloth World. The business never opened to the public.
“It’s really about preventing something like Sloth World from happening again. Because I promise you this: This type of stuff is happening everywhere, all the time,” Frost said in an interview with Inside Climate News. “It’s not just a Florida problem, it’s a national problem.”
Sloth World sparked outrage around the world. Florida regulators quickly imposed a two-month ban on sloth imports into the state and recently proposed new rules to strengthen protections for the animals.
However, a separate Inside Climate News investigation found that Florida regulators were aware of sloth deaths at the facility since at least August 2025 but saw no need to intervene even as the toll climbed. And an investigation from the Orange County Sheriff’s Office concluded that no crime occurred at the facility.
“We haven’t really seen anything of substance happen,” Frost said. Sloth World’s owner “should have been held accountable, and the fact of the matter is, he wasn’t.”
Sloth World owner Benjamin Agresta previously denied that he intentionally mistreated or neglected animals. He also called reports of sloth deaths “completely fiction” just before Inside Climate News published state records confirming dozens had died at his business.
Now, Frost and Lee hope their bill will prevent sloths from ever being put into this situation.
“Nowhere was there a clear cut, obvious prohibition on this type of commercial activity and the commercial capture and sale of sloths, and that’s the number one thing that we really wanted to crack down on,” Lee said in an interview.
Violators of the proposed law would face steep penalties, including a possible criminal fine of up to $100,000 and loss of federal import licenses. Sloth scientist Rebecca Cliffe and Sam Trull, co-founder of the Costa Rica-based Sloth Institute, worked with lawmakers on the proposal. Both women had called on state and federal authorities to intervene at Sloth World months before Florida officials announced a criminal investigation in May.
Cliffe and Trull said the bill could fundamentally reshape the U.S. roadside zoo and sloth industry because it would effectively cut off the supply of wild sloths to U.S. businesses that market hands-on encounters, photo ops and other exhibits. Only sloths already in captivity, and their offspring, could remain in commercial businesses or zoos. Between 2011 and 2021, people imported more than 1,100 live sloths into the United States, according to federal records.
“If we want to stop this permanently, like really cut off this sort of activity at its knees, then we’ve got to stop the sloths from being brought into the country,” said Cliffe, who is also the founder of The Sloth Conservation Foundation, based in Costa Rica.
She and Trull say the wildlife trade, which removes wild sloths from the tropical rainforests of South and Central America and ships them to zoos and private buyers, including facilities like Sloth World, is inherently cruel. Sloths are deeply sensitive to stress and biologically adapted to mostly solitary life in tree canopies. They lack the typical mammalian flight or fight response, and instead internalize stress, which can ultimately kill them.
Tourists often mistake sloths’ distress for docileness. They’re also psychologically sensitive, with some captive sloths exhibiting what researchers call stereotypic behaviors, such as swaying repeatedly back and forth, similar to the stress behaviors seen in elephants and other zoo animals.

She and Trull are fighting to end the trade on a global scale—starting with the United States.
“It’s really the only way to stop the suffering of sloths in places like Sloth World or other roadside zoos,” Trull said. “We can’t rely on people just not going to these places. … The only way to really stop the suffering is legislation.”
The bill, Trull added, has the potential to act as model legislation for other countries.
The bill includes narrow carve-outs. Under an exception for zoos accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums, facilities could exchange already captive sloths—such as between a U.S. and German zoo—to prevent inbreeding.
A second exception would permit importation of biological samples—such as skin scrapings—for research, but not live animals, so that scientific collaborations aimed at conserving wild sloths can continue.
“We wouldn’t want the import ban to stop important work that’s actually helping sloths in the wild,” Cliffe said.

A suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire over the weekend that broke out during mass disorder, French media report.
The clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall in the central city of Limoges were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.
The 40-year-old suspect is known for acts of violence against public officials and has been classified as an "S" subject, meaning he is a potential threat to national security, FranceInfo reported.
More than 120 people have already been imprisoned following widespread demonstrations across France, French Justice Minister GÃ©rald Darmanin told CNews-Europe.
Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets to protest against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Darmanin said he asked prosecutors to be "extremely firm" and "ruthless towards those who attacked police officers, gendarmes and firefighters, who looted shops and who attacked public buildings".
The justice minister insisted France did not need to be put into a state of emergency which would "deprive all French people of their individual freedoms".
But French Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu earlier said he had not ruled out imposing a state of emergency.
Targeted curfews introduced across France on Monday contributed to a quiet night following the disorder, Lecornu said.
Curfews were introduced across parts of central Paris, including Place de la RÃ©publique, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area.
Other measures restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were introduced in cities such as Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south, as well as Lille and other towns in the north.
Lecornu thanked police officers and gendarmes for enforcing the measures, adding that further curfews on Tuesday night would be decided depending on where they were necessary.
Writing in a post on X, he said decisions would be made "on the ground" by French regions and local mayors.
Earlier Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez admitted police had "lost control" in some cities.
He was strongly criticised by opposition politicians over authorities' preparedness for the disorder, leading him to offer his resignation on Monday, which was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron.
More than 2,500 people have been arrested since the disorder broke out, officials said on Monday. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured.
Protests first began last month with students demanding better school conditions but they have escalated to take in a broader range of concerns with numbers at demonstrations bolstered by trade unions and various protest groups.
More than 2,000 shops and other businesses have been directly impacted by the weekend's violence, the head of France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.
Rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings and looting businesses in Paris, Marseille and other cities and smaller towns.
Protest organisers have declared that a second round of protests will take place on Saturday across France.
The so-called yellow vests (gilets jaunes), who were responsible for France's longest-ever modern protests in 2018, has said "Act II" will take place this weekend.

In the Permian Basin of West Texas, methane gas billows from oil wells. It blasts out of pressure valves on pipelines, wafts from sprawling gas processing plants and rises up in plumes when companies air out systems during routine maintenance in the nation’s largest oilfield.
More than a decade of efforts to bring these practices under control has yielded slim results. The Obama administration proposed methane standards in 2015, but the first Trump administration rolled them back. The Biden administration developed a detailed set of rules, which the second Trump administration blocked.
Now, the Trump administration plans to release its own proposed rules for methane this month, according to a recent announcement by Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin.
Methane, a potent greenhouse gas, continues to flow freely from the Permian Basin and other U.S. oilfields, even as global temperatures break new records.
“Methane emissions are not slowing down,” said Sharon Wilson, an activist in Texas who has documented pollution from oil and gas for more than 20 years. “Nobody ever knows because it’s invisible.”
Wilson uses an optical gas imaging camera, a $50,000 piece of equipment, to visualize gases that the human eye cannot. Methane, the principal component of natural gas, occurs alongside oil underground and comes to the surface through wells. Much of it is captured to burn in power plants or to export overseas as LNG. Plenty, however, is simply released into the air as waste.
“People are totally unaware,” said Wilson, 72.
The founder of a group called Oilfield Witness, she travels the wide, rural expanses of Texas’ oilfields, recording gas releases from industry infrastructure. The largest releases follow blowouts at oil or gas wells, when equipment failures allow methane gas to erupt uncontrolled from the earth.
“There is still no sign that methane emissions from fossil fuel operations are falling, despite well-known and proven mitigation pathways,” said the International Energy Agency’s 2026 global methane tracker.
Wilson regularly records malfunctioning flares—chimneys meant to burn off gas for disposal—spewing invisible, unburned methane. She records tall plumes ejected from compressor stations to relieve pressure on backed-up pipelines. The emissions are almost never reported to state regulators or logged in official datasets.
Sometimes, during widespread disruptions like inclement weather, entire systems spanning hundreds of miles open emergency valves and hatches, letting untold volumes of methane escape—a practice known as venting.
Large methane releases occur constantly in the Permian Basin, said Gunnar Schade, an atmospheric scientist at Texas A&M University who has measured air quality in the area.
“There were methane plumes at all times of day from all directions,” he said. “The density of wells is so high in that area, you will probably not be able to assign that to any particular location.”
In a study published May 2026, Schade identified venting from oil and gas as the largest source of methane emissions.
A Potent Greenhouse Gas
Emissions of methane are the second-largest contributor to global warming, after carbon dioxide.
Methane absorbs more than 80 times as much heat as carbon dioxide on a pound for pound basis over a 20-year period, so relatively small amounts of methane can have outsize climate impacts.      
That’s why scientists years ago identified methane as a priority target in efforts to reduce near-term warming of the Earth.
“Cutting methane is the strongest lever we have to slow climate change over the next 25 years,” said a press release from the U.N. Environment Program in 2021. “We need international cooperation to urgently reduce methane emissions as much as possible this decade.”
So far, that hasn’t happened. Instead, atmospheric concentrations of methane continue to hit record highs. So does global production of coal, oil and gas. Now 2026 appears on track to be the warmest year on Earth since records began.
The livestock industry and landfills make up the largest global source of methane, according to a Global Methane Budget published last year by the European Geosciences Union. Natural emissions from wetlands are the second-largest source.
Fossil fuels, the third largest, account for 20 percent of global methane emissions.
Another EGU study, published this year, evaluated six major oil and gas producing basins of the world, identifying the Permian Basin as the top methane emitter.
A 2026 study published in the journal Environmental Science & Technology estimated Permian Basin methane emissions at 5.1 million metric tons per year. That’s almost 1 percent of total global methane emissions, by some estimates.
In Texas, the vast majority of those releases are never reported to state regulators, according to a March 2026 study by RMI.
The state’s oilfield regulator, the Texas Railroad Commission, “does not rigorously enforce reporting and seems not to test the validity of the gas volumes that are reported,” the report said.
For some companies, releasing methane typically makes more financial sense than capturing it and piping it to markets for sale. When gas prices rise, gas releases fall, according to RMI data.
When gas prices exceed $4 per thermal unit (MMBtu), “it appears to be economically advantageous for operators to sell rather than waste their gas,” said Kevin Gauthier, a geoscience advisor at RMI.
Prices in West Texas have hoovered mostly below that point for the last 15 years, RMI data show.
“Reliable reporting alone is unlikely to change the behavior of operators who are wasting gas and emitting methane,” the RMI report said. “Given the weakness of inherent economic incentives, stringent rules will be required.”

When Israel's far-right National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, reached voting age, he was rejected from Israel's army for being too politically extreme.
His views have not changed much in the 30 years since then - but Israel has. Once shunned by the political establishment, he is now part of the government's inner sanctum of ministers.
On the campaign trail ahead of Israel's general elections next week, Ben Gvir is often surrounded by a jubilant pack of fresh-faced young fans, waving huge party flags over the heads of his numerous security guards.
At the covered market in Ramle - a mixed city of Jewish and Arab Israelis - he told us his message to young voters was to get out and vote.
"We see the support, we see the love [and] we want to win!" he said.
More than half a million first-time voters will cast their ballots in this election, which many Israelis see as existential for Israel's future security and identity.
Polls suggest it will be a tight race, and the new young voters could help decide the result.
More than 16% are planning to support far-right parties - either Ben Gvir's Jewish Power or the Religious Zionism party of his far-right ally Bezalel Smotrich - according to a poll for one of Israel's most popular newspapers, Yedioth Ahronoth.
And almost three-quarters see themselves as "right or centre-right", according to another survey for Israel's leading Channel 12 television network.
"Itamar Ben Gvir gives me a sense of security," said 20-year-old Mordechai, one of the young fans accompanying the politician to Ramle.
"Like everyone in history, from Trump to Moses, there are slips of the tongue that are a bit less good. So what? 90% of the things by Itamar are amazing."
"Itamar will give us safety, and when we go to the army, someone will have our backs and be behind us," said 18-year-old Nadav.
"I think he's trying to show that we're a strong country. For many years, we couldn't show we're strong in our beliefs. We couldn't express our ideology."
Meir Schreiber, an ultra-Orthodox 23-year-old who grew up in London, said the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel, which triggered the Gaza war, also convinced him that Ben Gvir was the right choice.
"Young people understand that peace isn't something we can do," he told me, "because what happens to you when you're young shapes your personality - we saw October 7."
Ben Gvir is a divisive candidate in a divided nation: his political positions include annexation of the occupied West Bank, Jewish settlement of Gaza, and the "voluntary emigration" of Palestinians - positions and rhetoric that are widely condemned by liberal Israelis.
Several Western countries have imposed sanctions or travel bans on Ben Gvir and Smotrich for incitement against Palestinians. Both men are powerful ministers in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's governing coalition.
As he and his entourage pushed their way between the stalls, some shopkeepers threw sweets; others, dark looks.
"I don't like him, he sows discord," one stallholder said. "Ramle is a mixed city - Jews and Arabs. There's no problem here, even after 7 October, but his message preys on young uneducated people."
The fact that he appears more popular with 18 to 22-year-olds than with their parents' generation is often put down, at least partly, to the impact of the 7 October attacks.
But political analyst Dahlia Scheindlin, who previously ran many Israeli political campaigns, said it was more than that.
"For about the last 20 years, we've seen young Israeli Jews are more right wing than average, and significantly more right-wing on many measures than the 55+ group," she told me.
"They have grown up under a series of wars with no personal experience of efforts to achieve peace. But for the most part, they have been socialised into the most extreme terms of the debate [as] legitimate to discuss: annexation, settlement expansion and - after 7 October - annexation of Gaza. And now they're voting for the first time."
A series of classroom debates filmed by Israeli satirist Lior Schleien recently highlighted the extreme views of some young Israelis.
The debates, in which he challenges racist or extreme views, drew a lot of attention in Israel, and included one exchange in which a student advocates killing all Arab citizens of Israel. That particular video has since been removed from Schleien's website.
Surveys suggest that first-time voters here are highly motivated to cast their ballots, with more than 80% saying they are likely to do so. But the same research suggests they are also more sceptical about democratic institutions and less engaged by political protests or petitions.
In a race that is largely deadlocked between two stable blocs of pro-government and anti-government supporters, getting new voters to the polling stations could make all the difference.
Opposition parties have been engaging younger voters with warnings about threats to democracy, new social media videos and younger candidates.
"In 2022 [in the last election], only 59% of the citizens living in Tel Aviv voted - in the most liberal city in the whole Middle East! In places where they voted for Ben Gvir, they voted at around 90%," said Yonatan Shalev, a 24-year-old candidate with the centre-right opposition party, Beyachad ("Together"), led by former prime minister Naftali Bennett.
He told me that Ben Gvir had understood the power of social media faster than other politicians.
"The liberal politicians didn't believe in TikTok, didn't believe in Instagram, and he took advantage of that arena."
Shalev said he had pushed his own party to reach young voters through social media.
"Three months ago, Ben Gvir was still the politician with the most amount of views on TikToks, the most amount of likes on TikTok, and Instagram as well," he explained. "Right now, Naftali Bennett is leading [that]."

It’s been more than three decades since Democrats held a trifecta in Pennsylvania, but the prospect of a blue wave in next month’s elections has Gov. Josh Shapiro and party leadership optimistic that their time could come in Harrisburg.
After flipping the state House of Representatives in 2022, Democrats now have a chance to take advantage of flagging support for President Donald Trump and Shapiro’s positive favorability to gain control of the state Senate for the first time since 1993. If the gridlock breaks, legislators and environmental advocates see an opportunity to advance long-stalled proposals on renewable energy, data centers and greenhouse gas reductions.
“I think of it as a tectonic shift in Pennsylvania environmental politics,” PennEnvironment executive director David Masur said about a potential trifecta. “It’s a generational shift, and it really changes the playing field with the opportunity to move toward a green majority in the legislature.”
For years, Democratic legislators have operated with an “imaginative constraint” because of their inability to move bills through both chambers, said Sen. Nikil Saval, a Democrat from Philadelphia who is a member of the environmental resources and energy committee. If they secure the trifecta, quick action is possible on several House bills that have been blocked by a Republican-controlled Senate for the past four years, addressing solar power, siting reform for energy projects and guard rails for data center development.
Given the recent price hikes ratepayers have seen in their energy bills, offering relief would likely be among Democrats’ first priorities if they control the state government. One in four Pennsylvania families are struggling to pay their energy bills, and one in 20 carries significant utility debt.
“Energy has become a kitchen-table issue,” said Elowyn Corby, senior regional director for the Mid-Atlantic at nonprofit Vote Solar.
In this environment, community solar is the type of “low-hanging fruit” that should quickly move through the legislature, Saval said. Legislation that passed the House with support from more than a dozen Republicans would allow Pennsylvanians to subscribe to a local array and cut costs on their electricity bills. Several neighboring states have already opened the door to the practice.
Similarly, Democrats and advocates point to battery storage as a sensible solution with a clear path to law. Earlier this month the House passed a bill with bipartisan support that would require electric utilities to store energy for use during peak periods to lower overall costs and improve reliability. A proposal to make warehouses solar-ready has also sat in the Senate after clearing the House and could complement other actions on energy policy.
Rep. Elizabeth Fiedler, a Democrat from Philadelphia and chair of the House energy committee and co-sponsor of the battery storage bill, highlighted another idea to lower ratepayers’ bills: her proposal to rein in utilities’ profits by ensuring that their rates of return equal their demonstrated capital costs. That bill passed the House unanimously in June and has been stuck in the Senate since.
“Regardless of the election’s outcome, I believe our mission remains to do everything we can on the energy committee to lower peoples’ utility bills, generate more energy to meet demand, and hold big corporations accountable,” Fiedler said in a statement.
In the interest of energy generation, Rep. Mandy Steele, a Democrat from Allegheny County, has proposed a bill that would prevent municipalities from passing blanket prohibitions against renewable energy projects. This bill could be a “starting point,” Saval said. Pennsylvania is among a small number of states that lack a statewide energy siting policy, making it a target for reform.
“It would lower our energy bills in noticeable ways,” said Alex Bomstein, executive director of nonprofit Clean Air Council. “It would make our air cleaner. It would be a huge deal.”
Democrats could also approach renewable energy by updating the Alternative Energy Portfolio Standard, which sets requirements for the portion of the energy grid composed of renewable energy. Pennsylvania ranks 47th nationally in renewable energy growth, in large part because the standard has “flatlined,” allowing utilities to maintain the status quo, Masur said.
Of course, skyrocketing utility bills are inextricable from the proliferation of power-hungry data centers. There are already 70 in the state, and 93 more projects are proposed, according to the Data Center Tracker, heaping unprecedented demand on a grid already forecast by the Public Utility Commission to face 13 annual outages by 2030. Legislators and advocates said a House-approved proposal to regulate data centers and limit their impact on electricity bills could pass in a Democratic trifecta.
The environmental concerns around data centers go well beyond electricity. Rep. Danielle Friel Otten, Democrat from Chester County, said the Pennsylvania Water Resource Act, which she introduced in May, would be an important companion to any legislation, imposing a fee on users withdrawing more than 10,000 gallons per day.
“There’s an opportunity there to hold these large water users accountable and make it more expensive to do consumptive use in Pennsylvania,” she said.
Data centers are a key issue for Pennsylvania voters. Nearly three-quarters said they would oppose having one built in their community, according to a recent Quinnipiac poll. The stiff public opposition has given rise to calls for a moratorium on new data center construction.
“We should push pause until and unless the industry can show that their negative effects on the environment and public health and our pocketbooks can get resolved,” Masur said.

The Orionid meteor shower, which is capable of producing bright fireball meteors, is set to peak in UK skies this week.
While it has been active for most of October, the celestial spectacle will be at its best in the early hours of October 22.
Clear skies permitting, skygazers could be able to spot as many as 10-20 meteors per hour.
Where the weather is less cooperative, there will still be chances to catch a glimpse of the shower until 7 November.
Where do the Orionids come from and how can I watch them?
The Orionids are an annual meteor shower caused by debris left by Halley's comet in its journey around the Sun.
Every year, Earth passes through the comet dust and the debris burns with the friction caused by the atmosphere, creating a bright streak of light through the sky.
The Orionids are fast and bright, entering our atmosphere with speeds of around 41 miles per second. They can often produce long glowing trails and fireballs.
To spot them, find a dark spot with wide open skies, away from city light pollution and let your eyes adjust to the night sky for 20 minutes.
The meteors are visible to the naked eye so you won't need any specialist equipment like binoculars or a telescope.
The meteors will appear to originate from the constellation of Orion, near the red supergiant star Betelgeuse. This is known as the radiant.
Between midnight and dawn the constellation will climb higher in the sky to the south and then the south-west.
It is best to view the meteors slightly away from the radiant as they will be more visible.
Unfortunately, the Moon will be in the waxing gibbous phase on the night of the 21 October, throwing extra light into the night sky and reducing visibility.
However, conditions will improve once the Moon sets around 03:00 BST on Thursday morning.
What is the forecast for the peak?
Meteor showers are best seen in cloudless skies. Unfortunately for skywatchers, this week looks to be the wettest and windiest week so far this autumn with a strengthening jet stream propelling low pressure systems across the UK.
All is not lost, however.
While Wednesday is looking wet and windy for many parts of the UK, a brief ridge of high pressure could mean that there is a chance of clear spells for many parts of England, Wales and Northern Ireland for the second half of the night into Thursday morning.
There may also be some clear skies for a time for western Scotland.
Eastern Scotland looks cloudy and wet with a lingering front and the far south coast of England could also see outbreaks of rain.
Keep an eye on the latest forecast here or on the BBC Weather app.
