86982b7e6371.text: By — Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press By — Barry Hatton, Associated Press Barry Hatton, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/russian-missile-and-drone-blitz-kills-9-in-ukraine-as-zelenskyy-meets-u-s-and-european-officials-in-norway Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Russian missile and drone blitz kills 9 in Ukraine as Zelenskyy meets U.S. and European officials in Norway World Oct 20, 2026 1:30 PM EDT KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russia unleashed another missile and drone blitz of civilian areas in Ukraine, killing at least nine people, officials said Tuesday, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy sought more American and European help during a visit to Norway. Zelenskyy was joined in Norway by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end the war. Jared Kushner, another envoy who is U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, was due to attend a meeting with Zelenskyy by videoconference. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb were also scheduled to meet with Zelenskyy in Norway's capital. "We are maintaining all contacts that can help bring peace," Zelenskyy said in a post on X after he arrived in Oslo. He said officials gathered in Norway would discuss strengthening Ukraine's air defenses and joint production of weapons. Meanwhile, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Moscow hopes a meeting in Russia between the envoys and Russian President Vladimir Putin can be organized soon, perhaps as early as Wednesday. "We highly appreciate the mediation efforts of the American negotiators," Peskov said. Zelenskyy speaks with Rubio after U.S. support slows With further U.S. support for Ukraine in doubt as relations between Zelenskyy and Trump sour again, the Ukrainian leader said he spoke with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is on a trip to Asia. That conversation came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers Monday that he believes "some political decision has been made to slow down ... support for us." Ukraine has nearly run out of American-made Patriot air-defense interceptors that it needs to stop Russia's ballistic missiles, according to Zelenskyy, who has pleaded for Washington to send more. But he said the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that other countries have purchased for Ukraine. Zelenskyy also said he sought Rubio's help to ensure that the United States continues to share vital intelligence with Ukraine after Kyiv received no or belated warnings about Russian missile attacks in recent days. WATCH: U.S. must put pressure on Russia so Putin ends the war, Ukrainian official says The Ukrainian leader also said speed restrictions were still in place on his country's use of Starshield, the military-grade version of U.S. company SpaceX's satellite internet service Starlink, hampering battlefield operations. Trump also has waived sanctions on Russia, a move that Zelenskyy slammed as helping Putin push on with Moscow's full-scale invasion, which will hit the five-year mark in February. Zelenskyy said he had "a substantive conversation" with Rubio. "I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position," Zelenskyy said on social media. Rubio, who arrived Tuesday in India on an official trip, denied that the U.S. is withholding assistance from Ukraine. "Nothing has changed," he told reporters. The Patriot ammunition Ukraine needs is in short supply and is also required elsewhere in the world, Rubio said. "There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," he said. Europe is helping Ukraine avoid surrender, official says With the Russian army held up on the front line, Putin is trying to bomb Ukraine into submission while robbing it of vital U.S. support, Western leaders and analysts say. European countries, worried about Russia's plans on the continent and viewing Ukraine as a bulwark against Moscow's ambitions, are trying to take up the slack of any falloff in U.S. supplies, but some key assets are American-made. European countries and European Union institutions have allocated 237 billion euros ($266 billion) to support Ukraine, compared with 115 billion euros ($129 billion) from the U.S., according to Germany's Kiel Institute, which tracks assistance to Kyiv. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Tuesday questioned whether U.S. negotiators have been honest brokers in peace efforts. Ukrainian officials say the Trump administration has encouraged Kyiv to surrender land to Russia in return for peace. "Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now," Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin's terms "because Europe has been supporting Ukraine," Kallas said. Russian attacks cause power outages in 12 Ukrainian regions Four people were killed and 27 others wounded, including children, in Russian missile and drone attacks on the Kyiv region over the past day, regional police said. Three were killed and six were wounded in the Obukhiv district, where warehouses were damaged, police said. In the Bucha district, one woman was killed and 21 people were wounded, eight of them children, while hundreds of buildings were damaged, according to police. On Tuesday morning, three people were killed and four injured when two vehicles caught fire in a Russian attack on the Kyiv-Odesa highway, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. The dead included the driver of a shuttle bus that was hit. The bus transports people from Kyiv to the National Military Memorial Cemetery. Two more people were killed in a Russian attack Tuesday on warehouses on the outskirts of Dnipro in central Ukraine, authorities said. 99a5b5cc26d1.text: By — Rod McGuirk, Associated Press Rod McGuirk, Associated Press By — Charlotte Graham-McLay, Associated Press Charlotte Graham-McLay, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/driver-charged-with-intentionally-injuring-australian-federal-lawmaker Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Driver charged with intentionally injuring Australian federal lawmaker World Oct 20, 2026 1:08 PM EDT MELBOURNE, Australia (AP) — Police on Tuesday charged a driver with intentionally causing serious injury to an Australian federal lawmaker who is in critical condition after being struck by a car in an apparent escalation in political violence that has shocked the nation. Helen Haines, a 65-year-old independent politician, was in hospital in critical but stable condition after being struck by a car outside her office in the city of Wangaratta, in Victoria state, on Monday in what police alleged was a "targeted" incident. Brendan Nugent, from nearby Tarrawingee, was charged with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official, police said in a statement on Tuesday. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Suspect to face court on Wednesday Nugent has been in police custody since shortly after Haines was injured and a crowd of bystanders subdued him. He will appear in a Wangaratta court on Wednesday, when he could potentially be released on bail. His father, Rod Nugent, released a statement Tuesday describing Haines as a "deeply respected, valued and much-loved member of our local community." "Helen has been our friend for more than 20 years and what happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable," the father said, adding that he would cooperate with police. The incident shocked Australians as political violence is rare here and politicians have always been accessible to the public. Most lawmakers are not accompanied by security officers and go about their work and personal lives on their own. The prime minister thanks a bystander for intervening Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he phoned local barber Ricky Jefferies, who had run from his store to help members of the public detain the suspect, to thank him on Tuesday for intervening. "It's a reminder that at the worst of times, we see the best of the Australian character," Albanese said in Melbourne. Jefferies earlier told reporters he searched the driver's pockets and removed a knife. Police confirmed a knife had been found. Jefferies also said he did not consider himself a hero. "It was crazy," he said. "A lot of people got involved immediately and they didn't even check for danger. They just ran to help." The lawmaker's family says it's grateful for the 'swift assistance of bystanders' Haines's family released a statement expressing thanks for the "swift assistance of bystanders" as well as health workers and police. Haines, who was first elected to Parliament in 2019 and had been reelected twice since, was initially taken to a hospital in Wangaratta, a city of 30,000 people. She was airlifted later on Monday to a hospital in the state capital, Melbourne, 236 kilometers (147 miles) away. The Alfred Hospital didn't respond Tuesday to a request for comment on media reports that Haines had had a leg amputated. Albanese announced on Monday that the national counterterrorism team was investigating, incorporating police and intelligence agencies. Police have since said the incident appears to be isolated. "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear. We don't know what the motivation is," he said. Recent data has shown that threats of political violence have grown in Australia. The head of the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation spy agency, Mike Burgess, on Tuesday reiterated an earlier warning that politically motivated violence was a top security concern, along with espionage and foreign interference. Police reported in 2025 that threats against parliamentarians had doubled over the past three years. Official data showed more than 1,000 such threats against politicians in the 2025-2026 fiscal year. Military power rising as power of diplomacy falling, diplomats, crisis monitors, allies say
America is abandoning the rules, and the allies, it once kept safe.
DOHA, Qatar–International norms and humanitarian law are losing influence just as new military capabilities are becoming easier to access—a central theme of two days of talks among diplomats, government officials and humanitarian workers here.
“Conflicts are now a first resort in many cases. Diplomacy and dialog are being delegitimized,” said Pierre Krähenbühl, director-general of the International Committee of the Red Cross.
Krähenbühl was far from alone in his assessment at the Global Security Forum, hosted in this Gulf capital by the Soufan Center and the Qatar International Academy for Security Studies. Officials from Europe and the Middle East, as well as former senior intelligence officials from Australia and Britain, questioned the durability of the alliance structure that the United States and its Western allies put in place after World War II.
"The war in Lebanon today and on Lebanon shows that there are countries, Israel is a case in point, that do not need alliances, for they are engaged in an offensive war, and alliances in today's world are largely defensive,” said Deputy Prime Minister Tarek Mitri of Lebanon, which remains partly occupied by Israeli forces.
But that breakdown isn't happening on its own. Sir John Sawers, former chief of Britain's MI6 intelligence agency, pointed to the United States' declining commitment to its traditional security guarantees, even as the 8-month-old U.S.-Israeli war against Iran has exposed American partners in the Gulf to new threats.
Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates are reconsidering their security relationships with Washington, Sawers said.
“The United States was the guarantor of their security. And what of course these countries have experienced in the last six months is the attacks on them have been provoked by a U.S-instituted war of choice against Iran."
Europe is confronting similar questions as the Russian campaign against NATO grows more brazen and sophisticated. Sawers said America is eroding the international system it helped establish: one of the challenges to the rules-based order is “the United States losing confidence in the system which they designed and which has benefited America enormously.”
Sawers disputed the idea that Europe is rearming simply because of pressure by Donald Trump.
"The reason we're increasing money on defense now isn't because President Trump is telling us to do so. It's because the threat from Russia is much greater than it was before. And the reliability of the United States is less than it was before,” he said.The conference’s host country, Qatar, has found that its longtime efforts to play international mediator no longer keep it safe. The capital came under attack by Israel in 2025, and six months later by Iran.
“It was a surprise because it's the first time that a mediator has been attacked. This never happened,” said Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, Qatar's deputy prime minister and minister of state for defense affairs..
Al Thani identified three threats to Qatar: attacks on its sovereignty, disruptions to energy flows from Gulf Cooperation Council countries, and the spillover of regional conflicts.
Tom Barrack, U.S. special envoy for Syria and Iraq, said the United States remained committed to diplomacy and proposed a path out of the regional violence beginning with a ceasefire, reopening the Strait of Hormuz, and easing economic pressure on the Iranian people. But he cautioned against expecting any agreement to resolve the underlying conflict quickly.
"What we know in the Middle East is there's no such thing as a deal. There's no event. This process is going to continue,” said Barrack, a billionaire financier who served as a go-between from candidate Trump to Gulf princes during the 2016 campaign.Nick Warner, former director-general of Australia's Office of National Intelligence and former ambassador to Iran, put the issue more bluntly: "And the answer to how does the war with Iran end is: it doesn't."

When the sun hits the smog enveloping Indonesian Borneo, it turns everything the colour of rust. Cars, houses and streets appear and disappear out of a dim russet fog. There are few better words than "apocalyptic" to describe the way this looks.
But it's at night, in the quiet darkness, that mother-of-three Dianyra Eka Nastiti grows most fearful.
"Sometimes at night my baby's chest makes a rattling sound," she says. "She was hospitalised for bronchopneumonia when she was just a month and a half old, and every single night I worry: Will my child cough tomorrow?
"Those thoughts haunt me every night."
Dastiti lives in Palangkaraya, at the frontline of a months-long environmental catastrophe that has blanketed large parts of Southeast Asia in a toxic haze.
Wildfires have torched some 1.9 million hectares across Indonesia since the start of the year, according to open-access satellite platform Nusantara Atlas â an area roughly the size of the US state of New Jersey, or the entire nation of Fiji. One million hectares are thought to have burned in September alone.
But the toxic fallout is larger still. Swathes of smouldering forest, swamp and peatlands have turned the air thick with microparticles and carbon monoxide, creating a noxious cloud that has swaddled Indonesia and drifted as far as Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines.
As of mid-October, Indonesia's Health Ministry had recorded more than 277,000 cases of people suffering from chronic coughs and acute respiratory infections. More than 62,000 of those were infants and toddlers under the age of five.
"The forest fires have had a huge impact, especially on everyone's health," says 22-year-old Natari Victoria, who was admitted to a health centre in Palangkarya after suffering from a cough for more than a week.
"I have young cousins, including babies, who are coughing too. It's really taking a toll on them."
Haze and smoke from peat fires contain a complex mixture of pollutants that pose serious health risks to the human body.
Among these are tiny microparticles which can penetrate deep into the lungs and, in some cases, enter the bloodstream, causing inflammation, chronic lung diseases and increased risk of premature death.
Another concern is the toxic greenhouse gases that are being unleashed into the air.
"Here in Central Kalimantan, especially in Palangkaraya, the sky has turned yellow and hazy," says Riduan, head of the Palangkaraya Health Office. "So what are the residents actually breathing in? It's not fresh oxygen; it's carbon dioxide and pollutants. And what happens as a result? The body âÂ specifically the brain â doesn't get enough oxygen."
Children, older adults and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to the dangers of haze, especially during prolonged periods of exposure, when the health impacts can accumulate.
In places like Palangkarya, the official advice is to stay indoors and avoid going out. But Dastiti says this is unrealistic.
"I still need to buy vegetables, stock up on food, purchase school supplies, and take care of other necessities," she explains. "It's simply not possible, and I feel like the people who say things like that have no idea what is actually happening here."
Dastiti's utmost priority, however, is the health and wellbeing of her children. And when the haze grows heavy, she is quick to force them inside.
"With conditions being so unsafe, I have no choice," she says. "Our young children should be at the park, playing with their friends and going to school. Instead, they are locked inside the house."
Lola Macitri, a 37-year-old who lives in the rural village of Ramang, 50km (31 miles) north of Palangkaraya, has been similarly housebound. As the smog has deepened over the past few weeks â from dusty grey to amber yellow and, more recently, burnt orange â she and her family have come to spend most of their time indoors.
Her children, like many others in Indonesia's more haze-affected areas, have been doing their school classes online, she says, while she and other adults struggle to manage half-a-day's work out in the poisonous air.
Countless farmers, daily-wage earners and small vendors have similarly been forced to either sacrifice their livelihoods or endure the risk of stepping outside. Beyond that, many are left with no choice but to wait out the storm.
"If you ask whether we are afraid of the health risks, of course we are. But where else can we go?" says Macitri. "We just have to endure and stay strong through this situation, because there is simply no other option."
The government is under mounting pressure from the public to do more to stop the fires, with many criticising what they see as a woefully inadequate response by the authorities.
Authorities insist they have pursued a range of measures to try to extinguish the flames and, in turn, the smoke â from aerial waterbombing to experimental weather modification. Last week, the Indonesian government said it had deployed more than 60,000 personnel to carry out a "land operation", claiming they'd achieved an 80% success rate in extinguishing new fires.
"At this point, I think we need to use every safe and effective option available to suppress the fires," says Dr Nisa Novita, a forestry expert and peatland researcher at Indonesian conservation NGO Yayasan Konservasi Alam Nusantara (YKAN).
"It's a bit like trying to save a sinking ship: we need to act urgently, use whatever tools can help, and prevent further damage while we still can."
But those resources are fast depleting for responders on the ground.
For more than 100 days, Juni has been fighting wildfires that show only false signs of abating. On the surface, the flames are out âÂ but underground, smouldering blazes continue to burn through a deep understory of carbon, vegetation and peat.

Kenya is grappling with its first ever outbreak of Ebola, a disease which neighbouring countries, such as Uganda and Democratic Republic of Congo, are used to dealing with.
Nine cases have now been confirmed including its first patient, who travelled from DR Congo and died two weeks ago.
Four relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner have now tested positive, meaning they are all linked to him.
But concerns are rising that the virus could start spreading further, even as the government has sought to assure citizens.
The US has warned it citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.
Should Kenyans be concerned?
Kenyans have been expressing their concerns that the disease could spread more widely.
More than 4,000 people have died since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.
With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.
The latest outbreak has been caused by the Bundibugyo species, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Kenyans raised questions from the outset, about how the first patient was able to spend time in the region worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified. He died days after his arrival in Kenya.
As a regional transport hub, the risk of the outbreak spreading is a big concern.
The doctors' union in Kenya has expressed concerns at "lapses" at various border points, including with neighbouring Uganda and Tanzania, as well as at Kenya's main airport.
Dennis Miskellah, the union representative, told the BBC that border and port facilities were grossly understaffed.
However, Health Director-General Patrick Amoth on Tuesday evening sought to reassure people, saying that the eight patients were all improving and responding well to treatment.
What is being done to stop it spreading?
When the first case was announced, the authorities urged people not to panic, assuring them of heightened surveillance at airports and border crossings.
Kenya has since introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from 10 countries it considers to be at high risk: DR Congo, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.
The government has additionally designated treatment and isolation facilities across the country, and health workers have been trained to deal with the disease.
Amoth also said that a dedicated laboratory had been set up at the Kenyatta National Hospital Infectious Disease Unit to handle Ebola tests, to ensure that the hospital's laboratory was not contaminated.
In Kenya, 134 out of 135 people listed as contacts of the first patient remain in quarantine. That means about 99% of the contacts have been traced and isolated, in order to prevent Ebola from spreading to the wider population.
That all of those infected so far had links to the first victim shows Kenya's early response is working, according to the International Rescue Committee.
The government is also working with international partners, including Africa CDC and the World Health Organization (WHO), to support its response, including surveillance, communication and community engagement.
A toll-free emergency hotline, 719, has been provided to the public to report suspected symptoms.
Is Kenya prepared in case it starts spreading further?
Amoth said that none of the contacts of the first patients had showed symptoms before going into quarantine "and therefore the potential to spread to another person is very minimal, literally non-existent".
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
Despite that, Kenya's health ministry says nearly 5,000 healthcare workers have been trained to deal with Ebola at the national and local levels, besides the facilities that have been designated to handle the virus.
The ministry has urged people to remain calm and vigilant. It has also asked Kenyans not to stigmatise people identified as contacts of Ebola cases.
The ministry, along with the WHO, have produced posters to help people understand Ebola and support its containment. One message reads: "Stop stigma, choose support. Stigma can discourage people from reporting symptoms or cooperating with response teams."
In addition, the government has procured supplies of protective equipment.
Is enough being done to protect health workers?
Not according to the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Union (KMPDU).
With three health workers and a hospital cleaner among those infected, questions have been asked as to whether the government could do more to protect workers.
Health workers and carers can face a higher risk of Ebola infection because caring for infected patients may bring them into contact with blood and other bodily fluids.

a96beeac5adb.text: House Democrats' main super PAC is winding down its spending in several races where the party has struggled to make headway despite national trends working in their favor . Why it matters: Democrats' ambitions of winning heavily Republican districts are running into the reality of finite resources at the end of a long and expensive midterm campaign. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and its corresponding super PAC, House Majority PAC, have struggled to keep pace with their GOP counterparts' monster fundraising this cycle. Republicans also have the bonus advantage of a network of cash-rich outside groups, namely President Trump's MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk's America PAC . Driving the news: HMP pulled back its spending this week in three Republican-leaning districts, according to AdImpact and a source familiar with the matter. TN-05: Democrats were bullish about their star recruit, Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder, until redistricting made the district redder and embattled Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) lost his primary to former state Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher . HMP has drawn down its ad reservations in the district from nearly $1.6 million this month to a little over $500,000 as of Monday. Trump carried the newly reconstituted 5th district by 21 percentage points in 2024. Cook Political Report rates the race as "solidly Republican." FL-07: Facing a situation similar to Tennessee, Democrats liked their odds of unseating scandal-tarred Rep. Cory Mills (R-Fla.), who lost his primary to former local news anchor Ryan Elijah. Like Molder, Democratic candidate Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff, was a top DCCC recruit and is part of the committee's coveted "Red to Blue" program. HMP essentially halved its investment in the district on Monday, cutting ad reservations from $3.9 million to just $1.95 million. Cook rates the race as "likely Republican," though a poll released by the DCCC on Tuesday had the two candidates tied at 45% each. CO-03: A top target for Democrats when Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) represented it, the seat has become a heavier lift for the party since she abandoned it and Rep. Jeff Hurd (R-Colo.) took office last year. Democrat Dwayne Romero, a real estate company CEO and Army veteran, is seen by party operatives as having failed to build the kind of momentum shown by Jessica Killin in the neighboring 5th District. HMP halved its investment in this district too, from more than $2.1 million last week to less than $1.1 million as of Monday. Between the lines: The group has also made partial cuts — what it calls "shaves" — in districts where Democrats have struggled to gain traction but still see a glimmer of hope. That includes Arizona's 2nd District, where Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.) is locked in a rematch with former Navajo Nation President Jonathan Nez in a race Cook rates as "likely Republican." HMP has also taken some money out of Texas' 23rd District, where Republican Brandon Herrera, a right-wing YouTuber, is facing Democratic lawyer Katy Padilla Stout in another race rated "likely Republican." Yes, but: Some HMP triages are in districts where they feel confident the Democratic candidate will prevail. That includes Reps. Greg Landsman (D-Ohio) and Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Mich.), both of whose races are rated "likely Democratic" by Cook. The PAC has also pulled back in the districts of retiring Reps. Darrell Issa (R-Calif.) and Don Bacon (R-Neb.), which Democrats are increasingly bullish about flipping. The money from these cuts is funneled to districts the party views as more core battlegrounds — including some seats Trump carried by double digits in 2024 that Democrats nevertheless view as winnable. HMP has added at least $4.7 million to its existing investments in nearly two dozen districts over the last two days. What they're saying: Phil Gardner, a senior adviser for Blue Dog Action — a centrist group backing Dalton — told Axios of the cuts in Florida, "I'm not sure what HMP was thinking here." "The rest of the party is not triaging this seat," he said, citing the DCCC's poll and House Minority Whip Katherine Clark's (D-Mass.) plans to campaign there on Wednesday. Gardner said he agrees with "95% of the decisions HMP's made this cycle," but that it is "bonkers they're dumping so much money" into Maine's 2nd District "while leaving one of the party's best recruits high and dry in Florida." Blue Dog Action spent nearly $500,000 to help Dalton win the primary, but it hasn't yet invested any money in the general election. The bottom line: "We're focused on taking back the House," CJ Warnke, a spokesperson for HMP, told Axios in response to Gardner's criticism. Said Gardner: "I'm confident they'll rethink and make the right decision for the final week. Bale can win and hold that seat with everyone's help."

Elon Musk has said he likes the idea of a merger of Tesla and SpaceX, two of his most notable companies, and it is under active consideration.
"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts over the quarterly business results of SpaceX on Tuesday.
While Musk noted the certainty of such a merger should not be assumed, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies have been formed to examine the move.
"The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," Musk added. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."
With Tesla valued roughly $1.5 trillion and SpaceX valued at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.
Shares of SpaceX rose 8% in after hours trading.
The company, which builds space rockets and Starlink internet satellites, is now expanding into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, like Anthropic and Google.
That line of business has become the most profitable part of SpaceX, bringing in $7.5bn according to the latest quarterly results. Starlink also tallied revenue of $5.2bn.
SpaceX as a whole, however, is not profitable and has lost $1.1bn so far this year.
Shares of Tesla, which reports its own quarterly results on Wednesday, rose 2% after being down slightly for weeks.
Over the last year, Musk has taken to bringing more of his various companies under fewer banners. Before it went public earlier this year, SpaceX acquired xAI and X, the platform formerly known as Twitter, both of which Musk owned.
The recent launch of Terafab, a combined effort to manufacture computer chips between Tesla and SpaceX, was another signal that Musk sees his companies as potentially more effective when working together.
Musk said on Tuesday a full merger between the two companies would make sense for the work each is doing around chips, artificial intelligence, software and more.
Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after the SpaceX stock market debut earlier this year, said he is not included in either of the special committees considering the mega-merger.
He described himself as a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of Tesla and of SpaceX.
Even commenting on the possibility of a merger between the two companies, Musk compared to "tap dancing through a minefield".
He added a merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve the merger, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve".
Shareholders have supported Musk's desires before. Last year, a majority of investors in Tesla approved a compensation package for Musk valued around $1 trillion.
While Tesla is known as an electric car company, Musk has lately been shifting resources there to work around robotics.
SpaceX, with its growing focus on AI infrastructure, quickly outstripped Tesla on the stock market in terms of value when it made its stock market debut.

40b26bf82e23.text: White House envoy Steve Witkoff will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday and present him with an updated proposal to end the war in Ukraine, a U.S. official said. President Trump's son-in-law and adviser Jared Kushner will join the meeting virtually. Why it matters: The White House hopes Putin will show more willingness to compromise after Trump agreed to lift sanctions on Russian diesel sales and took other steps welcomed by Moscow. Driving the news: Witkoff will arrive in Russia after a day of talks in Oslo , Norway with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland and representatives from France, the UK, Germany, Poland, the EU and NATO. Zelensky said on Tuesday that the next step should be a trilateral meeting between him, Putin and Trump — something Russia has refused to do so far. The U.S. hopes the new proposal will "create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations," a U.S. official said. Zoom in: The discussions in Oslo focused on developing a unified proposal for a "framework agreement" to end the war. The U.S. official said Ukraine "brought forward new ideas and proposals, which were discussed in detail." The official said the parties made "meaningful progress" and now have "strong alignment at the working level" on next steps. Behind the scenes: Kushner joined the meeting virtually and again pressed Trump's demand that Ukraine halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, according to a source with knowledge. "Jared was very direct," the person said. Zelensky said after the meeting that he's prepared to cease strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow takes reciprocal steps. What he's saying: Trump said on Tuesday that he thinks "Russia would like to get it done" but expressed doubt that Zelensky wants to end the war. "If he does not, it's gonna be a very bad thing," Trump added. "We want Zelensky to make a deal … If they don't make a deal, it's just gonna get worse [for Ukraine]."

On the long drive to my kid’s sporting event this weekend, most drivers, myself included, cruised a few miles over the speed limit. A few drivers, though, blazed past in the left lane. Mindful of safety — and police cruisers — I didn’t follow suit.
Left unchecked though, a few bad actors can trigger social breakdown, researchers report October 21 in Proceedings of the Royal Society B. The truly deviant among us “basically take off the guardrails of the group,” says Lucas Molleman, a psychologist at the University of Amsterdam.
Molleman and his colleagues designed a thought experiment to show what it takes to sway people to bend or break the rules. They picked a contentious time: A week before the 2024 U.S. presidential election. The team recruited 750 U.S. participants, with roughly half identifying as Democrats and half as Republicans. The online participants watched an animated shooting star streak across a row of 100 squares and then selected which square shone the brightest.
Though the brightest square always appeared around the row’s middle, participants received more money for selecting squares farther to the right (the farthest-right square netted participants roughly the equivalent of $1.30). Dedicated rule followers, or those who always followed the rules, and rule breakers, existed in roughly equal numbers, with each comprising about a fifth of the larger group, initial tests showed.
The researchers then stirred the pot. Participants repeated the simple experiment several times while receiving information about a previous respondent, including their political affiliation and level of adherence to the rule. Rule followers rarely begot more rule followers, even when respondents belonged to the same political party, the team found.
The reverse held true for rule breakers, though. Receiving information that someone with the same political leanings had just disregarded the rules shifted selections rightward on average. Absent social cues, participants selected the farthest-right square roughly 23 percent of the time. That increased to almost 40 percent of the time after participants learned that a political comrade had made the most lucrative choice. Bad behavior, in other words, was contagious.
Most individuals’ rule-breaking levels mirrored or stayed below that of others. But just over 4 percent of individuals escalated deviant behavior beyond that of the previous respondent.
The researchers then created a computer simulation to see how those rule-breaking behaviors might play out across time. They designed a digital twin for each of the 750 participants and had the doppelgängers interact in groups of 100. In some scenarios, those few escalation-prone individuals could push everyone in the group toward wild rule breaking. But if the 100-twin selection had the same proportion of dedicated rule followers as the human experiment, overall deviance settled at a more intermediate level.
This study provides some keen insights into how humans might behave absent consequences, says behavioral economist Eugen Dimant of the University of Pennsylvania. “But that’s not how the world works.” His work suggests that to truly understand social contagion and the emergence of mobs, researchers must consider societal forces, such as punishments and social norms, that tend to keep behavior in check.
To Molleman, though, the study’s insights into individual behaviors are key. This pared-down experiment shows how just a few bad actors can cause entire groups to spiral out of control. Such findings could underpin everything from collective speeding to peaceful protests that turn violent, he says. “This is fundamental science … Obviously reality is way more complex.”

93bc3eb8d6f9.text: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy met with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff and European officials in Norway in a bid to avoid a further diplomatic rupture with President Trump. Over the past week, Trump has criticized Zelenskyy over Ukraine’s efforts to inflict heavy losses on Russia. The meeting was aimed at easing tensions ahead of Witkoff’s meeting with Vladimir Putin in Russia. Nick Schifrin reports. Amna Nawaz: Ukraine's President Volodomyr Zelenskyy met with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff and European officials in Norway today in a bid to avoid a further diplomatic rupture between President Trump and Ukraine. Geoff Bennett: Over the past week, President Trump has sharply criticized Zelenskyy over Ukraine's efforts to inflict heavy losses on Russia. Today's meeting was aimed at easing tensions ahead of Witkoff's trip to Russia tomorrow for more negotiations with Vladimir Putin. Nick Schifrin starts our coverage. Nick Schifrin: From a red carpet rollout, to a royal greeting, to a bro hug with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, Ukrainian President Volodomyr Zelenskyy received a warm welcome in this Nordic capital, an attempt to thaw the coldest moment in the U.S.-Ukraine relations in more than a year-and-a-half, with SpaceX restrictions forcing Ukraine to slow down and lose connection to its drones and Ukraine accusing the U.S. of withholding air defense missiles and the intelligence that goes into Ukraine's air alert system. The U.S. today blamed a technical fault. And Zelenskyy said the early warning system is again working. Volodomyr Zelenskyy, Ukrainian President: Hear when ballistic is coming, so we are thankful to American side. Now it works. It's great. Nick Schifrin: And flanked by Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finland's President Alex Stubb, the three said today's meetings made progress. Jonas Gahr Store, Norwegian Prime Minister: I'm happy that we were able to get together today to straighten out a few things and to agree that what matters now is to look ahead. Alexander Stubb, President of Finland: We have actually made a lot of progress. Under the radar in the past week or so. And now I feel that the process is back on track. Nick Schifrin: And multiple European officials tell "PBS News Hour" the U.S. program to sell weapons to Europe to give to Ukraine is still working, but there aren't enough air defense interceptors to go around, as Secretary Pete Hegseth said today. Pete Hegseth, U.S. Defense Secretary: We haven't changed our posture in any way toward the Ukrainians. But certainly with things like interceptors, we want to make sure our guys have the most possible as well. Nick Schifrin: But, tomorrow, Witkoff will travel to Russia to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin. And Ukrainian and other European officials fear that Witkoff and the Trump administration increasingly consider Putin a partner in peace and business, especially as, today, President Trump once again put the pressure on Kiev, not Moscow. President Donald Trump: Russia would like to get it done, but Ukraine has to want to settle this war. Zelenskyy has to want to settle this war. And if he doesn't, I think it's going to be a very bad thing. Look, we have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine. We've got nothing back, other than high diesel. Nick Schifrin: In fact, diesel prices have also spiked because of the U.S. and Israeli war on Iran. Volodomyr Zelenskyy: So, all of us want peace, Ukraine, Europe, United States, and we will see what will be tomorrow. Of course, we're not losing this war, but we are losing people. And because Russia attacks, we're losing people and time. Nick Schifrin: Including overnight, when Russian missile and drone attacks killed at least four and injured dozens, including children. The light of day didn't stop the terrifying bombardments on a main highway during rush hour. And while the owner of this coffee shop has no doubt the damage was caused by a Russian drone, he doesn't place the blame solely on Putin. Andrii Pakhalovych, Coffee Shop Owner (through interpreter): If Trump wanted to, he would have given us at least those weapons long ago so that we could defend ourselves, so that we could protect our power and heating plants. In a month, we'll have freezing temperatures. What are people supposed to do? Nick Schifrin: All Ukraine can do is prepare for more days like today. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Nick Schifrin.

f8ffb7a910e0.text: To discuss the tensions between President Trump and Ukrainian President Zelenskyy, Geoff Bennett spoke with David Kramer. He held a number of senior positions at the State Department during the George W. Bush administration. He’s now the executive director of the George W. Bush Institute in Dallas, Texas. Geoff Bennett: For perspective, we turn now to David Kramer, who held a number of senior positions at the State Department during the George W. Bush administration. He's now executive director of the George W. Bush Institute in Dallas, Texas. Thank you for joining us. David Kramer, Former U.S. Assistant Secretary of State: Thank you. Geoff Bennett: Let's start with this apparent reset, because, just days ago, as you well know, President Trump, President Zelensky appeared to be at a breaking point. Today, Zelenskyy says the critical U.S. intelligence sharing has been restored. You have European leaders talking about getting diplomacy back on track. Is this a genuine reset or simply a temporary reprieve? David Kramer: It's hard to say. I certainly hope it is more than temporary, because Ukraine has been suffering as a result of some of the disruptions in provision of intelligence, the Starlink and Starshield that Nick referred to, and Ukrainians have been losing their lives as a result. The war, let's not forget, was started by Putin initially in 2014, on a full-scale level in 2022. He is the one who has refused to negotiate and bring about an end to the war that he started. Ukraine and Zelenskyy have demonstrated repeatedly a willingness and flexibility to end the war and to end the suffering that the Ukrainian people have been enduring. Geoff Bennett: And we have seen this cycle before, a confrontation between Trump and Zelenskyy, followed by efforts to repair that relationship. What does that recurring pattern suggest about the fundamental challenge in the U.S.-Ukraine relationship right now? David Kramer: It's a strained relationship. We go back in this current administration to the February 28, 2025, infamous White House blowup, where the president and President Zelenskyy were essentially shouting at each other. And then the relationship got better, on a better track, and the United States imposed some sanctions on Lukoil and Rosneft, the two largest Russian energy companies. But, more recently, we have seen rhetoric coming out of Washington that suggests that the war is Ukraine's fault. Ukraine has been the victim of Russian aggression. That Zelenskyy and Ukraine refused to end the war. Putin is the one who refuses to end the war. And so there's been this seesaw that I think has been both exhausting and unnerving for the Ukrainians, but also deadly, because Russia is taking advantage of this and continues its strikes against Ukrainian civilian targets. Geoff Bennett: What do you believe Putin understands about President Trump that allows Putin to really shape President Trump's approach to this war? David Kramer: I think, on the Russian side, they have been dangling the prospect of improved U.S.-Russian relations, whether it's for business deals, nuclear negotiations. Of course, President Putin has offered the possibility of a summit meeting in Beijing next month, when President Trump will travel there for a major international conference. And the idea of Putin, Xi, the Chinese leader, and President Trump meeting to discuss Ukraine without Ukraine is something the Ukrainians would have great difficulty accepting. Geoff Bennett: What is in Russia's interest? What is Russia's incentive to end this war? Putin has suffered enormous battlefield losses. Russia's economy has come under considerable strain, and yet he continues fighting. Why? David Kramer: Putin doesn't view Ukraine as a truly independent state? He said this as early as 2008 to President Bush when they met in Sochi. He wants to put Ukraine under Russia's thumb. He wants to destroy Ukraine's identity. He wants to remove the duly elected government in Ukraine, President Zelenskyy, whose term has gone beyond its mandate, but that's because Ukraine had to declare a martial law because of Russia's invasion. And Putin wants to deny Ukraine the ability to choose its own future, to determine whether it wants to be a member of NATO or the European Union, and it wants to reduce its military. Putin essentially wants to eviscerate Ukrainian identity, sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence. And that's obviously something that Ukrainians find wholly unacceptable. Geoff Bennett: Would additional American pressure change Putin's calculations at this point? David Kramer: I think it is the way to end this war. I think it involves tightening sanctions, going after the shadow fleet that Russia depends on to bring in funding for its war effort. It includes going after Russian banks and more companies and individuals. It also includes resuming military assistance, whether it's through the system that the Europeans purchase American weapons and then provide those to the Ukrainians or direct military assistance. We have to remember that the U.S. Congress passed the Lindsey Graham legislation calling for more sanctions by 86-11 in the Senate and a sizable margin in the House. Americans, surveys show, support Ukraine. And so I hope that we will understand that pressure on Putin, not on Ukraine or Zelenskyy, pressure on Putin is the way to try to bring about an end to the war that the president has been talking about since he returned to office. Geoff Bennett: And you, of course, served in a Republican administration that viewed American leadership, support for Democratic allies, resistance to Russian aggression as fundamental national security interests. How do you explain, how do you understand the transformation of Republican foreign policy under President Trump? David Kramer: Well, there has been a major change. And America first places the priority on different issues. But I think there should be consistency throughout in recognizing

26433ff1e033.text: At a rally in Kansas on Monday, President Trump looked to boost Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in his reelection bid. Marshall faces a surprisingly close race with his Democratic challenger, Pastor Adam Hamilton. William Brangham discusses the Senate race with Jared Cerullo of PBS Kansas, the host of the weekly current affairs show, "Kansas Week." Geoff Bennett: President Trump is back on the campaign trail in the midst of a seven-day blitz that takes him to Greenville, North Carolina, this evening. On Monday, the president rallied Republicans in Kansas, a state that has long been reliably red, but where this year's midterm elections are proving surprisingly competitive. Our William Brangham has more. William Brangham: Last night in Wichita, the president sought to rally Republicans in Kansas to get out and vote. But his comments were often laced with ugly stereotypes. At one point, the present used an antisemitic slur while defending Republican Senator Roger Marshall. Marshall used to be an OB-GYN and has come under fire for suing dozens of his former patients over unpaid medical debts. President Donald Trump: He was given a bum rap because he was mandated by law to request strongly money owed from patients. You're not allowed not to do it. You have to, by law, go after those people. And they made it like, oh, he was some kind of a shylock-type guy. William Brangham: The president also made misleading claims about immigrants in Kansas and about Marshall's Democratic challenger, Pastor Adam Hamilton. President Donald Trump: He supports flooding Kansas with unvetted refugees who go around killing people literally for no reason. (BOOING) President Donald Trump: He used a lot of church money to fund all of this transgender crap that you're reading about, who openly mocks Jesus. He doesn't have our views, he doesn't have our values, and he happens to be, other than being a pastor -- he's a pastor, I guess, but he doesn't act like a pastor. William Brangham: So for more on this Senate race, we are joined by Jared Cerullo. He's a journalist with PBS Kansas and the host of the weekly current affairs show "Kansas Week." Jared, thank you so much for being here. Help us understand something. Why is this race so tight? I mean, Kansas is as reliably red state as they get. I don't think it's elected a Democrat to the Senate in something like 100 years. And yet here we have the president feeling the need to come and stump to support Senator Marshall. How did it get so tight? Jared Cerullo, PBS Kansas: Yes, you said it. A Democrat has not -- in many of our lifetimes has not been elected to this seat. So it seems obviously that Republicans are definitely feeling like they're in trouble. This race is so close because Adam Hamilton has been a viable candidate. Many times, we have seen in this state candidates who, quite frankly, aren't viable because Kansas has always been a Republican lock, and they know they're not going to win. Things really started to go downhill for Roger Marshall last year out in Western Kansas in a small town called Oakley. He held a town hall meeting and ended up walking out on that town hall meeting. There were several hundred people there, some of them protesters, and they started asking him challenging questions. And, by and large, they weren't demonstrating, they weren't protesting, but they were asking him challenging questions. And Roger Marshall got visibly upset and ended up walking out on the town hall meeting. And this was early last year. Democrats obviously began hitting him very hard after that. The second thing Roger Marshall has been coming under attack for is the billing issue. He -- as you mentioned, he used to be an OB-GYN in Great Bend, Kansas. And 81 people were sued by Roger Marshall for not paying their medical debts. And they weren't -- some of them even went to jail. And we're talking about low-income mothers, single mothers that went to jail because they ignored court orders. So that's ultimately why they went to jail. And the last thing is, Roger Marshall has largely come under attack because Democrats have largely claimed and his opponents have largely claimed that he doesn't even live in Kansas. There have been widespread speculation that he lives in Florida. He had a vacation home in Florida. He did finally start addressing that he does claim to live in Stafford, Kansas. He does have a mailing address there and claims that he has always lived in Kansas, but that's been widely disputed by his opponents. William Brangham: Kansas, as you well know, is a huge agricultural state, and the Iran war has driven up fertilizer prices, diesel prices. How much has that played into this race? I mean, that's got to be causing a lot of real pain for people there. Jared Cerullo: Oh, absolutely. Western Kansas especially is very largely agricultural, small towns, many small town -- Dodge City and Garden City are out in Western Kansas, and they're about 20,000, 30,000, maybe 50,000 size population, and that's about as big as it gets. Everything else is very rural in far Western and North Central Kansas. And many farmers -- and we see this in Adam Hamilton's ads -- many farmers are complaining that they are having a really hard time, harder times than what they are already facing, largely because of the fuel prices that have just skyrocketed. And it was interesting at the rally, at the President Trump rally yesterday, just north of Wichita. Roger Marshall took the podium before and after Trump spoke, and he said multiple times that we're going to lower grocery prices, we're going to lower fuel prices. But he didn't give any direct plans on how he would do that. But he said, if you elect me, we're going to lower these prices. The opponents may say, well, all of these prices have skyrocketed with Republicans in control. That's what they would say, I think. William Brangham: It's going to be an incredibly interesting race to watch. Jared Cerullo of PBS Kansas, thank you so m

e1bf75dd5909.text: In the final sprint to Election Day, more than 12 million votes have already been cast nationwide. That includes more than 65,000 in Philadelphia. The city’s voting processes have drawn President Trump's ire for more than a decade. In partnership with the Pulitzer Center, Lisa Desjardins takes a closer look at how officials in Philadelphia prepare for voting. Amna Nawaz: In the final sprint to Election Day, more than 12 million votes have already been cast nationwide. That includes more than 60-5,000 in Philadelphia, a city in the center of a usual presidential battleground state. The city's vote processes have drawn the ire of President Trump for more than a decade. In partnership with the Pulitzer Center, Lisa Desjardins takes a closer look at how officials in Philadelphia prepare for voting. Lisa Desjardins: Inside this warehouse in Northeast Philadelphia, workers are firing up the machines and paper that run the democratic process. Lisa Deeley (D), Philadelphia City Commissioner: These are what we call election activity boxes. So this box will have in it election materials for every division in the city. Lisa Desjardins: They hold poll books, rule books, posters, and pens, everything the city's 1,700 precincts need. Omar Sabir chairs the city's commissioner's board and says the preparations are working. Mr. Chairman, how ready do you feel for this election this year? Omar Sabir, Chair, Philadelphia City Commissioners: Born ready. Lisa Desjardins: Philadelphia's three elected commissioners, two Democrats and a Republican, run elections in Pennsylvania's largest city. Democrat Lisa Deeley and Republican Seth Bluestein say party allegiance does not factor into the job. Lisa Deeley: I would characterize the work that we do more as nonpartisan than bipartisan. Quite honestly, our job is to be umpires, to call balls and strikes. Seth Bluestein (R), Philadelphia City Commissioner: Running elections in Philadelphia doesn't require democratic values or Republican values. It requires American values. President Donald Trump: Bad things happen in Philadelphia, bad things. Lisa Desjardins: President Trump has singled out the city in every campaign since he was candidate Trump in 2016. Two days after the 2020 election, as the counting of Philadelphia's mail ballots cut into his lead in Pennsylvania, he lashed out. President Donald Trump: Detroit and Philadelphia, known as two of the most corrupt political places anywhere in our country. Seth Bluestein: Both Commissioner Deeley and myself were here in 2020, and we saw the danger of the type of rhetoric and what it could possibly lead through. We have both received death threats and harassment. Lisa Deeley: I'd never imagined that I would be at the Convention Center during a global pandemic with protesters on both sides. I had to leave my home and go live in a hotel. Lisa Desjardins: Then again, on Election Day 2024, Trump posted there was -- quote -- "massive cheating' in the city, though city officials said there was no substantive fraud complaints. President Donald Trump: Take a look at Pennsylvania. Take a look at Philadelphia. Lisa Desjardins: Since returning to the White House, Trump has said the federal government should step in. President Donald Trump: The federal government should get involved. Lisa Desjardins: He's repeatedly claimed without evidence that mail-in voting is rife with fraud, and he's pushed for federal legislation to overhaul elections. This month, he posted on social media that results in Philadelphia "will often take weeks to rig." Seth Bluestein: We have the receipts to show that there's not massive cheating in Philadelphia elections, quite literally. Lisa Desjardins: How safe is mail-in voting? What is the chance of fraud? Lisa Deeley: Mail voting is safe and it's trusted. This whole vote-by-mail rhetoric, again, dangerous. Lisa Desjardins: While there have been a handful of prosecuted cases of fraud in Philadelphia, the largest centered on some four dozen votes. And there's been no widespread documented fraud in a presidential general election. But convincing Republicans of that when the leader of their party says otherwise is a challenge for Bluestein. Seth Bluestein: I have a lot of interactions with local Philadelphia Republicans. And part of my job is to help them have confidence in how our elections -- how our elections are run. Lisa Desjardins: And how hard is that right now? Seth Bluestein: Well, it's about building trust, right? So it's about them having confidence in the work that we're doing so that they can say, you know what, I hear what the president is saying, but I know Seth. Lisa Desjardins: Counting the vote does take time. Bluestein says the reason is written into state law. Seth Bluestein: In Pennsylvania, we can't start the pre-canvass until election morning, when the polls open at 7:00 a.m. Lisa Desjardins: Meaning you can't open the ballots. Seth Bluestein: We can't even review the outer envelopes. We can't open the envelopes. We can't get the ballots ready to be counted. Lisa Desjardins: By law. Seth Bluestein: By law. Lisa Desjardins: Every mail ballot comes sealed inside two envelopes. in 2020, opening and processing the city's roughly 375,000 mail ballots meant more than a million pieces of paper. The count ran until the Saturday after Election Day. Lisa Deeley: We will never sacrifice accuracy for speed, and we never have. And since 2020, we have only gotten better. Lisa Desjardins: This year's ballots are already being mailed back. They will wait in a locked cage until Election Day morning, when processing starts. Officials hope to be done counting by midday Wednesday. But a specific 2026 worry is new growing pressure from Washington. President Donald Trump: Cheating on mail-in voting is legendary. It's horrible what's gone on. Lisa Desjardins: An executive order signed by Trump in March would have restricted whom the Postal Service could deliver mail ballots to. The Supreme Court blocked it

932a29c2b79e.text: A lawsuit in Missouri could have implications for the nation's historically Black colleges and universities. Current and former students at Lincoln University are suing the state for $549 million, alleging it systematically underfunded the school. The case could become a model for similar legal challenges across the country. Geoff Bennett spoke with Don Calloway for our series, Rethinking College. Geoff Bennett: A new lawsuit in Missouri could have sweeping implications for the nation's historically Black colleges and universities and the billions of dollars they say they have been denied over decades. Current and former students at Lincoln University are suing the state for nearly $549 million, alleging that Missouri systematically underfunded the school compared with the University of Missouri. The case could become a model for similar legal challenges across the country. Joining us now is Don Calloway, a former Missouri state lawmaker and attorney who founded The 1890 Project to challenge longstanding funding disparities at historically Black land grant universities. He's also leading this lawsuit against Missouri. This conversation, we should say, is part of our series on higher education called Rethinking College. Don, it's great to see you. Don Calloway: Good to see you, Geoff. Geoff Bennett: So we know for decades HBCUs have been receiving less funding than their predominantly white counterparts. But you're arguing that what happened at Lincoln University in Missouri, you're saying that this wasn't simply unfair, that it was illegal. What exactly did the state do wrong and what makes this a violation of federal law? Don Calloway: So, from 1987 to 2020 -- really to the present, but through 2020 on paper, we see for the first time, because the federal government started tracking -- based upon the states' -- individual states' own reporting, the federal government started tracking and then publishing exactly what each state allocated to its land grant institutions. So it's an important context here. Every state in the country has a flagship university, your University of Missouris, your Auburn Universities. That is an 1862 land grant institution, which the government gave thousands of acres to place a school and give -- then gives millions of dollars a year to each school to fund. After slavery ended, in 1890, there came a series of those land grant institutions for the freed slaves to educate them concurrently. And what we have found is that, from the inception, every state has not met its obligation to fund the 1890 equitably with the 1862. As a result, we didn't see that data published until 2023. It goes back to starting in 1987, which was the first year that the feds began to aggregate that data. And so our lawsuit is based upon the notion that the state of Missouri underfunded Lincoln University as compared to the University of Missouri, to the tune of about $361 million, since we have begun tracking the data. Geoff Bennett: So we're talking about hundreds of millions of dollars. Those numbers can feel abstract, but what has the loss of funding actually meant for generations of students at Lincoln University? Don Calloway: Yes. Well, a couple of things. I'm glad you asked that. First of all, it's not just Lincoln, but there is an aggregate across the 1890s of about $12.6 billion of the 16 states who did not properly fund their 1890, as compared to their 1862. But there are real, tangible damages here. You take career earnings of a FAMU graduate compared to a Florida State graduate, a Fort Valley graduate in Georgia, as compared to the University of Georgia graduate. When you attend an institution that has been hampered by demonstrable underfunding, the facilities are in disrepair. That has a definite effect on the quality of life on campus. The programmings, access to advisory facilities, access to all of the things that one believes goes into the standard of life that one expects from a reasonably competitive college are diminished. And we see the results of that as you enter the professional sector, whether it's private or public, through end of life. Geoff Bennett: You used to serve in state government. Don Calloway: Yes. Geoff Bennett: So you know that states can say, look, we make funding decisions based on enrollment, institutional needs, performance, budgetary issues. Where is the legal line between a legitimate funding decision and unconstitutional discrimination? And how can you prove that Missouri crossed that line? Don Calloway: Yes, that's a great question. Well, one of the ways that Missouri underfunded Lincoln is, it created a five-metric rubric. And so it has -- gets a certain amount of money from the federal government. The state of Missouri is supposed to match that. Well, what it did in Lincoln's case is created a five-metric rubric that apportioned 20 percent of its state match, which was mandatory, upon Lincoln hitting these certain metrics. They didn't apply that metric to the University of Missouri. So that is facially unconstitutional, inasmuch as, number one, the state had no precedent to create this thing. But, secondly, they didn't apply it equally to the University of Missouri to determine its match. So that, in and of itself, whether or not we ever achieve the remedial fund of the corpus of $361 million, that funding metric can be destroyed immediately. And that provides us the prospective relief. But that's just one of the ways that we make a very clear legal argument that this was fundamentally and facially unconstitutional. Geoff Bennett: The $549 million number, how did you arrive at that? Don Calloway: That's a figure with nominal interest. The 548 is salacious. It makes it a bigger headline, but that's with nominal interest calculated. I hope that we don't have to get that because we'd be glad to settle for the objectively indisputable 361 that was withheld from Lincoln. Geoff Bennett: As you were putting this case together, did you happen upon

360d2aefa02e.text: House Republicans are entering the final two weeks of the midterms with a rare but razor-thin fundraising advantage over House Democrats. Why it matters: Democrats outraised Republicans by $84 million in 2024 and $74 million in 2022. Now, Republicans are holding their own financially even as they face mounting political headwinds. The National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) outraised the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) by $1 million ($250 million to $249 million) so far this cycle, Axios has learned. "The NRCC spent this cycle building a war chest to amplify Republican wins and make Democrats answer for their failures," NRCC Chair Richard Hudson (R-N.C.) told Axios in a statement. By the numbers: The NRCC raised $50 million in the third quarter of 2026 and entered October with $61 million cash on hand. The DCCC raised $50.5 million in Q3, and entered October with $55.7 million cash on hand. The NRCC raised $28.5 million in September (the last month of Q3) including a $14 million transfer from the Republican National Committee, compared to $26.3 million raised by the DCCC. Between the lines: Hudson's fundraising success comes as Speaker Mike Johnson has also built a formidable fundraising operation of his own. Johnson has raised more than $220 million for House Republicans since becoming speaker in October 2023, a turnaround from early concerns about whether he could fill the void left by former Speaker Kevin McCarthy.

777a3ec22572.text: Poland has been one of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. But many of its people are slowly turning against the one million Ukrainian refugees given sanctuary over the past four years. Divisions between Poles and Ukrainians are being exacerbated by bitter cultural memory of a World War II massacre. Special correspondent Malcolm Brabant reports. Amna Nawaz: Poland has been one of Ukraine's staunchest supporters since the full-scale Russian invasion. But many of its people are slowly turning against the one million Ukrainian refugees given sanctuary over the last four-plus years. Divisions between Poles and Ukrainians are being exacerbated by bitter cultural memory of a World War II massacre, as special correspondent Malcolm Brabant reports from the Polish capital of Warsaw. Malcolm Brabant: Warsaw's Central Station in March 2022 two weeks after the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the concourse was packed with refugees fleeing the war; 4.5 years on, nearly a million Ukrainian refugees remain here. Only Germany provides sanctuary for more. After enduring the war for a month, Natalia Klimenko escaped to Poland with eternal gratitude. Natalia Klimenko, Ukrainian Refugee (through interpreter): When I came, do you understand, I still can't talk about it without crying. They welcomed us as if we were family. I was stunned by this welcome, like relatives on the border. Malcolm Brabant: What a difference four years makes. In 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, 94 percent of all Poles were in favor of welcoming Ukrainians fleeing the front lines. But now, according to the latest public opinion survey, more than half the nation, 52 percent, to be precise, oppose the idea of giving sanctuary to those running away from the war. Occasionally, Polish antipathy towards Ukrainians escalates to violence. This couple was attacked after their assailants heard them speaking in their native tongue. Dmytro Dymydyuk mans a hotline at a Ukrainian help center. So palpable is the hostility in Warsaw that he maintains a very low profile. Dmytro Dymydyuk, Coordinator, Ukrainian House Foundation: I try not to use social media. I don't write any comments. I don't take part in this holy wars in social media. So I just try to live normal life, job, house, shops, et cetera. So I try to avoid any places, any manifestations where someone from Polish side can attack me. Natalia Panchenko, President, Stand With Ukraine: Last few months, we have every month more and more calls, when people are calling us, and they need support because they are victims of hate crimes. Malcolm Brabant: Natalia Panchenko, president of a nonprofit called Stand With Ukraine, blames extremist politicians. Natalia Panchenko: The role of politicians is very important on everything which I'm talking to you about, because hate speech or hate crime is a result. First, politicians start to show Ukrainian community in Poland as someone very bad. Grzegorz Braun, Leader, Confederation of the Polish Crown: Polish crown This is Poland. This is not some Ukropole. Malcolm Brabant: Grzegorz Braun is an ultra-right politician who is not easily ignored. In the 2025 presidential election, he surprised his critics by winning 1.2 million votes. Grzegorz Braun: With people coming from other countries, we get social diseases, and not only social diseases. As a bonus, we get costs. Malcolm Brabant: Braun shocked Poland during a sacred Jewish holiday when he extinguished a menorah in the Polish Parliament. Braun is brazen about his antisemitic beliefs and hatred for what he calls the Ukrainization of Poland. But isn't it the decent thing to do as a neighbor to offer sanctuary to your neighbors when they're under threat from one of the most powerful militaries in the world? Grzegorz Braun: OK. 6699f3005eec.text: By — Leah Willingham, Associated Press Leah Willingham, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/woman-who-accused-cornell-students-of-rape-says-university-presidents-response-made-her-feel-unsupported Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Woman who accused Cornell students of rape says university president's response made her feel 'unsupported' Nation Oct 20, 2026 6:06 PM EDT A woman who accused seven Cornell University students of raping her at a fraternity house says the university's president questioned why she waited to report the alleged assault, leaving her feeling "unsupported and disbelieved." READ MORE: Polymarket stops users from wagering on possible felony charges for Cornell students accused of rape Her secondhand account of the president's remark, which Cornell disputes, comes as faculty prepare for a potential vote of no confidence in the Ivy League school's leadership. She sent a letter to faculty leaders last week, which The Associated Press obtained Tuesday. The sexual assault allegations by the former student, called Jane Doe in court documents, have sparked campus protests, renewed scrutiny of the university's disciplinary system and a state investigation into the alleged October 2024 assault. In the letter, Jane Doe said her sorority president told her that Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff questioned why she waited until the following month to report being assaulted. The sorority leader, who spoke with Kotlikoff in November 2024, interpreted his remark as casting doubt on her story. "President Kotlikoff's initial response was along the lines of, 'Why did she wait so long to report it?'" Jane Doe wrote in the letter. She said the conversation made her less confident that the administration could handle what happened with the sensitivity and fairness she expected. Cornell's dean of faculty, however, offered a different account of the conversation. In an email Tuesday to faculty senators and verified by the AP, professor Chris Schaffer said another official who was present at the conversation recalled Kotlikoff asking why bystanders had not reported the alleged assault sooner through the school's anonymous tip line, especially since the allegations were already circulating on social media. Schaffer said he waited to share Jane Doe's letter with faculty senators until he could get another account of the conversation. He said he forwarded the letter to university lawyers, who passed it on to an independent team investigating Cornell's response. Schaffer said at a meeting last week that he was against the proposed no-confidence resolution, saying it identified no specific failures or fixes, but acknowledged faculty frustration. "The anger in our community is justified and I share it." Kotlikoff did not respond Tuesday to an email inquiry about Jane Doe's letter. A statement from a university spokesperson also disputed her account of the conversation, saying Kotlikoff was asking about bystanders' actions rather than Jane Doe. Her letter, transmitted through her attorney and first reported by The New York Times, comes as Cornell faculty consider a resolution declaring no confidence in the university administration's ability to address what some faculty members have described as an "ongoing crisis" of sexual assault on campus. Faculty members began debating the resolution at a meeting last Wednesday, where Kotlikoff faced pointed questions about the school's response to sexual assault allegations and its oversight of fraternities. The Faculty Senate is expected to resume debate on Oct. 28 before holding an electronic vote. In her letter, Jane Doe said she wanted faculty members to have information that might be relevant to their deliberations. She emphasized that she was not trying to tell them how to vote. "My intention is not to prescribe how the Senate should interpret this account, but rather to provide information that its members may wish to consider or investigate further," she wrote. Messages seeking comment were left for Jane Doe's lawyers, Thomas Giuffra and W. Whitney Seals. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.
