A famed dusky shark in South Korea is still lingering near a canal that it was guided out of on Wednesday.
The shark, nicknamed Bukangi, became an unlikely sensation after it was spotted swimming in a canal in the south-eastern port city of Busan last month.
For weeks, rescuers tried in vain to get her back to the open sea, using nets to move it out.
On Thursday, authorities said they had reinforced barriers to prevent Bukangi from returning. But it has yet to swim out into the open sea, and instead has been seen circling back repeatedly to the mouth of the waterway.
In a livestreamed operation on Wednesday, rescue workers took more than eight hours to delicately guide the three-metre-long (10ft) shark with a net towards open water in a harbour.
Hundreds of adoring fans gathered at the park overlooking the canal, cheering and waving goodbye to the shark.
But then, on Thursday morning, Bukangi reportedly swam back into the canal after breaking through a barrier installed by authorities.
For some time, Bukangi was trapped in a tight space between two layers of nets in the canal.
Rescuers freed it by removing the outer layer, and have since fortified the remaining layer of nets to prevent it from going back in.
Since then, authorities said, Bukangi has been swimming further out but keeps circling back.
A government official told the BBC on Thursday afternoon that rescuers had concluded their operations to free the shark.
It is thought that Bukangi might have been drawn to the canal by unusually warm waters and plenty of fish. With the sea getting warmer each year, experts say Busan may play host to more sharks in the future.
In the month that she has been in the canal, Bukangi had already attracted more than 1.6 million visitors.
Its popularity gave a welcome boost to Busan's tourism, and the city has embraced her as an unofficial mascot.
But authorities were also concerned about Bukangi's well-being as she appeared to be injured and was not eating.
Social media users have been circulating videos of Bukangi swimming in the canal with what appears to be a bloodied snout.
There were concerns the shark would be further weakened by falling water temperatures.
Before this week's operation, there had been two earlier failed attempts to guide Bukangi out of the canal with nets.
Residents and visitors interviewed by the BBC were divided over whether the shark should stay or go.
Some felt it was safer for the shark to remain in the canal. The BBC saw two people holding up cardboard signs protesting against Bukangi's eviction.
One of them was Cho Hannah, who had travelled for two hours from her home in North Geongsang province to see the shark.
Bukangi, she insisted, was "a rare gift" to Busan.
"This shark has made this canal her home, and we are kicking her out unnecessarily. I am afraid the shark might die tangled with the net, or die out at sea," she said.
But others like Yoon In-taek said it was only right that Bukangi leaves.
"Bukangi seemed much larger when I first saw her on 18 September, when she first got here. Now she seems gaunt. I'm worried for her health if she stays," he said.
"It doesn't sit right with me that she keeps returning here. It will be best if Bukangi leaves, doesn't come back, and lives and feeds freely in the open sea. I'd love to see her find a healthy, free life out there," said Shin Seungmin.
Bukangi has "brought so much joy to us", he said, adding that he was sad to see her leave.
"But she should go and live her normal shark life."
Additional reporting by Leehyun Choi.

The Scene
MIDLAND, TX â This should be a glorious era for Diamondback Energy. In the 15 years since the oil company went public, it has leveraged savvy fracking skills and astute acquisitions to grow from a scrappy West Texas driller â its stock ticker is FANG â to a behemoth responsible for about 4% of US oil production. This year, thanks to the surge in oil prices caused by the war in Iran, Diamondbackâs second-quarter profits per share more than doubled from last year; Wall Street expects another boost when third-quarter earnings are released in a few weeks.
But CEO Kaes Vanât Hof isnât celebrating. âWe donât like when prices are too high,â he told me. Oil prices north of $100 per barrel â the US benchmark is around $99 this week â âare great for a month or two, and then I get called to Congress and called a price gouger.â
High fuel prices could be a decisive disadvantage for US President Donald Trump in the looming midterm elections. As he scrambles abroad for barrels, the Permian Basin â the countryâs biggest and richest oilfield, the bedrock of US energy security at a time of unprecedented turmoil in global markets â remains the place where his battle will be won or lost. And indeed, production here is higher than ever.
But many Permian drillers are ambivalent about this growth. Diamondback, like its peers, has been hesitant to answer Trumpâs repeated calls to âdrill, baby, drillâ; the companyâs latest production target for the year is only about 4% higher than it was before the US-Iran war. Across the Permian, daily production is only 1.5% above where it was when the Strait of Hormuz crisis began in February, despite US oil prices rising 50%.
That circumspection is the result of some hard lessons from a century of booms and busts. Despite major engineering strides in driving down production costs, and a wave of industry consolidation that has concentrated resources and decision making in fewer hands, executives like Vanât Hof are less willing than ever to take billion-dollar gambles adding rigs just because the president wants them to. No matter how attractive oil prices look today, many in the Permian believe a price crash is inevitable, either because Trumpâs daily âjawboningâ keeps futures traders feeling bearish, or because of a genuine security breakthrough in Iran, evaporating consumer demand owing to high prices and the clean energy transition, or the influx of foreign barrels from places like Venezuela.
Thatâs a market reality that Washington often seems to miss: Trumpâs overall âenergy dominanceâ strategy relies on companies like Diamondback to drill more, but sets them up for failure if they do too much.
âWeâre the only business in the country where neither side of the aisle wants you to make money,â Vanât Hof said. ââDrill, baby, drillâ is basically drill as much as you can to commit economic suicide.â
Timâs view
Standing on the site of Diamondbackâs newest frack, I began to understand why an unprecedented oil supply crisis has not unleashed a corresponding gold rush in the Permian.
Here, you can hear this vanguard of US oil drilling before you see it: the earth-shaking racket of a dozen semi-truck-sized gas generators, powering more than a dozen equally huge pumping machines, pushing sand and fluids into four brand-new wells. To get these wells pumping, three dozen people, including workers from Halliburton and several other subcontractors, work in round-the-clock shifts for at least a week, using explosives and high-pressure fluids to âfractureâ deep shale rock formations along the length of a horizontal well that can run for miles parallel to the surface so oil and gas can be siphoned out. This is the basic technology that revolutionized US oil a decade ago, and made the country by far the worldâs top producer. But it was always somewhat odious to oil company shareholders, who found it a money pit that didnât make sense if crude prices werenât high.
When prices picked up this year, no one expected Chevron or ExxonMobil to suddenly drill more in the US. Their monster capex budgets change direction slowly, and both companies have their hands full with far-flung global drilling adventures. But in booms of the past, small and midsize drillers would have jumped to cash in. Married at First Sight Australia is facing fresh controversy after police launched an investigation into the hit reality TV show.
New South Wales told BBC News that inquiries had taken place "following a report of inappropriate content being shared".
Channel Nine, which broadcasts Married at First Sight Australia, confirmed that it was "aware of a police investigation" involving the show's production company.
It is the latest blow for the show, after a BBC News investigation earlier this year into MAFS Australia revealed cast members said they had not been told their partners had previous drug and violence convictions.
Those revelations led to a warning from Australia's media watchdog, which called them "serious and disturbing".
The British version of Married at First Sight, known to many as MAFS UK, was separately plunged into crisis in May after BBC Panorama reported rape allegations from two female cast members - allegations the men involved have denied.
MAFS UK is made by a different production company to the Australian version.
The Dark Side of Married at First Sight
Panorama investigates allegations that raise serious concerns that welfare procedures on Married at First Sight UK have failed contributors, leaving them at risk of harm.
Watch on iPlayer now
Married at First Sight shows single people agreeing to "marry" total strangers after meeting for the first time at their mock weddings.
The marriages are not legally binding, but viewers see the couples go on "honeymoons", before moving in together and navigating their relationships - all while being filmed, almost every day.
According to industry news website TV Blackbox, external, a male cast member on the current series of MAFS Australia made a formal complaint to the police after producers allegedly shared private information about him with his on-screen bride.
A spokesperson for New South Wales Police Force told BBC News: "On Monday 24 August 2026, officers attached to South Sydney Police Area Command commenced an investigation following a report of inappropriate content being shared.
"Following inquiries, the matter will be referred to WA [Western Australia] Police Force."
BBC News has approached WA Police Force, who said the referral has not yet been received.
A spokesperson for Channel Nine said: "We are aware of a police investigation involving Endemol Shine Australia and all enquiries should be directed to them."
Endemol Shine Australia, which makes MAFS Australia, has not responded to multiple requests for comment over the latest developments.
In June, a BBC News investigation heard from nine former cast members from MAFS Australia, who urged the show to improve its background checks and to stop allowing individuals with previous convictions or allegations on the show.
One woman from last year's Australian series told us she was not told the man she had been matched with had a previous drug conviction and only found out after the show ended. "There should be informed consent," she told us.
Responding to those claims at the time, Channel 9 and Endemol Shine Australia said they had "strong protocols in place to ensure participant safety and wellbeing".
MAFS UK review due back 'any day now'
As well as being a huge hit in Australia, the show is popular in the UK and is shown on Channel 4.
The broadcaster pulled all the UK episodes of MAFS from its streaming service just hours ahead of the transmission of the Panorama investigation in May, but MAFS Australia remains available to watch.
In July, BBC News revealed that a cast member from MAFS UK had been arrested on suspicion of rape following the Panorama programme.
The individual is not being named; nor is the alleged victim. Anyone who makes an allegation of rape is entitled to anonymity by law.
The media regulator Ofcom has also launched an official investigation into the hit Channel 4 show.
The UK version, which has been running for 10 seasons, is one of Channel 4's biggest shows, with audience figures often topping three million.
The broadcaster has commissioned a review into contributor welfare on the show. However, it only intends to publish "a summary of findings", rather than the full report.
Channel 4's chief executive previously said the review was due back in the summer, but it has not yet been published.
Speaking to MPs earlier this week, Ofcom boss Dame Melanie Dawes said the report was due back "any day now".
BBC News has approached Channel 4 for a response.
Lawyers for CPL, the independent production company that makes the UK version of the show, have previously said its welfare system is "gold standard" and industry-leading.
If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.uk

The News
As President Donald Trump continues buying government stakes in private companies, the rest of Washington is starting to appreciate the power of his new tool.
The Trump administration has so far announced 43 equity stakes in firms producing everything from minerals to semiconductors, 36 of which were negotiated without explicit legal authority â and more are yet to come. The administration may be negotiating even more stakes under the radar, since SEC filings for unrelated deals mention the possibility of warrants.
Unwinding the administrationâs investments would prove legally and politically difficult â but Democrats likely wonât want to, at least not right away. Theyâre already weighing how to use equity stakes for their own ends, signaling that Trumpâs government intervention in the private sector may be the start of a permanent trend.
âThe Trump administrationâs approach to government equity stakes has completely lacked transparency and accountability,â Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., told Semafor. âWhile this is something future administrations may want to consider, itâs clear that to actually serve Americans, it would require a totally different approach.â
Thanks to the precedent Trump has set, a future Democratic president could reap multiple benefits from equity stakes in private companies. Among them, as former Biden administration officials suggested: reining in the AI industry, shrinking defense spending, boxing China out of critical sectors, and pressuring gun and oil companies.
Even demanding an equity stake as a condition for government assistance â whether itâs a loan, grant, or other federal permit â is a powerful tool thatâs now more readily at the White Houseâs disposal, no matter which party controls it.
âWeâre through the looking glass,â said Democratic strategist and former Biden administration official Doug Farrar.
Van Hollen isnât the only 2028 Democratic contender whoâs focusing on overseeing Trumpâs deals rather than discontinuing them.
In a statement to Semafor, California Gov. Gavin Newsom trolled Trump as âTHE LEADING SOCIALIST OF OUR TIME,â crediting him with unlocking âA BOLD NEW ERA OF GOVERNMENT-RUN BUSINESS â¦ WITH HIS GLORIOUS GOVERNMENT TAKEOVERS.â
The next president may well also have more power to purchase equity stakes; legislation moving through the Senate would give the Pentagon explicit legal authority to do so.
âThe skyâs the limit, because the patternâs been set,â said Tad DeHaven, who helps track the equity stakes at the Cato Institute.
Know More
Some Republicans donât want any administration making forays into the private sector with public money. Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, recently introduced legislation that would require the government to dissolve any equity stakes after eight years.
âWhether itâs President Trump or somebody else like Bernie Sanders who might be president someday, I donât trust the federal government being a long-term investor in American companies,â Husted told Bloomberg TV.
But no one else has signed on to his bill. And some progressives are already embracing taking stakes.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced this month that his Economic Development Corporation, helmed by Bidenâs former FTC chair, Lina Khan, would invest $30 million in a quantum technology lab in exchange for 15% of its profits.
Already, âthe [Trump] administration keeps gaining footholds in the industries that make up the supply chain for the AI buildout,â said Farrar, who worked for Khan at the FTC. âThat could be an important point of leverage for a future president of either party â but especially a Democrat who wants to seriously regulate this industry.â
Sanders, one of the leftâs leading critics of the AI industry, went a step beyond profit-sharing by suggesting this summer that its companies surrender half of their stock to the government.
âThe Trump administration has opened up Pandoraâs box with this approach to state capitalism,â said Bloomberg economist Chris Kennedy, who served on the National Security Council during the Biden and Trump administrations.
Some Democrats fear Trump could sell off his equity stakes following the next presidential election. Others pray their party, as it prepares to take back at least some power in Washington, can dig into Trumpâs equity stakes without creating too much pressure for a selloff after he leaves office.
Any future Democratic president would seek to âfigure out a way of imposing some sort of governance scheme over all of these equity interests that strikes the right balance,â said Bharat Ramamurti, the former deputy director of the Biden White Houseâs National Economic Council.
âI hope there is not an overreaction to one of [Trumpâs equity stakes] not panning out, especially because many of the other ones may end up being quite successful for taxpayers,â Ramamurti added. âAnd youâll be making a losing financial decision if you decide to cut all of that off.â
Room for Disagreement
Given that Trump has built three campaigns around his skills as a dealmaker, the White House has plenty of reason to argue that his opponents wonât use his playbook. In a statement to Semafor, White House spokesperson Matthew Middleton appeared skeptical that a Democrat would hang onto Trumpâs existing stakes.
âThrough voluntary equity investments in willing companies, the Trump administration has partnered with the private sector to rebuild Americaâs industrial base,â Middleton said, adding that âitâs justifiable to doubt that Democrats will want to build on President Trumpâs legacy to revitalize American industry and strengthen our economic independence.â
Eleanorâs view
Itâs easy to envision a future Democratic president using Trumpâs model to advance a more progressive agenda, as Mamdani already has in New York.
But one Republican asset that Democrats will have trouble replicating is the man whoâs largely responsible for the Pentagonâs investments: Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg.

Israel's general election takes place on Tuesday 27 October.
It's the first election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel and its subsequent conflicts in Gaza and with Iran, Hezbollah and the Houthis.
Many view it as one of the most pivotal elections in Israel's history, with global implications.
Who are the main contenders?
Current polling puts incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu in a tight race with Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israel Defense Forces, to become prime minister.
Eisenkot's popularity stems partly from his military credentials and his relative newness in politics, having formed his Yashar Party only last year.
He lost his son, a soldier, in the first months of the Gaza war, and served in Israel's war cabinet under Netanyahu until resigning in 2024 over disagreements about the conflict. He has built his campaign on calls for accountability over the security failures that led to 7 October.
Other opposition leaders include former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman - both right-wingers who take hardline positions on security and advocate permanent Israeli control over much of the occupied West Bank - and Yair Golan, a left-winger who supports Israel's withdrawal from large parts of the territory. Despite their differences, they could work with Eisenkot to form a government.
Netanyahu's current government is the most right-wing in Israel's history. In order to remain in power, he will likely have to rely on the support of some of his existing far-right coalition partners. Some hold ultra-nationalist positions, such as calling for Israel to annex the West Bank and for the "migration" of Palestinians from Gaza - which could amount to the forced displacement of civilians. Some members of Netanyahu's own Likud party have also called for Palestinian "migration" from the territory.
There are two Arab party blocs in the running too, as about one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. In theory, they could prove kingmakers. But all but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out working with them.
How do the elections work?
Israel's parliament - known as the Knesset - has 120 seats, meaning a government must hold 61 seats to command a majority.
Israel uses a proportional representation voting system, meaning governments have always been coalitions of multiple parties.
This means that after election day, it may take weeks or even months before the next government is formed - with different parties wrangling for concessions and deals being struck.
If no bloc can form a majority, it is possible a minority government could take power.
What are the main issues?
The dominating topic has been security - with the challengers to Netanyahu all heavily criticising the security failures that led to the 7 October attacks, in which nearly 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken back to Gaza as hostages. Nevertheless, Netanyahu has once again framed himself as "Mr Security", pointing to strategic victories in Israel's wars since 2023.
Conscription is also a major topic. Historically, ultra-Orthodox Jewish men in full-time religious study have been exempt from military service, but since war broke out this has become an increasingly divisive policy.
Judicial reform has also featured heavily during the campaign. Netanyahu's government is still pursuing contentious plans for reforms to the judicial system, which led to mass protests before 7 October. Critics say the plans would compromise the independence of the judiciary and threaten democracy.
As in many countries, cost of living is another key issue. Food and housing costs have grown steadily in recent years.
What does it mean for Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank?
A year on from the ceasefire in Gaza, Israel continues to carry out near-daily strikes on the territory - saying it is targeting Hamas operatives - and maintains control of more than half of it.
More than 74,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza since 7 October 2023, according to the Hamas-run health ministry - whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
In the West Bank, attacks by Jewish settlers are at an all-time high, according to UN records, while Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law, are rapidly expanding.
So for Palestinians, the shape of Israel's government is a major factor in their lives.
On Gaza, the two leading camps - headed by Netanyahu and Eisenkot - hold similar positions - with both supporting Donald Trump's peace plan, which would see Hamas give up its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal from the territory. Eisenkot recently pledged to end Hamas rule in the territory within 18 months, through military means if necessary.
In the West Bank, Netanyahu's camp largely wants to continue with its policy of settlement expansion.
Eisenkot supports Israeli settlements in general, but opposes proceeding with the controversial E1 settlement project which would, in effect, split the West Bank in two. He also wants to close some unauthorised settler outposts built on Palestinian land, create conditions for a final peace settlement with the Palestinians, and crack down on extremist Jewish settlers.
For decades, many mainstream Israeli politicians advocated for a two-state solution - the creation of an independent Palestinian state in peaceful coexistence alongside Israel - although Netanyahu has long opposed it. But support for the idea has been declining for years. In this election, none of the leading Jewish parties are campaigning on it, and many have outright rejected it.
When will we know the results?
At 22:00 local time (20:00 GMT) on election day, Israeli broadcasters will publish exit polls. These will give some indication of the direction of voting, but can vary significantly and current polling suggests a clear projected winner is unlikely.

Two people were killed and eight others injured in an attack on an airport in Dammam, eastern Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, the kingdom's General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) says.
Those killed at King Fahd International Airport were a Saudi citizen and an Indian resident, while the injured were Saudi, Indian, Yemeni, Bangladeshi and Nepalese nationals.
The GACA did not say what type of attack occurred, but Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement has repeatedly targeted the kingdom's airports with drones and missiles.
On Wednesday morning, two people were killed by debris from a drone that was intercepted over Eastern Province, where Dammam is located, the Saudi energy ministry said.
The ministry said the drone was intercepted as it attempted to target a processing facility owned by Saudi Arabia's state oil company Aramco in the Shaybeh oil field, where a contractor's vehicle was set ablaze.
It identified the dead as residents from the Philippines and Nepal.
Another four drones were also intercepted on Wednesday night, according to the Saudi-led coalition that is supporting the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis, but they have previously said they are attacking Saudi airports, energy facilities and military bases in retaliation for deadly Saudi air strikes on the territory they control in western Yemen.
At least 21 people have been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities.
One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others â the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
The Houthis' military spokesman said on Wednesday that they had targeted military equipment at an airport in the southern Yemeni city of al-Mukalla, which it said had been transported by Saudi Arabia for use by pro-government forces.
Meanwhile, Houthi-run media reported that at least six people had been killed and 11 injured in air and artillery strikes over the previous 24 hours.
According to the Houthi-run health ministry, 155 civilians have been killed since Yemen's devastating civil war flared up three months ago.
The government's health ministry has said at least 1,574 people have been killed in the conflict over the same period.
The UN says more than 256,000 people have also been displaced.
The war began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated the next year, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
Earlier this month, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a counter-offensive with Saudi air support.
However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib, al-Jawf, Dhale and Shabwa provinces.

After petting a carriage horse in New York's Central Park at the age of five, Alexus Lawson was hooked.
She has driven a carriage in Manhattan's most famous park, pulled by her horse, for six years. But since Lawson heard about the city's vote this week to outlaw the carriages over animal and public-safety concerns, she has been worried.
"What am I supposed to do with my horse?" asked the 28-year-old, who has been driving in the park for six years. "You're going to tell me I can't work with her anymore? How am I supposed to ensure her health?"
Lawson is one of roughly 200 horse-drawn carriage drivers in Central Park. Use of the carriages has been an at-times controversial tradition for over 160 years that has become a popular tourist activity.
On Thursday, New York City Council is expected to vote to pass a ban on the carriages that would start in June 2028. The proposal is backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who says he will help develop a transition plan for workers in the industry.
But several drivers who spoke to the BBC said they did not want new jobs, and disputed claims their horses are mistreated - even as many New Yorkers and tourists welcomed the ban.
"There were a few cases of horses dying in the middle of the park. You can clearly see that they're not taken care of," said New York resident Ron Tsur. "That's not what they're supposed to be doing."
Since 1982, 40 horses working in Central Park have died, according to the Manhattan Borough President's office, which blames issues including overheating and collisions.
New York leaders previously sought a ban, under pressure from animal-rights activists, but faced pushback from city council members and unions representing the workers.
But the ban movement found new momentum this summer after the death of a teenager.
In June, Romanch Mahajan, a tourist visiting New York with his family from India, was in a carriage when the horse bolted, causing the 18-year-old to fall out and die. The planned ban - named Romanch's Law after the teen - also follows the death this year of a carriage horse, Deniz, who ate a toxic plant in Central Park.
'Horses are working animals'
Several Central Park horse carriage drivers who spoke to the BBC said they were devoted to their horses and that the rides did not pose a safety risk.
Lawson, who was nearby on the day Mahajan fell to his death, called the deadly incident "extremely tragic". But she said if the city was really worried about the safety of the horse-drawn carriages, it would outlaw them immediately - not in two years' time.
The Central Park Conservancy, the non-profit organisation that manages Central Park and supports the carriage ban, said that over the past 13 months alone, there had been seven "horse-related incidents". In May, a driver was taken to the hospital after a spooked horse hit another carriage, causing it to tip over. In January, another horse, named Destiny, ran into traffic near the park, causing a multi-car collision.
Lawson, who owns six horses, pointed out that New York City carriages were the most regulated in the country and said horses enjoyed the stimulation.
"They look at an animal in harness and they see a trap," Lawson said of officials pushing for the ban. "They see a job as something that's terrible. Horses are working animals."
Medet Fidan, a carriage driver for 12 years, feels similarly attached to his horse, calling allegations of mistreatment a joke.
"I spend more time with my horses than my wife and my kids," he said. "They're telling me I'm abusing my horse? No way."
Fidan said he was angry, and that officials were passing a ban without talking in-person to drivers and others in the industry. "If you don't listen to me, how can you come and kill my business, destroy my family's, my livelihood?" he asked.
The city council held a hearing in July, inviting community members, including horse-carriage drivers, to comment.
The legislation to end horse-drawn carriages proposes an "industry transition framework" including potential job placement, training, career counselling, and financial compensation for those in the business.
A spokesperson for Mamdani said his office was involved in planning to find new jobs for these workers - who make around $60,000 (Â£ 44,000) to $70,000 a year, according to drivers who spoke at the city council hearing.
But the Transport Workers Union, which represents the drivers, said the plan did not include guarantees - including compensation - and that the workers would be "economically wiped out".
The union also raised concerns about a lack of funding for individuals and organisations who eventually take in the horses. It argued that thousands end up at slaughter auctions each year.
The bill forbids selling horses for slaughter or for similar work.
'Confining for the horses'
Though carriage drivers say they are committed to the health of their horses, concerns over the animals' well-being have been raised in the city for decades.
The carriages have been opposed by animal-rights groups, including one that was founded in response to New York's industry. In 1866, after Henry Bergh witnessed the brutal beating of a carriage horse, he established the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA) to protest horses' treatment and other instances of animal abuse.
People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) and a coalition of organisations supporting the horse-carriage ban also oppose the carriages.
Horses can work up to nine hours a day. They are currently restricted to certain entrances of the park, where they stand and wait with drivers to be hired. Customers pay $72.22 for a 20-minute ride, plus $28.89 for every extra ten minutes.
Vanessa Stolle, a German tourist, said she and her family had horses at home - and that they do not belong in a noisy park pulling passengers.
"To stand the whole day here â it's loud for them and they can't go to the countryside," she said.

Job-Based Health Plan Costs Rise, With Little Relief in Sight
Rising healthcare costs aren’t a problem just for those who buy their own health insurance. Increases hit employers and their workers this year, too, and more are expected for 2027 plans — adding to growing concerns about affordability heading into the midterm elections.
Polls show that healthcare costs — and affordability, in general — are among top concerns cited by likely voters. Much attention has been focused on mounting costs and declining enrollment in Affordable Care Act plans, the insurance used by roughly 19 million people who buy their own. But work-based plans are adding financial pressure for the more than 150 million Americans covered through their jobs.
One of the biggest changes this year, for instance, came in the amount workers pay toward their own coverage, rising an average of 9% to $7,471 annually for a family, according to a broad annual survey released Oct. 22 by KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. That’s up from the 7.6% jump seen from 2024 to 2025.
Their employers, too, faced additional costs, with the average family coverage premium rising 5% to hit $28,303, according to the survey.
In response to that increase — which comes on the heels of a 6% increase the previous year — 44% of large employers, with at least 200 employees, said they upped what workers had to pay toward coverage.
“When we start to see higher use or higher prices, there are only a limited number of things employers can do” to try to slow premium increases, said Matthew Rae, associate director of the Program on the Health Care Marketplace at KFF.
Employers reported taking other actions in the past year to hold down their costs, such as increasing deductibles (the amounts people pay toward their care before insurance pitches in), changing insurers, adding preapproval for some services, or offering workers a narrower choice of healthcare providers, the KFF report said.
Workers’ earnings rose an average of 3.7% this year, the survey found, while overall inflation was 2.7%.
People who work for small companies, with fewer than 200 employees, paid more for healthcare than their counterparts at larger companies.
For example, health plans at large companies had a $1,772 average annual deductible for an individual employee, while small workplaces averaged $2,624.
Overall, though, the share workers pay toward the total premium across all companies ticked up only slightly from the previous year, hitting 27% of the cost for family coverage and 18% for individual coverage, with employers picking up the remainder.
Driving Up Costs
Other groups have recently posted projections of what employers might face next year.
Consulting firm AON, for example, projected employers could pay 9.5% more next year, the fourth consecutive year of big increases, while a similar company, Marsh, estimated 8.2%, the highest jump since 2003. Costs are going up for many reasons, from people utilizing more services to skyrocketing prices of prescription drugs and rapidly rising hospital prices, the reports say.
Also helping drive up costs is artificial intelligence, say other reports, including one from the Business Group on Health, a membership organization of self-insured employers. The report said hospital systems and other medical providers use the technology to maximize insurer and patient billing.
The business group predicted a median premium increase of 9.2% next year, although employers might reduce that by making benefit changes.
Until recently, employers absorbed the lion’s share of cost increases, “but that’s starting to change a bit,” said Jim Winkler, chief strategy officer for the group. “When open enrollment starts, most people will see their out-of-paycheck costs and probably their out-of-pocket costs going up.”
Looking ahead, the group suggests employers take further action to forestall increases in 2028, Winkler said. One idea is to offer lower copayments for some health providers based on their prices or quality, similar to “tiered networks,” a strategy employers and insurers have tried, with only 4% of companies sticking with it, according to the KFF survey. “What’s old is new again,” Winkler noted, saying it might work better now because it’s easier than ever for apps to show consumers the providers with the lowest copayments, which would be set by an employer or insurer.
Overlooked in much of the discussion on rising health costs, said Elizabeth Mitchell, president and CEO of the large employer organization Purchaser Business Group on Health, is the role played by the healthcare industry — from hospitals to drugmakers to insurers.
She asked: Why are the customers — the employers, in this case — being asked what they are doing about it? “The industry is doing absolutely nothing to control costs, as evidenced by the relentless growth in costs,” she said.
Businesses are using new pricing information made available under federal rules to contract directly in some cases with hospitals and other providers and to invest in primary care.
Mitchell and others say Congress should also get involved. Health policy researchers at Georgetown University, for example, suggest capping annual deductibles, setting hospital price caps, and extending lower drug prices negotiated by Medicare to the private sector.
Keeping Costs Flat
Not all companies saw an increase this year.
Take KFF survey respondent Phifer Inc., a company based in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, that makes insect screens and precision woven products, such as outdoor furniture fabric. Its health costs remained flat this year, likely because it has put a strong focus in recent years on providing zero-cost primary care to its workers through on-site clinics and direct contracts with doctors’ offices, said Russell DuBose, the company’s vice president of human resources.

d954ab55359a.text: Vice President Vance 's call for fellow Republicans to "stop whining" about Vivek Ramaswamy's controversial attack ad in Ohio's race for governor showed a key part of his political mindset ahead of his expected run for president in 2028: Never back down. Why it matters: Channeling President Trump, Vance has shown contempt for what he sees as the old-guard GOP's reflex to cave under pressure from Democrats and the media. He thinks too many Republicans sacrifice allies to make controversies go away, and that giving critics a political scalp only encourages them to demand another, according to people familiar with his thinking. It's an approach with some risk — namely whether Vance, entering a critical period in his political career, has the political muscle to get away with Trump's no-apologies approach. Driving the news: Vance on Wednesday defended Ramaswamy amid bipartisan outrage over an ad featuring the estranged mother of Ramaswamy's Democratic opponent, Amy Acton . In the deeply personal ad, Acton's mother calls her daughter a liar, and says Ohioans shouldn't vote for her for governor. Not mentioned in the ad: Acton and her brother were removed from the mother's care as children after Acton accused her stepfather of sexual abuse. Her mother sided with the stepfather, leading to an estrangement that has lasted nearly 50 years. Appearing at a campaign stop for Ramaswamy in Ohio, Vance showed little concern about the criticism over the ad. Vance said he was "disgusted" by fellow Republicans criticizing it, telling them to "stop whining." Asked whether the ad was appropriate, Vance said it was "not really my concern," and that politics is tough. The other side: The backlash has included Republicans and Democrats who believe the ad crossed a moral line by exploiting Acton's traumatic childhood. "I would not have run that ad," Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, who appeared alongside Vance and Ramaswamy at a campaign rally Wednesday, told the AP . Former UN ambassador Nikki Haley called Ramaswamy "a bad guy," adding: "It's a shame he continues to get away with it." Acton told CNN that she hopes her story of recovering from abuse inspires others, and that she "was not stunned" at "the antics of an out-of-touch billionaire," referring to Ramaswamy. Behind the scenes: Vance's refusal to denounce allies dates to his 2022 Senate campaign in Ohio. During a March 2022 debate, Vance refused to condemn then-Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) for appearing at a rally organized by white nationalist Nick Fuentes. "She is my friend, and she did nothing wrong ... I'm absolutely not gonna throw her under the bus," Vance said then. In the final days of Ohio's 2024 Senate primary, Vance aggressively defended GOP candidate Bernie Moreno amid a controversy over an adult dating website account linked to Moreno's work email. As vice president, Vance has refused to disavow his friend Tucker Carlson amid accusations of antisemitism — even as Carlson's relationship with Trump was fracturing. After racist and antisemitic messages surfaced in a leaked Young Republicans group chat, Vance declared on X that he wouldn't join the "pearl clutching." During a December 2025 speech at a Turning Point USA event, Vance rejected political "purity tests," declaring: "I didn't bring a list of conservatives to denounce or to de-platform." What they're saying: "There is nothing JD has more personal disdain for than weak Republicans who reflexively kowtow every time the Dem-media demands a scalp," a source close to Vance told Axios. "It drives him crazy to see the cucked reaction from some establishment operatives and politicians in the GOP, who he views as nothing more than useful idiots for the left." The intrigue: Some Republicans see Vance as influenced by Trump and Vance's mentor, tech billionaire Peter Thiel, who has embraced a similar no-apologies mantra. "The president's refusal to kowtow to the left is one of the things JD admires most" about Trump, the Vance source said.

92061763f22b.text: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, with some agents attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources tell Axios. Why it matters: AI agents are becoming a nightmare for America's banks, making their way into banking systems faster than financial institutions can respond. The difficulty in distinguishing between a human and an unauthorized bot is forcing banks to block the technology and rapidly rewrite their terms of service. Driving the news : Banks including Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and others are racing to contain agent risks. Some are aware of unauthorized access, people familiar with the issue said. These are generally situations when an agent or AI assistant accesses a human's account with the user's permission and login credentials. Even if permitted by the user, this goes against the guidelines of most banks requiring that humans log in to their own accounts. This presents significant security risks : banking executives fear the steps agents with login access might take, especially if a user has granted purchase authority or the ability to shift funds. In other instances, some banks have tracked activity when agents — programmed to fulfill requests or complete tasks on a user's behalf — contact call centers or appear to take actions independent of user instructions, the people said. What they're saying: Bank executives described the situation as horrifying, with one official saying the industry has grave concerns about agents gaining access to customer accounts and taking steps that could impact user finances. State of play : The concerns are at the root of the decision by several banks to restrict third-party AI agent access, the people said. Morgan Stanley has begun blocking third-party agents from accessing its platforms, sources familiar with the decision said. JPMorgan , Bank of America and Citi are also restricting agents . A Chase spokesperson said customers should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone. A Morgan Stanley spokesperson said the bank hasn't observed instances of "rogue AI agents accessing our platforms." Zoom out: Most banks have authorized or are moving in the direction of allowing read-only access , which should allow agents to see customer financial information without taking action. Banks already grant such access to third-party apps like Quicken for budgeting and other activities. Reality check: Several industry and bank executives told Axios they recognize the need to find a middle-ground with AI agents. Customers will want to use these agents going forward, which banks recognize. But for now, the risks of being too permissive are too high. Threat level: Many banks are broadly not able to parse whether agent account activity is user-directed, sources said. One bank executive told Axios they struggle to differentiate between agents, as well as whether an agent has been authorized by a user or has gone rogue and gained access to a customer account. What we're watching: On one hand, banks are best positioned to respond to the threats and opportunities of AI given their cash on hand and experience as critical infrastructure. But money isn't necessarily enough to solve this problem, one source said, because of how quickly the technology is developing and revealing new weaknesses in real time. Banks are investing in preventing worst-case scenarios, but they are also preparing for when those could happen, including with "day after" scenario planning that would allow them to quickly secure or restore customer access, sources said. The bottom line: The rapid pace of AI advancement is becoming a security nightmare for America's financial institutions.

The Trump administration has hinged federal funding for states on whether they end or loosen powerful but controversial laws that regulate the construction of new hospitals — with a handful of states poised to comply.
A chunk of the $50 billion available to states through the five-year Rural Health Transformation Program is partly contingent on policy commitments. The administration told states it would score their applications higher if they walked back their certificate of need, or CON, laws, which give a state approval authority over the expansion or construction of any healthcare facility. Six states indicated plans to revisit their laws in their applications.
Certificate of need laws, which require that a healthcare provider prove a community need for a new service, were intended to curb monopolies and rising costs. But critics of the laws say they’ve instead raised healthcare prices, stalled needed facilities, and barred rural patients from new technology. More than 30 states, plus Washington, D.C., enforce some sort of certificate of need law, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Legislators in several states have been pushing to end the laws, which have faced scrutiny for decades — under Republican and Democratic administrations. But the Trump administration’s aggressive approach to tie the policies to funding has forced states to reckon with their laws quickly.
The Rural Health Transformation Program was added to President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act as an initiative to modernize healthcare in remote areas. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, in its notice to states applying to the program, called certificate of need laws “an additional expense and burden on rural facilities” and explained how states with fewer certificate of need rules would get higher scores.
“It’s not the first time the federal government used funding as a state carrot (versus using a stick) to encourage alignment on an administration’s policy goal,” Maureen Hensley-Quinn, a researcher at the National Academy for State Health Policy, said in an email. She noted that President Barack Obama’s administration included millions of dollars in performance bonuses for states that made it easier for children to enroll in federally funded health insurance.
Hensley-Quinn said the funding “carrot” was an opportunity to take a hard look at whether policies like certificates of need were truly worth it.
“States need to carefully weigh the trade-offs of supporting a ‘voluntary’ federal policy no matter what,” she said, “and additional federal financing, especially in tight state budget years, can tip the scale.”
Obama, Trump on Same Page
Since the Rural Health Transformation Program became law last year, Tennessee has taken the most concrete action. In a bipartisan vote in April, state lawmakers passed a bill that will unravel most of its remaining certificate of need rules over the next four years. Alaska, Connecticut, Delaware, Iowa, and Mississippi have also said they would consider ending or loosening their laws.
“If there’s an issue where you can have President Obama and President Trump in agreement on something, that tells you the idea probably has some merit,” Wes Climer, a Republican state senator in South Carolina, said in 2021, supporting the repeal of that state’s certificate of need law. The legislature voted in 2023 to end most rules in the law, and in January it will stop requiring certificate of need applications for new hospital construction or expansion, leaving them only for nursing homes.
Some certificate of need laws require approval for changes as minor as a new piece of expensive equipment. In North Carolina, a hospital that won a certificate of need to build a much-needed facility was mired in a court battle for three years before breaking ground in 2026.
As more states consider removing their certificate of need laws, Hensley-Quinn warns of unintended consequences: Fewer records will exist that help states track hospital ownership.
Hensley-Quinn said frustrated state officials have come to her years after their states repealed certificate of need laws, saying that even with a licensure process, they don’t have insight into the financial state of their health systems or facilities, or how they’re managed. Certificate of need laws force companies seeking a new foothold in the state to submit voluminous applications. Once the laws are gone, few regulations force transparency. That leaves states unaware when a health system contracts with private equity to provide hospital services, for example.
“Without CON, without ownership reporting, and without an entity that monitors transactions or providers in that way, there’s no way for you to know,” Hensley-Quinn said.
Tennessee’s Certificate of Need Law
Tennessee lawmakers had pushed to change the state’s certificate of need law for years but didn’t pass sweeping legislation until it faced losing out on federal funding. Like all states, Tennessee is set to receive an equal share of half of the Rural Health Transformation Program’s grants, while the other $25 billion in funding is contingent on other factors, including states’ policy commitments.
In 2024, the state’s hospital association opposed a repeal effort in a letter penned by 12 hospital and health system leaders, many serving rural areas, though that more limited legislation passed anyway.
A repeal would harm vulnerable patients by driving up costs and thinning existing hospital staff, said Martin Chaney, CEO of Maury Regional Health, a system in rural Middle Tennessee south of Nashville. Ending the law would create rural healthcare deserts, Chaney wrote in the letter, because hospitals would choose to expand in areas that were already the most profitable, where residents had a range of health insurance providers.

‘Go to Canada’: Trump Touted Americans’ Access to Cheaper Drugs. A New Rule Threatens It.
The import regulation was set to take effect Oct. 22 but was pushed back three months.
Days before it was to go into effect, the Trump administration pushed back a U.S. customs rule threatening the supply of vital prescription drugs imported by millions of Americans.
Under the rule, Customs and Border Protection and the FDA will require coding on packages that makes it easier to know what’s in them. It is aimed at collecting tariffs on even low-value imports, and at catching illegal drugs like fentanyl. It will also add costs and complex paperwork to each order.
Now the regulation, which was set to start Oct. 22, is delayed until Jan. 20.
While it is illegal to import most FDA-approved prescription drugs, the U.S. has allowed Americans to import legal medications in small quantities for personal use since 2003. The FDA rarely inspects the parcels.
“The information we have is there’s going to be a complete shutdown on Oct. 22,” Tim Smith, general manager of the Canadian International Pharmacy Association, said in an interview in early October. The 51 licensed retail pharmacies in his organization urged their hundreds of thousands of U.S. customers to file extra orders before Oct. 9 to be sure as many medications as possible arrived before the clampdown, Smith said.
“These are people in every case who have gone to the doctor, gotten a prescription for whatever, gone to the pharmacy to fill the order, seen how expensive it’s going to be, and then looked for an alternative,” he said. “Those are the people who’ve been coming to us for years.”
As Donald Trump campaigned in 2016, allowing people to import drugs was part of his platform. In his first term, President Trump let states buy cheaper drugs from Canada. He told Floridians at 2020 rallies that their state could “go to Canada” to obtain drugs for them.
But while Florida and Colorado joined the importation program, neither state has brought in any drugs yet.
Patients have, however, and they flooded authorities with at least 109,000 letters urging the FDA to clarify that the rule won’t stop personal-use drug shipments, said Ken Hunter, executive director of the Campaign for Personal Prescription Importation. And Trump ally Laura Loomer called the rule a case of stupidity or sabotage, under a headline that asked, “So Why Is Someone in His Administration Trying To Make Prescription Drugs More Expensive Before The Midterms?”
Seventy-one congressional Democrats signed an Oct. 1 petition led by Reps. Jan Schakowsky of Illinois and Mark Pocan of Wisconsin to warn about the potential impact of the rule. Three House Republicans from Florida wrote separately to CBP and the FDA, noting that Floridians, unlike Americans in Northern states, can’t easily drive to Canada to buy medicine.
By cutting off imports, Hunter said, “they are going to lose millions, maybe billions in tariff revenue.”
“Why would you want to cut off this massive revenue source?” he asked. “Why would they want to cut people off from lifesaving medications two weeks before midterms?”
Pressure by advocacy groups may have led the agency to back off, said Lucia Mueller, president of PharmacyChecker, which helps patients find legitimate pharmacies to obtain cheaper drugs.
“Loomer’s political argument is sound,” she told KFF Health News. “We know she’s had Trump’s ear before.”
The agency’s Oct. 14 news release on the delay said it would help “avoid disruptions to certain international postal shipments.” It didn’t specifically refer to drug imports.
“This is an important short-term success,” said Gabriel Levitt, founder of Prescription Justice, a nonprofit that advocates for more-affordable drugs. “However, the underlying threat to personal prescription drug importation remains, and the next 90 days will be critical.”
A 2020 study found that 2.3 million Americans regularly imported medications from abroad, and some surveys show much higher numbers. About 4 in 10 Americans in a recent KFF survey said cost had led them to not take medications as prescribed over the past year.
When he was diagnosed with atrial fibrillation years ago, Leslie Waters learned that a 90-day supply of the blood thinner Eliquis, or apixaban, would cost $486. “Holy crap!” said the retired computer scientist, who said he lives off a monthly $1,886 Social Security check. Waters, of San Jose, California, learned about the Canada option on the internet and has been buying 90-day supplies from a pharmacy there for $57, including shipping.
Under previous administrations, orders worth $800 or less weren’t taxed or saddled with extensive paperwork. The new rule will require shippers of even low-value international parcels to transmit detailed information about their contents to CBP, along with tariff payments, which must be transmitted through a licensed customer broker.
Zonos, a U.S.-based company that handles logistics for mail from Canada and other countries, told clients in early September that its understanding was that CBP would no longer allow in personal prescription drug packages after the rule took effect, said Smith, of the Canadian pharmacy trade group. In an Oct. 6 webinar, Zonos senior broker Angela Macke said that the company would continue to ship the drugs but that it didn’t know whether the agencies would let them reach patients.
The pharmacy announcements have frightened thousands of customers, said Bill Hepscher, whose company, Canadian Medstore, has six Florida storefronts that help patients import drugs.
“It’s really been hair on fire,” he said. “I could spend my entire day fielding phone calls from people saying: ‘Can I no longer get my Eliquis? I could have a blood clot or stroke!’”

Rising food prices. Supply chain disruptions. Wars. More extreme weather.
The confluence of these factors in 2026 has prompted researchers, advocacy groups and farmers around the world to more forcefully question the architecture of an increasingly stressed global food system—and the money, both public and private, that supports it.
Coinciding with harvest season in much of the world this month, critics and activists are using a handful of agriculture- and food-focused events to home in on the structural problems of a system they say disadvantages developing countries, fattens rich ones and fails to “feed the world” as it claims to.
“It does produce food,” said Jeff Conant, a deputy director with the advocacy group Friends of the Earth. “It also undeniably produces something on the order of a third of the world’s greenhouse gas emissions. It produces illness. It produces dispossession of land-based peoples. It produces obesity and it produces wealth for the corporate elites at the expense of the rest of us.”
This month, Friends of the Earth and more than a dozen advocacy groups published a report tracking the profits of the world’s largest food companies. “It is not, in fact, a food system,” Conant said. “It’s an agribusiness financial complex.”
On Friday—the United Nations’ “World Food Day”— hundreds of farmers from around the world protested against the World Bank and International Monetary Fund, accusing the institutions of undercutting public support for agriculture and worsening hunger.
The protest, organized by La Via Campesina, a grassroots movement of small-scale farmers, came as the institutions concluded their weeklong annual gathering in Bangkok.
Earlier this month, farmers and advocacy groups convened, also in Bangkok, under the movement’s newly coined slogan, “Feed the People, Not the Debts!” The issue, they say, is that low-income countries spend so much money on debt payments they can’t feed their own citizens or invest in agricultural improvements to make food production more resilient.
“We owe 12.23 trillion Kenyan shillings,” said Kenyan farmer Susan Owiti, who traveled to Bangkok to join the protest. “This is a crisis. So what we are saying is we don’t need more debts. What we want is a trade framework that is based on food sovereignty.”
As climate-fueled weather events batter the world’s farms, the ongoing war in Ukraine cuts grain exports and fertilizer shipments remain stalled in the Strait of Hormuz, food prices have soared, making the situation especially fraught.
“Farmers are increasingly integrated into a global supply chain that controls fuel, fertilizer and grain. Every time a disruption happens—COVID, Ukraine, the war in West Asia and others—it leads to a major increase in input prices, pushing us further into debt,” said Zainal Arifin Fuat, a farmer from Indonesia and member of La Via Campesina, at the Bangkok conference. “Then the World Bank and IMF approach us with more loans, which come with even stricter conditions.”
The World Bank did not answer questions from Inside Climate News.
According to a 2023 report from the United Nations, about 3.3 billion people—more than half the world’s population—live in countries, mostly in the Global South, that spend more on interest payments than health or education. This “crushing debt crisis,” as U.N. Secretary General Antonio Guterres has called it, prompted Guterres and many economists to urge overhauls of IMF and World Bank lending policies, which they argued have favored developed countries.
The debt makes it harder for countries to feed themselves while coping with repeated climate-driven droughts, heatwaves and flooding.
In a workshop on food prices held for journalists last week, Raj Patel, a research professor at the University of Texas at Austin and food systems expert, explained that the indebtedness of countries in the Global South locks them into a food-impoverishing pattern. In order to pay back loans in U.S. dollars, he said, countries are forced to grow crops for export rather than using their land to grow food for their own consumption. When selling into the international market, farmers get hammered by exchange rates, which ultimately means the countries have to cut spending on healthcare and education.
“Debt repayment is actively siphoning off the fiscal space countries need to fund the very transition required to survive climate change,” Patel explained to Inside Climate News. “The protesters are calling out the architecture that demands austerity in the Global South to maintain liquidity in the North.”
The beneficiaries of this northern liquidity are the world’s largest agricultural and food companies.
In the new report, “Food, Land and Money,” Friends of the Earth and fellow advocacy groups take a broad swipe at the corporate agribusinesses that have dominated the global food economy, from the 1950s, when the term “agribusiness” was coined by Harvard economists, to the present.
A handful of businesses control the global food system, the report says, using huge swaths of the planet and its resources to grow commodities that don’t actually provide sustenance but instead have become financial instruments.
The report identifies the 100 food and agriculture companies with the largest revenues and then points to the global financial institutions that underpin them.
The top-earning “agrifood” businesses made $4.5 trillion in revenue in 2022, the report found—with the top 10, including Walmart, Cargill and Costco, making up nearly one-third of the total. The report goes on to note that only a handful of financial institutions effectively own the food system, with giant asset managers Vanguard, BlackRock and State Street owning more than one-fifth of the shares in the top 100 companies. The Trump administration is at odds over an executive order targeting housing affordability, people familiar with the talks told Semafor. The White House has grappled with how to address the cost of living ahead of the midterms, which are less than two weeks away.
A six-section draft viewed by Semafor would make it easier for some homeowners to âproactivelyâ cancel their mortgage insurance; create an interagency task force on manufactured housing; allow more homeowners to refinance without title insurance; and direct the Agriculture and VA departments to lower interest rates for single-family home loans.
Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte is pushing for Trump to sign it as soon as this week, some of the people said, while others in the administration are pumping the brakes. Housing groups have expressed concern over some proposed changes, the people said, which they warn could wind up boosting prices.
The White House and Pulte did not comment.
âItâs definitely on everyoneâs radar, and I think people are really just hoping that itâs not something thatâs done for theatrics; that if it is done, itâs more real and has substance to it,â one industry representative said of the executive order. âI mean, people arenât against stabilizing housing costs, right? But they just want it done in a cautious and safe way.â
Scotsman Guide earlier reported on the talks.

The News
SIOUX CITY, Iowa â President Donald Trump will touch down on Thursday in Iowa, the site of perhaps the tightest Senate race in the country. Strangely enough, both candidates are welcoming him.
Only one, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, will be at his rally on Thursday, but Democrats are banking that Trumpâs presence helps them due to his unpopularity.
âItâs good. â¦ He needs to see what the policies, like the tariffs and the war in Iran, cuts to healthcare, have done to a state like Iowa,â Democratic candidate Josh Turek said in an interview.
A couple hours away in Greenfield, Hinson denied any tension between her and Trump, despite her recent calls for him to end the Iran war and stop cutting deals with Russiaâs Vladimir Putin.
âPresident Trump knows where I stand,â she told Semafor. âI nag him a lot to get priorities for us all the time.â
At an event on Tuesday in Des Moines, she disclosed that Trump recently called her right after she dropped off her kids.
âAshley, itâs your favorite president. Howâs it looking, how are you feeling about the polls?â Hinson recalled Trump asking her. She said she asked how a deal to export more soybeans was coming together.
Know More
The Senate race is absolutely everywhere in Iowa, which is also home to three competitive House races and a governorâs race (Democrat Rob Sand is now favored to defeat Republican Zach Lahn). The Senate race appears to be the one Republicans are most worried about. Trump will swing through Iowa twice in October, a sign that Republicans need him to juice turnout in a state he flipped that hasnât flipped back to Democrats.
The radio ads are inescapable, the TV spots are relentless, and Trumpâs visit puts an exclamation point on a race where the National Republican Senatorial Committee and the RNC are both spending millions in coordinated advertising on behalf of Hinson. The top Senate GOP super PAC, Senate Leadership Fund, is also spending money to counteract Turekâs competitiveness.
âYou know what that means. They wouldnât be coming unless they knew that this race was winnable for us,â Turek said.
Democratic groups are spending a lot on Turek as well, identifying his race as a top pickup opportunity in a cycle where Democrats need to net four Senate seats to retake the majority. Hinson said Trumpâs visit will help remind Iowans why they voted so strongly for him in 2024, the third straight cycle the state backed him.
âLook back to where things were two years ago, before we had President Trump securing our border,â she said. âIowans found the choice that they have in this election: somebody who wants to again go back to those policies of two years ago or move our country forward and continue working.â

Two women - a Swiss and an Austrian â have been freed after more than a year in captivity in Niger and handed over to authorities in the Libyan city of Benghazi.
Swiss national Eva Gretzmacher, 76, and Austrian Claudia Abbt, 69, were kidnapped separately in the northern Nigerien city of Agadez in January and April last year.
No details have been given about who was holding them or their demands, although some reports have previously linked the kidnapping to Islamic State militants. The circumstances of their release were not disclosed.
Libyan officials were reported as saying the women would be handed over to authorities in their respective countries after necessary procedures were completed.
Libya's al-Masar TV showed the two women entering what looks like an ambulance and later being attended to by a health worker.
Speaking in French, the women thanked Khalifa Haftar, military commander of eastern Libya, and his son, Saddam Haftar, for their release.
Gretzmacher was an aid worker who had lived for many years in Niger, while Abbt had spent several years living and working as a community worker in Agadez.
A plane was expected to leave Benghazi on Thursday, first stopping in Vienna to transfer Gretzmacher to Austrian authorities before continuing to Switzerland with Abbt, privately owned Air Info Agadez news outlet reported.
Libya has struggled to recover from the chaos that followed the 2011 Nato-backed uprising that toppled long-time ruler Muammar Gaddafi.
It is split between two administrations - one in the east backed by Haftar, and the other in the west in the capital Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah.
Niger and the broader Sahel region have faced years of jihadist violence, including kidnappings and deadly attacks, carried out by different groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State.
The country has been under military control since 2023 when Gen Abdourahmane Tchiani deposed the country's elected President, Mohamed Bazoum.

At rush hour in Nazareth, the largest Arab-majority city in Israel, students are handing out leaflets by the roadside urging motorists to vote in next week's closely fought, general election. Polls indicate that Arab parties could be left holding a critical balance of power.
Disaffection has often driven down past turnout among Arab Israelis - who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. But this election, there is a strong push to get rid of the most right-wing governing coalition in the country's history - an alliance between veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.
"I see it as our duty to bring down this extremist government. They treat us as second-class," says Arkan Badran, 23, who is with the students giving out flyers. "I call on all young men and women to vote for Arab lists, which represent us, because this is our future."
Most opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu and his partners nor the main "Change Bloc", led by centre-right former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a parliamentary majority.
If they are right, after the election anti-Netanyahu parties wanting to form a governing coalition would either have to go back on pledges not to work with the prime minister or make a deal with Arab-majority lists.
A major sticking point is that Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values.
Israel's politics and society have been changed by the deadly, unprecedented Hamas-led assault on the country on 7 October 2023, and subsequent war in Gaza. There is increased mistrust of and hostility towards the country's Arab minority.
"After October 7, we were treated as enemies of this country," says Suha Salman Mousa of the Mossawa Centre in Nazareth, which advocates for equal rights for Arab citizens. "There was shrinking space for freedom of speech. There were major arrests, there was also firing of people from their workplaces because they put something on social media or they went out against the war on Gaza."
Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis. Civil society groups say they have disproportionately cut budgets for Arab communities. The government says reductions are needed to fund wartime defence and security spending.
There have also been politicised campaigns against Arab physicians working in Israeli hospitals and racially motivated attacks on Arab bus drivers by Jewish Israelis.
Some electioneering has sought to capitalise by deepening social divisions. The far-right Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has vowed to "Judaise" parts of the northern Galilee and southern Negev regions where most Arabs live, likening this to expanding settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The majority of Arab Israelis are descendants of Palestinians who remained within what became Israel during the war that surrounded the creation of the state in 1948, when hundreds of thousands were forced from or fled their homes. Israel's current government often frames them as a threat to the state's Jewish identity. Recently, the prime minister has claimed that his rivals plan to team up with Arabs and form a "dangerous government".
To make this point, his campaign has put up billboards, including one at a road junction at the main entrance to Nazareth. They suggest a choice between: "Right or Palestine" - with pictures of main opposition figures, including right-wingers, depicted as representing the latter not the former. The Netanyahu campaign has also used AI-generated videos to present his opponents embracing Arab leaders.
At Radio Nas, a popular Arabic-language station in Nazareth, I meet news anchor Mohammed Magadli, who is also an analyst for Israel's Channel 12. His father, Raleb Magadli, served as Israel's first Muslim minister between 2007 and 2009, representing the Labour party.
I ask the younger Magadli what he makes of Change Bloc leaders refusing to join forces with Arab parties.
"In a word it's racism. But if we're trying to explain why, it's because of the political interests of Benjamin Netanyahu," he says. "He's trying all the time to pull the legitimacy of the Arab parties - because they're Arab, because they're Palestinian. This is affecting the majority of the Jewish parties in Israel."
Polls this week have suggested that both Eisenkot's bloc and Netanyahu's religious-nationalist bloc could each win around 50 seats of the 120 in Israel's parliament while 13 or 14 seats in total could go to Arab-majority groupings.
These are the Joint Arab List, a coalition of Hadash, Balad and Taal, and the smaller United Arab List, an Islamist party headed by politician Mansour Abbas.
While Abbas's party was originally created as part of the Islamic Movement in Israel - which has socially conservative values - he has become known for joining with Jewish partners. He prioritises solving the problems of Arab Israelis and speaks relatively little of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.
Abbas has had a taste of power. In 2021, he became a minister in a previous, short-lived Israeli government led by Naftali Bennett - now a right-wing member of Eisenkot's bloc.
For this election, he has taken the surprise step of giving the number two position on his slate to a Jewish former police official and centrist member of parliament, Yoav Segalovitz. Abbas believes Eisenkot and others will be more open to an alliance with his party after the election and insists he wants to join the next government.
"We've reached the conclusion that parliamentary representation is not enough to serve Arab society. We decided to take responsibility, to become part of the solution to our problems and to offer hope to both Arabs and Jews," he tells me.
"That's why our approach has been driven by a desire to reach a position of influence, not merely representation."

Time is running out to meet key targets within Stormont's energy strategy by 2030, a committee has said.
The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) report followed an inquiry into the Department for the Economy's (DfE) delivery of the net zero strategy.
The PAC heard that Northern Ireland could lose out on significant economic opportunities if action was not speeded up.
Committee chair Daniel McCrossan said the government had a "responsibility to create the conditions needed for investment to proceed, otherwise there is a real risk it will go elsewhere".
During its inquiry, the PAC heard from business and energy sector representatives that uncertainty around future policies and delivery timescales was affecting investment decisions.
It heard investment could be diverted to Great Britain, Ireland and other European markets where existing factors were seen as more certain.
PAC members said it was unacceptable that delays were affecting projects which could support economic growth, create jobs and strengthen energy security.
Published in 2021, the NI energy strategy included a plan to fully decarbonise by 2050 and ensure that at least 80% of electricity consumption comes from renewable sources.
McCrossan, said that despite the strategy presenting a major economic opportunity for Northern Ireland, the evidence heard "pointed to growing frustration among businesses and investors over delays, policy uncertainty and a lack of clarity around delivery".
The PAC chair added: "Our message is clear - there can be no further delays. We want to see barriers removed so that delivery can be accelerated.
"Almost Â£124m of public money has been spent on energy-related programmes, since 2020. We need assurances that Northern Ireland is on track."
Report makes 18 recommendations
He said that despite the DfE "consulting widely" during the development of the strategy, the PAC found "that significant weaknesses had undermined its implementation".
PAC deputy chair Tom Buchanan said: "The next four years are critical. We need to see decisive action, stronger oversight and a clear focus on results.
"Our report makes 11 recommendations, including the publication and regular updating of the department's Energy Policy Statement. Funded plans must also be brought forward to address grid, infrastructure and energy storage constraints."
While the committee noted the department's confidence in achieving the strategy's ambition of a Â£2bn green economy, members said the challenge was turning ambition into results so that Northern Ireland could realise the investment, jobs and wider benefits promised by the transition to net zero.
