From the day they were born, just seven weeks ago, twins Raghad Hassan and her brother Raad have been battling for survival.
They came into the world prematurely, as fighting surged in Yemen's long-running civil war between Houthi rebel fighters and government forces.
When the Houthis reached their village in the Kahboub mountains in south-west Yemen, their family of seven was forced to flee amid bombs, missiles, and drone attacks â the twins protected only by blankets.
What followed was three days on foot heading for the port city of Aden.
"It was very difficult," says their father, Bajash Ali Sagir Hassan, a softly spoken shepherd. "We didn't find cars or transportation. One kind person brought us here [on the fourth day] while others refused."
As the family walked, the twins got weaker, according to their mother Lina. "They were exhaustedâ¦ there was cold and dust. Their vomiting and diarrhoea got worse."
By the time the newly homeless family arrived at al-Sadaqah hospital in Aden, the twins were barely clinging to life. "Just skin and bone," said a doctor, shaking his head, as he looked at their wasted limbs.
Raad was the sicker of the two - his ribs visible and his chest heaving as he took rapid, shallow breaths. He was barely bigger than the hands of the nurse who carried him gently to be weighed and measured.
Bajash looked on, worry etched on his face. He told us the twins were fed twice a day, but sometimes he could only give them water - after the war drove up the price of baby milk.
The diagnosis came quickly - severe acute malnutrition. That can be as deadly as a bullet.
Malnutrition in Yemen is a crisis within a crisis - another frontline in a devastating civil war. Hunger did not arrive with conflict, but it's spreading with the latest bloodshed.
The United Nations says around 800,000 people can no longer receive lifesaving aid and more than 250,000 have been displaced, after an informal ceasefire collapsed in the summer.
Since then the Houthis have made a lighting advance along the Red Sea coast, and they have now completely cut off Yemen's third largest city, Taiz.
The UN says civilians there are "at grave risk" and lacking food due to soaring prices.
The internationally-recognised government is fighting back against the Houthis - or trying to - with the help of Saudi air strikes.
Caught in the middle of all this are fathers like Bajash, fighting to get help for their children. We saw another mother with a malnourished baby being turned away.
We followed Bajash as he rushed through the corridors, trying to get the all-important admissions slip. He found an ally, a forceful supervising nurse, Aisha Ragab, who had run from the war herself, back in 2018.
"I feel for them," she said, "because I have already lived through the situation myself."
Two beds could not be found, but Aisha was undeterred.
"I will settle this by having the twins share a bed... so that we can save them. By God, I will convince them [the doctors]."
Within an hour the twins were lying on a single bed, their tiny bodies taking up little space.
Lina was feeding them sips of fortified milk from a tiny bottle, but Raad could not keep it down. He was cradled in her arms - his eyes wide and his cheeks sunken. Asked if she thought her twins would recover, Lina replied quietly, "God willing."
As we walked through the unit with its pink walls, some doors were padlocked shut.
There are 22 beds, but staff told us only 13 patients were admitted at a time - the most critical cases - due to the lack of international funding, staff, and equipment.
That's a bitter pill to swallow for Dr Noor Mohammed, a harried young doctor.
"It's sad to say, but we lose patients [because of the conditions]," she says.
"We don't have good equipment like ventilation machines, and oxygen bottles," she adds. "There are no good resources. A lot of laboratory investigations... it's very hard to do them."
A recent flare-up in fighting has left civilians in the firing line.
Even before the latest escalation, the UN calculated that half a million Yemeni children would suffer from severe acute malnutrition this year.
The malnutrition unit in al-Sadaqah hospital is a conveyor belt of suffering. As one severely ill baby leaves, another arrives. And some of those discharged are back all too soon.
"Sometimes a child comes back to us after a week, or two days," says Dr Mohammed. "Sometimes it is the same day. They come back and we admit them and the story begins again."
They return because parents cannot afford proper nutrition or vitamins or antibiotics.
"Every child here, his parents came because they don't have anything," she tells me. "They don't have money or insurance. They are here because they can't afford a private hospital."
She does her best for them, she says, and she cries for them.
Many parents - like Bajash - are trying to outrun both war, and poverty. He is now a shepherd without a flock. When he fled, he had to leave 10 sheep behind. They were his only livelihood.
As doctors monitored his twins, he cared for his three older children - all aged under five. They lingered on a bench in hospital reception without toys, bedding or baggage of any kind. But they could not sleep there.
So, they spent the night outside, on the street - one more family with war wounds that cannot be seen but will disfigure a generation.
Additional reporting by Wietske Burema, Lee Durant and Suaad Al Salahi

f933891c89f2.text: The U.S. Embassy in Canada accused Canadian leaders of "openly" describing plans to "influence American politics," doubling down on Ambassador Pete Hoekstra's claims of potential election interference. Why it matters: The accusation further deteriorates Washington's relationship with its northern neighbor under President Trump's costly trade war that's put political pressure on Republicans. Canada targeted its retaliatory tariffs on politically salient states and products ahead of the U.S. midterms. Driving the news: The embassy cited Canada's targeted tariffs as part of the influence accusations laid out in a Wednesday fact sheet . It cited remarks from Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, including an August press conference where she said Canada was "targeting products that will target states in the U.S." She added, "we're being wise and strategic to put political pressure." Joly has echoed that message throughout the trade tensions. The fact sheet also cited Joly's meeting with Democrats. She recently huddled with Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker. What they're saying: Asked about the accusations during a news conference, Prime Minister Mark Carney said "all of our actions are in the interest of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy." Zoom out: The fact sheet also singled out conservative Ontario Premier Doug Ford over a 2025 anti-tariff ad campaign featuring excerpts from a Ronald Reagan speech . It also cited Liberal MP Anthony Housefather's campaigning for Florida Democrat Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz. The memo read, "The Canadian government brushes off concerns about potential interference in U.S. elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances." Catch up quick: Hoekstra said in a recent podcast interview that American officials were "closely watching" Canada for potential election interference. Joly said last week it was "absolutely not" fair to characterize Canada's actions as election interference. Her visits, she said, were aimed to attract investments. Carney, after cheering Canada's reduced dependence on the U.S. in a speech earlier this month, joked, "Careful, they might think that's election interference," seemingly a jab at Hoekstra. Worth noting: The Trump administration has taken an increasingly antagonistic approach to Canada, from trade tensions to threats over its sovereignty . In August, Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario, which straddles the U.S.-Canada border, to "Lake America." He's also continuously said Canada should become the "51st state." The big picture: Trump himself has openly weighed in on politics beyond U.S. borders, including during Canada's 2025 election campaign and ahead of Israel's elections this month. On Sunday, Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection just nine days before Israel's national vote. Go deeper: Escalated U.S.-Canada trade talks threaten fallout

58603b7b289a.text: By — Mark Kennedy, Associated Press Mark Kennedy, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/tom-skerritt-emmy-winning-actor-with-roles-in-alien-top-gun-and-picket-fences-dies-at-93 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Tom Skerritt, Emmy-winning actor with roles in 'Alien', 'Top Gun' and 'Picket Fences,' dies at 93 Arts Oct 22, 2026 7:17 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Tom Skerritt, the Emmy-winning actor who embodied a solid, wry authority figure, whether as a flight instructor in "Top Gun," a tough-but-fair sheriff on TV's "Picket Fences" or the doomed captain of "Alien," has died. He was 93. Skerritt died Wednesday of natural causes, his family said in a statement. "While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity and the love he brought into our lives. He cared deeply about imagination, creativity, storytelling, service, veterans, the natural world and helping others find and share their own voices," the statement said. Skerritt was twice nominated for an Emmy — both for "Picket Fences," winning outstanding lead actor in a drama series in 1993. Other career highlights include playing the patient husband of Shirley MacLaine in "Turning Point," Sally Field's husband in "Steel Magnolias" and a scheming opportunist who stands in the way of Jodie Foster's attempt to communicate with extraterrestrial life in "Contact." "A writer once described me as a character actor locked in a leading man's body, and I've always loved that. It's a nice compliment. I've been able to walk the line between television and features," he told the Seattle Post-Intelligencer in 1997. Onstage, he was the narrator in "Our Town" at Seattle's Intiman Theatre in 2004 and made his Broadway debut in 2013 in an adaptation of John Grisham's "A Time to Kill," in which The Associated Press wrote he "nicely pulls off a charming disgraced and drunken lawyer." Skerritt's early life Skerritt grew up in a middle-class Detroit family, his father a small businessman and his mother a housewife. He had two brothers; a sister died as a child. He spent four years in the Air Force, attended Wayne State University and then switched to the University of California, Los Angeles, to study filmmaking, inspired by a viewing of "Citizen Kane." His performance in a Los Angeles theater production of "The Rainmaker" led to his first film role — a supporting role as a sergeant in the 1962 scrappy, $250,000 independent Korean War film "War Hunt." The movie marked the debuts of Skerritt, Robert Redford, Sydney Pollack and Francis Ford Coppola. Redford and Skerritt were vying for the same lead role, with the former winning out. Years later, Redford, now directing, paid Skerritt back with compound interest in "A River Runs Through It," handing him the plum role of the stern Rev. John Maclean, a minister whose governing passions are his faith and fly-fishing. The New York Times was impressed by his "halting, thoughtful manner." Redford, who died last year, became a lifelong friend. "There was such a deep connection we made with each other that it matured into a level-headed friendship," Redford told the Seattle Times in 2007. "His values were close to mine, and he kept his integrity." 'Alien' and 'Top Gun' After "War Hunt," however, Skerritt still struggled for screen time, landing a small role in "M.A.S.H." and "Thieves Like Us" for Robert Altman, and doing a bit part as a motorcycle cop in "Harold and Maude" for Hal Ashby. Things changed with "The Turning Point," which earned him a National Board of Review win. Then came "Alien," with Skerritt playing the beleaguered and doomed captain of the ship Nostromo, crouched in a dark, claustrophobic duct, hunting the alien with a sputtering flamethrower. He told the Seattle Times that what appealed to him in the script was that the lead actor disappeared and "the woman becomes the hero. I really like that idea." Things shifted again after that, including a memorable role as Tom Cruise's instructor in the landmark "Top Gun": "Gentlemen, you are the top 1% of all Naval aviators. The elite. The best of the best. We'll make you better," he told the students. "This school is about combat. There are no points for second place." Skerritt achieved perhaps his best notices as the kindly sheriff in "Picket Fences," a comedy created by David E. Kelley that won 14 Emmy Awards — one for Skerritt — and a Golden Globe over its four-year run from 1992 to 1996. Skerritt co-starred opposite Kathy Baker, playing his doctor wife in the community of Rome, Wisconsin, a place with bizarre happenings, like having a robber leaving a trail of frogs or the pope becoming the primary witness to a murder. "It was written by the best writer on television," he told the A.V. Club in 2019. "That was the magic and brilliance of it. Because I wasn't trying to do a series, but then they said Kathy Baker was going to do it, and I thought, 'She's fabulous — what do they want me for?'" Also on the small screen, Skerritt played William Walker on ABC's "Brothers and Sisters," Jimmy Ford on TNT's "Leverage" and he had the recurring character Evan Drake on "Cheers." He starred in the Hallmark movie "What the Deaf Man Heard," co-starring Matthew Modine, Judith Ivey and James Earl Jones. He also modeled for Guess jeans. Directing and writing — his initial dream — had been overtaken by a career in front of the camera, though he managed to direct and star in the 1997 television movie "Divided by Hate." "Things happen," he told The Ottawa Citizen in 1992. "You get hired for a film and the roles kept coming for me. I kept telling myself that if I stuck with acting it would be a really good training for what the problems are in directing. Then the family came along and I had to support them. The years flew by and there was a time when I said I would give up acting and really try to get into directing. But it hasn't worked out

dc3e5a89323a.text: By — Gene Johnson, Associated Press Gene Johnson, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/teacher-injured-in-oregon-school-shooting-says-she-had-no-chance-to-protect-students Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Teacher injured in Oregon school shooting says she had no chance to protect students Nation Oct 22, 2026 7:06 PM EDT A teacher wounded in last week's attack on a special education classroom at an Oregon elementary school never had a chance to try to shelter any of the children inside, she said Wednesday in a statement issued by a family friend. READ MORE: Oregon father is the latest armed civilian to confront a gunman in a U.S. mass shooting Becky Drury said she ran to see what was going on but immediately saw the shooter and rushed back to the classroom. "I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there," Drury said. "Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground." Her left hand was nearly severed by a gunshot, and her right arm was struck as well. Unable to get up or defend herself or others, she said, "I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again." Three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and a teacher were killed at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, last Thursday when a former student there, 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, blasted his way through locked doors with a shotgun and attacked the classroom. Another student was critically injured. The pump-action shotgun used in the attack was purchased legally, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said in an update to the city council Wednesday. But he didn't say who bought it and added that investigators are still piecing together how it ended up in the shooter's hands. The Associated Press previously reported it had been purchased by the shooter's mother, according to a law enforcement source who was not authorized to discuss the investigation. Authorities said another teacher threw her phone at the attacker and then tackled him and wrestled with him for control of the weapon, likely saving lives before the shooter was shot by a father who followed him into the building. Some news reports had suggested that Drury threw herself on top of one student to protect her. Drury, who remains hospitalized, said she wanted to correct the record. "Accurate, respectful reporting is a truly important service that will help heal the wounds inflicted by that awful day," she said. The district closed schools after the shooting but reopened them Wednesday everywhere but Silver Rail. Dozens of officers were at each school to welcome children, the Bend Police Department said. "We do have some families that are still not ready yet, and we most certainly have some Silver Rail families that are still going through a lot of processes," said Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook. In a social media post, the police department said its investigation includes serving search warrants at the attacker's home, as well as on his electronic devices and social media accounts. Associated Press journalist Hallie Golden in Seattle contributed. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Heat-related deaths in Europe’s urban areas exceeded 50,000 in the summer of 2026, as repeated waves of record-breaking temperatures swept across the continent from late May through August.
More than 32,000 of those deaths were attributable to human-caused global warming, driven primarily by the burning of fossil fuels, according to studies published in Nature Health.
Urban areas of Europe’s major economies, Italy, France, Spain, Germany and the United Kingdom, recorded the highest estimated death tolls. The work by researchers at the Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine warns that Europe’s cities are struggling to keep pace with the growing health risks posed by extreme heat.
“This summer has been another dramatic reminder that climate change is everybody’s problem,” said co-author Pierre Masselot, a health researcher at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine.
The research findings point to the growing reach of heat-related mortality beyond the oldest and most vulnerable populations and underscore the need for governments to improve adaptation efforts, including expanding health care for populations most vulnerable to extreme heat, he said.
Scientists examined 854 urban areas across 30 European countries, covering about 40 percent of the population. The countries included the 27 European Union member states, plus Norway, the United Kingdom and Switzerland.
They compared actual summer temperatures with a model of what they would have been without human-caused warming, then combined it with historical data on heat and death rates to estimate monthly heat mortality. The late-June heat wave was the deadliest, accounting for about a third of the summer’s total mortality.
Between June 17 and July 1, daily mean temperatures across the entire region were more than 9 degrees Fahrenheit (5 degrees Celsius) above the 1991 to 2020 average. The scientists concluded that, as “fossil-fuel driven climate change has pushed temperatures higher, the proportion of deaths attributable to climate change has grown too.”
During the summer of 2003, the proportion of heat-related deaths attributable to human-caused warming was 42 percent; in 2022 it reached 59 percent and rose to 65 percent this year, one of the two new papers shows.
The historical comparison comes from the study examining summers from 2000 to 2025. The second paper, which has been accepted for publication, applies the same analysis for the summer of 2026. Together, the analyses show how the share of heat-related deaths attributable to human-caused warming has increased over time.
Behind these statistics are “real people whose lives were lost and real families who grieve for them,” said Clair Barnes, a research associate at the Grantham Institute, Imperial College London, who focuses on how climate change affects extreme weather. Targeted interventions to protect the most vulnerable people are urgently needed, said Barnes, the lead author of both papers.
The research also highlights the growing need to “rapidly transition away from fossil fuels to slow the pace of change and limit future warming,” she added.
With the extreme heat this past summer, mortality soared in northern regions like the United Kingdom that are traditionally cooler. People older than 85 accounted for more than half the total heat-related deaths, but the study also showed that, across the 30 countries, 6,000 people under the age of 65 died during heat waves. 
Age isn’t the only factor that makes people more vulnerable, said co-author Garyfallos Konstantinoudis, a health and heat researcher at the Grantham Institute, ImperialCollege London. In a study published in early October, he and other researchers found more heat deaths in populations that are “socially deprived.” That includes limited access to education and other key social vulnerability factors, Konstantinoudis said.
The estimated death toll of 4,500 in the United Kingdom serves as a warning that other areas with historically moderate climates need to prepare for extreme heat impacts now, said Andrew Hartle, a professor of anesthesia at Imperial College London and an intensive care consultant at Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust.

In the U.K., summer is usually the quietest time of the year for health emergencies, but the heat drove demand for care and strained hospitals to levels usually only seen during a severe winter flu season. Patients were overheating while receiving treatment for other conditions, and the heat increased the risk of medical equipment failure, he said.
Much of the country’s hospital infrastructure is “not built to withstand these temperatures,” Hartle added.
The summer’s extreme heat also helped spark some of the largest public climate protests since the height of the Fridays For Future movement in 2019. About 40,000 people demonstrated in Amsterdam in mid-September, followed by tens of thousands more joining subsequent protests in Germany, Belgium and Austria.
Across the demonstrations, protesters called on their governments to do more to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and protect people from extreme heat.

The body in charge of Britain's electricity network has given assurances that the lights will stay on this winter after concerns were raised by some of its engineers.
The National Energy System Operator (NESO) said the country's electricity system was prepared and "resilient to the challenges it may face" during the colder months.
However, its winter outlook report comes after an independent investigation found engineers had "high levels of stress and concern" about their ability to ensure adequate supply due to differences between renewable and gas-fired power generation.
NESO said supplies were expected to remain secure throughout the winter, though warned there could be "tight days".
It added that such days would result in it deploying notices to power producers that additional electricity generation may be needed. It said such an announcement was not a warning of power cuts and was routine.
"While we never take resilience for granted, households and businesses can be confident that Great Britain's electricity system remains secure, reliable and among the most resilient in the world," said Deborah Petterson, director of whole energy system resilience at NESO.
In a separate report, National Gas, a private company that owns and runs the country's gas network, and is separate from NESO, said it expected to have sufficient supply to meet demand this winter, but forecast gas for power generation to increase at peak demand due to the "intermittent" nature of renewables.
Supply under scrutiny
The release of the two reports comes as Britain's energy generation and security falls under increasing scrutiny, given the wars in the Middle East and eastern Europe have pushed prices up and sparked supply fears.
The country's electricity is generated from a wide range of sources, including renewables such as solar and wind, as well as more traditional gas-fired and nuclear power stations.
Wind power was the largest generator of electricity in Britain last year, accounting for almost 30% of all power, marginally above gas.
However, there appear to be challenges in the transition to renewables in ensuring supply keeps up with demand, according to findings from an investigation into practices at NESO, which was commissioned following allegations over operational decision making and record keeping at the grid operator.
'High levels of stress'
Law firm Eversheds Sutherland, which carried out the independent investigation, said there were "high levels of stress and concern" within NESO's Electricity National Control Centre over the "current state of the energy industry generally" and the longer-term ability to keep it balanced.
It said this was, according to evidence gathered from staff, due to the fact that traditional methods of electricity generation such as gas were "easier to manage", compared to renewables, which were "less flexible", and were making the job of ensuring supply meets demand "more difficult".
The probe also found there to be a "significant disconnect" between those working in the control room and NESO's leadership.
Multiple witnesses expressed the view that those in senior leadership and executive positions "do not fully appreciate or understand either the way in which the control room works, or the reality of the pressures faced by those on the frontline who are responsible for 'keeping the lights on'", Eversheds' report said.
The investigation was prompted after Conservative shadow energy secretary Clare Coutinho said in July she had been contacted by a whistle-blower alleging that NESO had been "hiding information about how securely our grid is being run".
One of the claims was that control room staff were encouraged to conceal or alter records to avoid leaving a paper trail linked to efforts to stabilise the grid during a period of extreme heat in June.
This was done in order for NESO, which is owned by the government, to avoid public scrutiny or reputational damage, according to the allegation.
Eversheds said its investigation did not substantiate any of the allegations from whistle-blowers but did identify "cultural, governance and control issues" that it said were "significant findings in their own right".
Fintan Slye, chief executive of NESO, said the investigation identified "areas where we could improve how colleagues can raise concerns and how we respond to them".
"I want all colleagues at NESO to feel heard. We will act on the recommendations, working closely with our trade unions, and be open with colleagues about the progress we make," he added.

40039b3b5985.text: A small group of Rep. Brandon Gill's fellow House Freedom Caucus members are privately questioning whether he still belongs in the hardline group, Axios has learned. Why it matters: The 32-year-old Texas freshman's rapid rise through House Republican ranks has transformed him into one of the party's most prominent young stars — and earned him a growing list of critics. Driving the news: Multiple House Republicans told Axios that Gill is the future of their party, but several Freedom Caucus members told Axios that his engagement with the group has faded as his national profile has grown. The lawmakers spoke on condition of anonymity to offer candid assessments of a colleague. "He's not really in the Freedom Caucus. He's just using it for conservative bonafides," one HFC member told Axios. The Freedom Caucus is "livid" at Gill, another member told Axios. The intrigue : Four sources familiar with the conversations said members have privately discussed kicking Gill out, though the conversations have been informal and the issue has not been raised at a HFC meeting. It's unclear if there would be enough support within the group to boot Gill if there ever was a formal vote. The other side: "Congressman Gill is laser-focused on getting out the vote and ensuring Republicans hold the majority this November," a spokesperson for Gill told Axios in a statement. State of play: Gill has become a favorite in President Trump's orbit, has won praise from GOP leadership and has launched an ambitious bid to head one of the House's most powerful committees. Asked about the criticism from Gill's colleagues, Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) flatly told Axios in an interview earlier this month that Gill "needs to be out front. I don't care where it is," adding, "Brandon is the future of our party, and his communication skills are phenomenal." But his ascent has fueled resentment, with colleagues accusing him of burning bridges and treating fellow Republicans as stepping stones to greater power and influence. Zoom in: Members say Gill benefited from introductions to HFC donors but hasn't adequately financially supported fellow members in difficult races. "For those of us who have been in meetings, who have been in the tough votes over the last two years, he's been M.I.A.," one HFC member said, adding that he's "totally looking for the ladder climbing." Gill, who is in a R+11 district, raised $4.7 million in the third quarter, a massive haul for a freshman member. Gill's office pointed out that he's given to over a dozen HFC members' campaigns. What they're saying: Freedom Caucus Chair Andy Harris (R-Md.) accused the media of "ginning up stories about Republicans based on anonymous sources," insisting the group is "united and laser-focused" on advancing Trump's agenda. One HFC member defended Gill, telling Axios: "I'm glad that young talented patriots like Brandon are not only coming into politics but that they are climbing quickly...Of course I would like to see him stay in HFC." "I'm not frustrated with Brandon at all," Rep. Mark Harris (R-N.C.), also a freshman member of the caucus, told Axios. "He comes to meetings. I don't know why they feel like he doesn't." "HFC is its own worst enemy sometimes," one GOP member told Axios. "They've managed to kick out, alienate some of their members that help them fundraise." The Freedom Caucus has kicked out members before. In 2023, the group voted to oust former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) over a fight with Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), and in 2024, the group ousted former Rep. Ken Buck (R-Colo.) for "nonattendance." Friction point: Gill's bid to become the top Republican on the powerful Oversight Committee is also creating friction beyond the Freedom Caucus. Republicans Axios spoke with questioned whether Gill's success at generating viral hearing moments makes him qualified to lead the committee, while others have raised concerns about his history of publicly attacking fellow Republicans like Rep. Maria Salazar (R-Fla.) over her immigration bill . "He's kind of skipping a few steps here, and he doesn't necessarily have the credentials to do it," one House Republican told Axios. Gill has also sought to build influence within the broader conference, contributing $1.1 million to the National Republican Congressional Committee in September. Behind the scenes: A House Republican said Gill stopped returning texts and began treating colleagues differently as his national profile grew, echoing complaints from Gill's Freedom Caucus colleagues. The lawmaker told Axios that there was a sentiment among some Republicans that Gill's fame had gone to his head. Gill, who is president of his freshman class, is a frequent guest on Fox News, including during coveted primetime hours. The big picture: The Freedom Caucus is on the cusp of an identity crisis — at least 10 of HFC's more than two dozen members will not return next term, including some of its most prominent voices . Gill has been viewed by some in the caucus as someone who could fill that void and emerge as a leading voice for the next generation. But the group could gain influence at the highest levels of leadership: Founding member Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) is being floated as a potential minority leader if Republicans lose the House. That could reshape the group's relationship with GOP leadership, which the hard-line caucus has made a habit of challenging . The bottom line: "He's already kind of left the Freedom Caucus," an HFC member told Axios. "The only question is whether you formalize it or you don't."

Geoff Bennett: With a proper welcome to the "News Hour" now, we should say we had a technical issue at the start of tonight's broadcast. So thank you for bearing with us. Now, with the midterm elections less than two weeks away, a new legal battle is raising questions about the federal government's role in policing who is eligible to vote. A federal judge in California has blocked a Department of Homeland Security effort to identify noncitizens on voter rolls. I spoke earlier about it with our White House correspondent, Liz Landers. So, Liz, this federal judge issued this ruling with now less than two weeks before Election Day. So there's some clear urgency here. Liz Landers: Yes, the Department of Homeland Security has been engaged in this operation since August, according to this lawsuit. And this federal judge in California ruled yesterday that they must restrict their field operations to look for voter fraud and noncitizens on voter rolls. DHS cannot do stops in field interviews unless they think someone is a noncitizen. This applies to nine different states, California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington, and Wisconsin. There are hundreds of DHS agents who are assigned across all states to look for voter fraud. This has been dubbed the Unlawful Voter Initiative. And the judge here is concerned that the lists created by DHS had errors and did have citizens' names on them. The judge is allowing this to go into effect tomorrow, so that the government has time to appeal. Geoff Bennett: And there's a separate lawsuit the DOJ has brought in California related to mail ballots? Bring us up to speed. DOJ has alleged that there are 20,000 noncitizens on the voter rolls there. The L.A. County registrar's office told me today that they have not stopped the ballot processing there. This is still playing out in a court of law. This is a hearing. The next hearing on this is going to be next Tuesday. And the attorney general, Todd Blanche, was asked about the department's intentions behind the lawsuit earlier today. Todd Blanche, U.S. Attorney General: We're not trying to create chaos. It continues to baffle me why anybody, if presented with evidence that there are tens of thousands, 20,000 ineligible voters that are receiving ballots, that there isn't some motivation, anything to do something about that. And this lawsuit says that there are -- that the Trump administration is using unfounded voter fraud claims to influence how the elections are conducted. Geoff, I want to be clear here that there are very few, but there are examples of noncitizens voting in elections. New Jersey uncovered a few months ago a software glitch -- this happened years ago -- that allowed noncitizens to register and vote in that state. It was a mistake. There were 6,600 people that registered to vote; 340 of those actually vote. Geoff Bennett: When the DOJ alleges that some 20,000 noncitizens are on the voter rolls in California, where is that number coming from? Liz Landers: So the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security are compiling lists based on state data that they're getting, but it's not complete data sets. And that's why you are seeing states like California, like the secretary of state and the Los Angeles County registrar, saying, we don't know if this is an accurate list. And, in fact, some of those lists that they have been giving back to states saying, hey, we think that all these people are noncitizens, as it turns out, especially in Nevada -- this was a recent example -- there were many people on that list, in fact, all of them in Nevada, who were U.S. citizens. Geoff Bennett: Now, beyond all this, you have also reported today that the Justice Department is preparing a large-scale election monitoring effort? What did they announce? Liz Landers: Yes, a senior Department of Justice official briefed reporters on this and said that they're going to send more than 1,000 election monitors across all 50 states in the country. The agency regularly monitors elections, but this year is a big spike in that number. A DHS -- a DOJ official, I should say, told us that the 2022 midterms had 388 people serving as monitors. So this year would be more than double that. These efforts are guided by federal statutes like the Voting Rights Act. And the DOJ official was very clear that their monitors must follow state and local guidance. This is supposed to be a passive act. These election monitors are supposed to observe and take notes. And monitoring these elections is supposed to be a way to ensure that voting rights laws are being followed, Geoff. Geoff Bennett: And how are state and local officials responding to all of this? Liz Landers: Secretaries of state have started to receive these letters from the Department of Justice about this election monitor program. The Kansas Republican secretary of state, Scott Schwab, he said he got notified earlier this week by DOJ. He's going to allow the election monitors to come to Kansas. 40c84d231ced.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/iran-says-7-oil-tankers-damaged-in-strait-of-hormuz-and-other-middle-east-news Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Iran says 7 oil tankers damaged in Strait of Hormuz, and other Middle East news World Oct 22, 2026 6:48 PM EDT Iran's state television reported on Thursday that seven oil tankers were either struck by attacks or hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz overnight, possibly the largest single-day number of vessels damaged in the waterway since the Iran war started on Feb. 28. Here is the latest news from the Middle East. 7 oil tankers reported damaged in Strait of Hormuz Iran's state television reported that seven oil tankers either caught fire or were damaged by mines overnight Wednesday into Thursday after being targeted or striking naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz. If verified, it would be the largest single-day number of vessels damaged in the waterway since the start of the Iran war on Feb. 28 when the United States and Israel launched joint strikes against Iran. READ MORE: Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall in debate blames Ukraine war, not Iran war, for high diesel prices Quoting a statement by the Revolutionary Guard's navy, the Iranian report said four of the tankers were transferring oil when they were targeted and caught fire. Three more were damaged and immobilized after hitting naval mines. The report didn't provide details about possible casualties or the tankers' flags. Shipping data and analysis company Lloyd's List Intelligence said Thursday that tanker operators willing to risk the voyage have been transporting oil from Gulf producers through the strait at night, using a U.S. military-protected lane near Oman's coast with their location systems and mobile phones switched off. The oil is then transferred to other tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman for shipment to customers in Asia. Oil company says volume bypassing strait via pipeline has surged The president of Saudi oil company Aramco, whose sites have been targeted by Yemen's Houthi rebels, says the amount of oil moving through a pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz has more than tripled. The East-West pipeline's capacity has surged from 2 million to 7 million barrels each day, President and CEO Amin Nasser said in an interview with Saudi-owned television Al Arabiya Business. Built in the early 1980s, the pipeline played a crucial role in Saudi Arabia's ability to export oil following the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war. Nasser said the company has used drones to assess damage caused by oilfield attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels and to help with firefighting. UN chief says Egypt is 'vital' to solving Mideast crisis United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said Egypt has a vital role to play in resolving the Middle East crisis, citing its "defense of the rights of the Palestinian people" and its mediation efforts in the U.S.-Iran conflict. Guterres, who is due to arrive in Egypt on Friday, said he would also discuss the war in neighboring Sudan, the situation in Libya and hostilities in Yemen, including the siege of Taiz and Houthi rebel attacks on civilian targets in Saudi Arabia. He called those attacks "totally unacceptable." Yemen says rallies in support of Houthi rebels could be targeted Yemen's Defense Ministry said Thursday that rallies and mobilization programs by the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels will be considered legitimate military targets and warned residents in Houthi-held areas against taking part. READ MORE: Iran-backed Houthi rebels strike Yemen's government forces with ballistic missiles, killing at least 53 The announcement on social media is considered a major escalation against the Houthis and civilians living in areas under their control. Pro-Houthi rallies are regularly staged on Fridays, the Muslim day of prayer. Deliberate attacks on civilians could be a war crime. Rallies and what Houthis call "cultural courses" are one of the Iranian-backed group's main tools to mobilize supporters and fighters. The Defense Ministry said Houthis are also mobilizing children for combat. Saudi airport strike death toll rises to 2 Saudi Arabia's Civil Aviation Authority said Thursday that the number of people killed in an attack the night before on the King Fahd International Airport has risen to two — a Saudi citizen and an Indian national living in the kingdom. Another eight people suffered injuries in the attack, which occurred late on Wednesday, the statement said. Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for the attack in a statement posted Thursday on Telegram. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree also claimed the Houthis targeted an Aramco facility in Yanbu that ignited a fire, as well as the Saudi Defense Ministry in Riyadh. Saree didn't provide any evidence for the ministry strike. King Fahd Airport in the country's east near Bahrain and Qatar has been attacked previously amid a wider wave of Houthi missile and projectile strikes targeting major Saudi airports. Strikes kill 4 in Gaza Strip At least four people were killed and several others wounded Thursday in Israeli strikes and gunfire in the Gaza Strip, hospital officials said. One person was killed when a car was struck in Gaza City, according to Shifa Hospital. Another was killed and others wounded in a strike on a gathering in a street in the southern city of Khan Younis, according to Nasser Hospital. The Israeli military said those strikes targeted Hamas militants. A woman was also killed by Israeli military fire in the northern city of Jabaliya, Shifa Hospital said. And an Israeli strike that hit a refugee camp in Nuseirat, in the central region, killed one person, according to the Awda Hospital. c9174e301e14.text: Ukrainians are desperate for more defense systems to repel Russia's relentless onslaught of drones and ballistic missiles. For the missiles, no system is more valuable than the U.S. Patriot interceptor. But years of use in Ukraine and by the U.S. and allies in the war with Iran have depleted thin stocks. Special correspondent Mike Cerre has an exclusive look at the Patriot manufacturing process. Geoff Bennett: As Kyiv burns night after night, Ukrainians are desperate for more missile defense systems to repel Russia's relentless onslaught of drones and ballistic missiles. For the missiles in particular, no system is more valuable than the U.S. Patriot interceptor. But years of use by the Ukrainians and by the U.S. in the war with Iran have depleted thin stocks. Special correspondent Mike Cerre has this exclusive look at the Patriot manufacturing process, and also from the ground in Ukraine, where their need is so acute. (SIRENS BLARING) Mike Cerre: It's now 4;15 in the morning in Kyiv, and we're hearing the sirens for the first time. But, earlier, we have heard three sets of explosions and the warnings to get to the bomb shelter, which has become a normal pattern here in Kyiv. The hotel bomb shelter was a new experience for this group of American relief volunteers on their very first night in Kyiv, especially for volunteer Richard Bew, who works for Lockheed Martin, the major defense contractor that builds the Patriot interceptor missiles the Ukrainians need every day and can't get enough of. You sure you don't have an extra Patriot in your backpack? Richard Bew, Lockheed Martin: I think we just spent a couple of them just now, but it sounds like they did their job. Beauty giant L'Oreal says the rise of weight loss drugs has affected beauty and skin care sales, as it designs products to specifically target some side effects of rapid weight loss.
The company's head Nicolas Hieronimus said the beauty market was proving resilient in a challenging global context, and that the use of GLP-1s was "a very important phenomenon for us".
He told an investor call that the rise in their use was "having an impact on beauty consumption and skin care consumption in particular".
L'Oreal, which owns other popular brands including Maybelline and La Roche-Posay, announced on Thursday that sales in the three months to September rose by 7.7%, above analyst expectations.
The use of GLP-1s has boomed in popularity in recent years, after drugs developed to treat diabetes such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro were found to also lead to significant weight loss because they supress the appetite.
While it is not caused by GLP-1 drugs directly, rapid weight loss can, for some people, come with a side effect of loose skin - including around the face.
Hieronimus said L'Oreal's brands SkinCeuticals and Kiehl's have products "that have been designed to work alongside and complement GLP-1 and its side effects on skin sagging" and other effects related to rapid weight loss.
L'Oreal has also moved further into the clinical aesthetic space, increasing its stake in dermatology firm Galderma to 20% last December.
Both companies have been testing products on GLP-1 users worried about loose skin in separate clinical trials, according to Reuters.
Galderma owns popular aesthetic products including Sculptra, an injectable aimed at stimulating collagen production, and Restylane, which is an injectable dermal filler.
Last year the aesthetic firm released a report into the rise of GLP-1 use and related concerns about changes in facial appearance.
Its own survey of weight loss medication users found the vast majority had noticed changes to their facial appearance after using those drugs.

Scotland is braced for a wet and windy weekend as two named storms hit in two days.
Storm Austen is the first to sweep across the country, with the Met Office issuing a a yellow warning for rain, external in central and eastern areas from 06:00 on Friday until midnight.
Forecasters say some places could experience 60-80 mm of rain, with a risk of flooding and travel disruption.
Storm Boelo will follow hard on its heels on Saturday, with another yellow weather warning issued, this time for high winds, for the whole of mainland Scotland, the Western Isles and Orkney.
The wind warning will come into force from 18:00 on Saturday and last until 21:00 on Sunday.
The wind speeds are expected build on Saturday afternoon, reaching a peak overnight.
Gusts of 50-65mph are forecast widely and could reach 80mph in exposed locations.
The storm will also bring wet and windy weather across the whole of the UK on Saturday with poor travelling conditions expected due to surface water and spray on faster roads and motorways.
Network Rail Scotland said that trains on Friday will be slowed down to keep people safe in the areas expected to see the heaviest rain.
Speed restrictions will be in place on parts of the West Coast Main Line and East Coast Main Line, as well as routes across southern and eastern Scotland.
It said some journeys would take longer as a result, but that the restrictions meant trains could continue running through areas where the weather is at its worst.
Safety priority
Speed restrictions for trains are also expected in some areas as the second storm moves across the country over the weekend.
Craig Gorman, head of operational weather strategy at Network Rail Scotland, said: "We can't control the weather, but we can make sure we're as ready as possible for whatever it brings.
"We know any disruption from these storms will be frustrating, particularly as it's the weekend, but we'll do everything we can to keep people moving wherever it's safe to do so."
Mark Ilderton, ScotRail service delivery director, said: "Safety is always our top priority and with weather warnings in place as Storm Austen and Storm Boelo bring heavy rain and strong winds to parts of Scotland this weekend, there is an increased risk of flooding and disruption on the railway."
He advised customers to check services before they travel.
Power cuts are possible, which could also affect mobile phone coverage and other services.
There is a small risk of damage to buildings, including roof tiles being blown off, while flying debris could pose a danger to the public.

A United Nations fund to help developing nations pay the costs imposed by climate change voted Thursday to allocate money for Nepal as the country recovers from devastating flooding in August.
It was a historic step for the fund—the first time it has allocated money to a vulnerable country in an immediate response to climate impacts. But that also highlighted the severe limitations it faces.
It was 2022 when nations agreed to create the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage. The aim was for wealthy nations to contribute money that would flow to developing countries to cover irreversible economic losses caused by climate change. The fund has yet to disburse any money.
The disaster in Nepal, where flooding unleashed by a landslide and glacial collapse killed some 1,500 people, with more than 5,000 still missing, was exactly what the fund was meant to address. Several members of its board recognized this during a live-streamed virtual meeting Thursday that was called specifically to consider a request for support from Nepal.
“Loss and damage are no longer a future concern,” said Tomás Soley Pérez, representing Costa Rica. “They are a present reality for many vulnerable countries. Today it is Nepal. Tomorrow it will be any one of our countries.”
Yet while the outcome was widely praised by government representatives and civil society groups, many said it underscored the fund’s weakness and inability to meet its mandate.
The decision by the board, composed of 26 representatives from governments around the globe, did not actually provide the money, $20 million, but merely allocated it—Nepal must now formally apply and have its request approved. Assuming that final step is taken, which could come at the next board meeting in December, the amount distributed would represent less than 1 percent of the initial economic loss and damages from the flooding, which the Nepali government said is at least $2.69 billion. Another $4.71 billion is needed for initial recovery and reconstruction, the government said.
Harjeet Singh, global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign and founding director of the Satat Sampada Climate Foundation in India, said the vote came only after civil society groups and developing nations launched a relentless campaign pressing the board to take immediate action. Even with this success, he said, Nepal is unlikely to receive any money until next year at the earliest.
Ali Tauqeer Sheikh, representing Pakistan on the fund’s board, called during the meeting for his colleagues to move faster, and criticized the lack of a schedule for the money to flow.
Despite the shortcomings, many people who have supported the fund praised the board’s decision. Raju Pandit Chhetri, lead climate finance negotiator for the least-developed countries at the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change, said in a statement: “The Loss and Damage Fund Board’s approval of $20 million for Nepal’s flood response shows that when countries come together, they can reach swift, effective consensus to address the urgent needs of vulnerable countries.”
As of March, 27 countries had pledged $822 million to the fund. The largest amount has come from the United Arab Emirates, which pledged $100 million. Actual contributions were only $630 million, and some of that has yet to be transferred in. The United States contributed $17.5 million in 2024, before the Trump administration withdrew from the Paris climate agreement.
“We don’t have sufficient money, that’s the heart of the problem,” Singh said. He added that wealthy countries have been delaying the disbursement of money and “will continue to delay it because the moment that fund is empty, there’s pressure to fill it again.”

While many developing nations called for this more rapid response to Nepal to serve as a model for the fund to take swift action, representatives of some wealthy countries, including Germany and Japan, said the vote should not set a precedent for future emergency funding outside the board’s standard process.
So far, 119 countries have sent 176 requests to the fund, seeking a total $2.8 billion in support. The board is expected to consider its first funding decisions beyond the emergency money for Nepal at its next meeting in December, with up to $350 million available.
How the board will choose among the requests, with only a fraction of the needed money to spend, Singh said, is “the billion-dollar question.”
Toward the end of Thursday’s meeting, the board heard from Maheshwar Dhakal, a representative of Nepal, who thanked his peers for their support and stressed the severity of what people in his country were experiencing.
“In some of the hardest-hit communities, entire settlements have been wiped out, leaving no survivors to report who has perished or who has survived,” Dhakal said. He added that the vote represented a powerful example of solidarity and hope, saying, “behind these numbers are human lives.”
Inside Climate News reporter Bob Berwyn contributed to this article.

Elon Musk has restored Ukraine's Starlink internet access, US President Donald Trump has said after restrictions hampered Kyiv's armed forces.
Trump made the comments after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said connectivity to the military-grade Starshield network, which is provided by Musk's satellite-based Starlink system, had yet to be fully restored.
Musk previously denied he was behind the slowdown, which affects Ukraine's ability to use drones to attack Russia and protect itself from attacks.
Trump refused to be drawn on a report that he had called Musk to ask him to lift restrictions to the service, but when asked about it he said: "Bottom line, he put it back."
The Trump administration previously denied instructing Musk's company to restrict access.
The connectivity restrictions came as Trump put pressure on Zelensky to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, which he has argued have caused prices to rise.
Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move which has been criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.
Ukraine relies on Starlink - owned by Musk's SpaceX company - for a range of battle communications and early warning systems during Russian missile attacks.
Earlier on Thursday, Zelensky said the speed of the system used by Ukraine's military had still not been restored fully.
Speaking at a press conference, he said the speed "has not been restored to 400 [km/h; 250mph] yet", adding: "We are working on it."
He continued: "I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so."
The Ukrainian president made the comments shortly before the Wall Street Journal, external reported that Trump called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink.
The US outlet reported that Trump told Musk he was frustrated the Starlink system's speeds were still capped at around 160km/h, according to officials.
The speed limit made Ukraine's offensive drones and interceptors powerless against Russian attacks.
The journal reported that the system was working more normally on Thursday, shortly after their conversation.
BBC News has not confirmed the Wall Street Journal's report. It has also contacted the White House and SpaceX to ask for an explanation.
Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing on 14 October.
Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink which Ukraine uses for some of its operation. He said the system was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions.
The White House has repeatedly said it did not order access to be restricted.

The Prince of Wales has made a surprise appearance on the Graham Norton Show, as part of a special edition to mark the Earthshot Prize.
During the episode, which airs on Friday, he joined Cate Blanchett, Robert Irwin and Hannah Waddingham, who are all involved with the prize.
As Norton spoke about the initiative with the trio he surprised the audience by then inviting the prince out to join them on the sofa.
They discussed the need to pair optimism and urgency when tackling climate change. The prize was founded by William to "celebrate and scale the solutions that will repair our planet".
The guests also chatted about William's long-time support for Aston Villa, and his love of Christopher Nolan films.
William set up the Earthshot Prize in 2020, drawing inspiration from US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely.
There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate. Each winner receives Â£1m.
The future king has committed himself to the prize until 2030. This year's winners will be announced at a ceremony in Mumbai in November.
Last year, the ceremony for the prizes drew famous faces such as former Formula 1 driver Sebastian Vettel and then-UK prime minister Keir Starmer. Pop stars Kylie Minogue and Shawn Mendes performed at the ceremony in Rio de Janeiro.
The 2025 winners included Lagos Fashion Week, for "transforming one of the world's most wasteful industries" by requiring designers to demonstrate their commitment to sustainability.
At last year's ceremony, William said the winners were "proof that progress is possible".
The Graham Norton Show is on BBC One at 22.40 Friday.

Federal prosecutors arrested a prominent Virginia lawmaker on Thursday over allegations she oversaw a criminal marijuana enterprise.
Democratic state Senator L Louise Lucas and six other people, including her family members, have been charged in relation to a sweeping racketeering case that allegedly involves fraud, drug violations, and bribery.
Lucas, 82, claimed the prosecution was politically motivated in a statement on X.
"I will not be intimidated," she wrote. "I will not be bullied. And I will not back down."
While she has not entered a formal plea, Lucas' attorney, Anthony Capozzolo, told the BBC she would plead not guilty.
Capozollo said in a statement they were "surprised and disheartened" to learn of the indictment, and that Lucas "denies these charges in their entirety."
Lucas and her co-conspirators are charged with obtaining and illegally distributing large amounts of illegal marijuana. The government has also accused her of using her political influence to benefit herself and her family.
Lucas was herself charged with five counts, including racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to distribute marijuana, conspiracy to launder money, conspiracy to commit honest services fraud, and maintaining a drug involved premises.
Other alleged participants were charged with a firearm charge and wire fraud.
Lucas is not running for re-election. But her daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke, who is also charged in the indictment, is running for the city council of Portsmouth, Virginia.
"I grew up under Jim Crow," Lucas wrote on X in response to the charges, referencing an era of legal segregation in the US. "I've seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my entire life fighting back, and I'm not stopping now."
At a press conference on Thursday, US Attorney General Todd Blanche accused Lucas of overseeing a criminal "enterprise", arranging for the "acquisition and distribution of marijuana," and using her power as a lawmaker to influence legislation that would benefit herself and her family.
Lucas has served in the Virginia State Senate since 1992, and assumed the powerful role of Senate president pro tempore in 2000. She has publicly spoken about her cannabis dispensary and her support for legalised usage, as well as her opposition to President Donald Trump and Republican lawmakers.
"I'm a 78 year grandma who legalized pot and now has her own cannabis store. And I'm the last thing standing between The GOP and total control of Virginia. That's worth an RT!" she wrote on X in 2022.
While small amounts of cannabis are legal in Virginia for personal or medical use, major restrictions remain in place regarding its sale and consumption.
Lucas has backed legislation to legalise recreational marijuana.
She is an owner of The Cannabis Outlet in Portsmouth, Virginia, which opened in 2021 after the state decriminalised simple marijuana possession and legalised personal possession of certain small amounts of marijuana, according to WAVY News., external
The Virginia Mercury reported in 2022, external that products sold in her shop may have contained substances and dosages that conflicted with state law at the time.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) raided Lucas' office and a cannabis business in May as part of a long-running inquiry, the Washington Post reported at the time.
It is unusual for the justice department to announce major actions involving lawmakers, candidates, or other electorally sensitive matters in the weeks before an election. Early voting is already under way in the US midterm elections, which are held on 3 November.
However, the justice department has announced a series of inquiries against lawmakers and election officials in recent days, including conducting a raid on the home of Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar as the government investigates her immigration status.
Referring to Lucas' case, Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, wrote on X: "The timing of this indictment undermines the US Department of Justice's previously longstanding policy of not taking legal actions â to include indictments or significant investigative steps â close to an election."
She added: "And sadly, this timing further erodes the trust the American people deserve to have in the Department of Justice."

A Florida police officer has been accused of stealing the identity of a man he found dead during a welfare check call and then moving into his home, authorities say.
Brian Louis Sguros, 35, a police officer in Lauderhill, Florida, was arrested this week by the Broward County Sheriff's Office.
Investigators allege he impersonated the deceased man, Dennis West, moved into the house he found West dead in, and then renovated the two-story south Florida home. Police say he lived there for years undetected.
Sguros has not commented on the charges. It's unclear whether he has legal representation yet. He has been placed on administrative leave from the Lauderhill Police Department.
In 2022, police were called to check on a 71-year-old resident of Lauderhill, Florida, Dennis West.
Officer Brian Louis Sguros was called in as back-up for the welfare check. When he found West dead of natural causes, he allegedly "created a complex scheme to take control of the individual's home," the Broward County Sheriff's Office said in a news release.
Investigators say Sguros told the medical examiner's office he was West's friend, though authorities found no indication the two knew each other, according to the news release. Court documents detail that the officer appeared in body cam footage during the welfare check and did not appear to have a prior relationship with the man.
He also allegedly told the county medical examiner that West had no living relatives, which authorities say say was also untrue, the release states.
Sguros then had West's body cremated, according to the BBC's news partner CBS.
According to a joint investigation by the sheriff's office and the Broward County Property Appraiser's Office, Sguros took possession of the home in August 2022 and moved in.
Authorities say in 2025, he allegedly filed paperwork with the property appraiser's office stating that his possession dated to August 2022.
Sguros said he took possession of the home because it was hazardous, and he wanted to prevent people from squatting, according to court documents.
He paid utility accounts which were in the deceased man's name. He also applied for a permit to replace exterior doors and windows, at the cost of $8,000 (Â£5970), according to court documents.
Sguros claimed he has increased the property's value, spending more than $214,000 (Â£159,717) on the home, according to the sheriff's office.
Sguros faces charges of official misconduct, criminal use of a deceased person's identification, criminal use of personal identification information, offense against a computer user, and unlawful use of a two-way communication device.
He was released from jail on a $25,000 bond.
Local law enforcement were made aware of the situation when West's heirs tried to sell the property, according a police affidavit.
Once Sguros eventually returned the keys to the property's rightful owners, he allegedly demanded reimbursement for improvements he had made to the property, court documents state.
The Lauderhill Police Department told BBC News that Sguros has been relieved of his duty and was placed on administrative leave with pay.

The eventual nominee, Rep. Mike Collins, has struggled to keep pace with fundraising juggernaut Sen. Jon Ossoff (D). GOP money is in retreat. 🦞 Maine: Schumer endorsed Gov. Janet Mills, but Graham Platner's implosion left Democrats with backup Troy Jackson against Sen. Susan Collins. ⛴️ Michigan: Abdul El-Sayed defeated Rep. Haley Stevens and made a name for himself nationally. But he won by just one point even though primary polls showed him up by double digits. He's now polling within the margin of error against the GOP nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers. 🏈 Minnesota: Peggy Flanagan ran as a progressive, said she would not support Schumer as leader and bested establishment-backed Rep. Angie Craig. But Cook Political Report moved her race against former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya toward Republicans even as it shifted other races toward Democrats. Joe Manchin, who flipped to independent in 2024 after being elected as a Senate Democrat, is campaigning for Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), as Semafor reported. Former Sen. Are yearlong deployments the Navy’s new normal?
That's what officials are telling sailors' families in Japan, where two destroyers are slated for 12- and 14-month cruises.
When the U.S. Navy destroyer John Finn left home in January, sailors expected to be home in March. Now, after extensions on top of extensions, their families have been told to expect them next March—after a 14-month deployment.
The Mustin, another Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, switched homeports this year, leaving San Diego in February and arriving in Yokosuka, Japan, in March. As the sailors stepped off the ship, they were told they needed to be ready to deploy “tomorrow.”
The Mustin actually left Japan in April for a deployment that was supposed to end in August. Now its crew has been told they will return in April 2027, the spouse of one of the sailors told Defense One.
These marathon deployments—a month or more longer than the carrier Abraham Lincoln’s record-breaking 322 days—may be the new normal for U.S. warships. Last week, a Navy official told families at Yokosuka that all ship deployments and patrols, stateside and overseas, will be 10 to 12 months long for the foreseeable future.
Asked about that statement, a Navy spokesperson told Defense One, “It is U.S. Navy policy not to discuss future operations or movements due to operations security.”
But last month, Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle said that sailors and their families should expect “longer deployments” until “I can grow the Navy we need.” The service’s battle force currently consists of about 290 warships, down from 295 two years ago but up from about 275 a decade ago.
In recent decades, the Navy has generally kept deployments to six or seven months, although that is not a set-in-stone policy, said Katherine Kuzminski, vice president of studies at the Center for a New American Security. But, she said, “that commitment is being violated now.”
“Certainly, depending on operational needs and demands, I think service members and their families are fully on board with providing—with the requirements that are put on them in ongoing operations,” Kuzminski said. “A potential way that the Navy can mitigate this is actually to just commit to the longer term upfront and be clear with service members and their families.”
After initial reports of the Lincoln’s woes emerged, some veterans of other services and other conflicts were quick to post online about their own longer deployments. But the issue, Kuzminski said, is not so much the length of the deployment, but the “dissonance between what was said at the beginning and what is happening in actuality.”
That dissonance is particularly pronounced for the John Finn, one of several “forward deployed” guided-missile destroyers based at Yokosuka. While other Navy ships tend to deploy for about six months and then return home for a year, forward-deployed ships typically leave for two or three months at a time, then return to port for two to three months of maintenance before heading back out to sea. Those deployments are designed to keep the ships ready for combat in the region, deter aggression from China, and “maintain a free and open Indo-Pacific.”
Last year, the John Finn left home in June for a “normal” deployment in the region and returned in early November. But much of the following two months were spent in hasty preparations to return to sea.
“We really only saw him a collective 20 days,” the spouse of a sailor on the ship told Defense One.
In early January, the ship left again, for what was expected to be a deployment of perhaps 45 to 60 days. It headed to the Indian Ocean and was involved in the boarding of a Venezuelan oil tanker before being directed to the Arabian Sea, shortly before Operation Epic Fury began.
The ship was part of the initial attack on Iran, the spouse said, and they’re “still there.”
Earlier this month, the sailors were told they would likely not be home until March 2027.
“There’s cars that were left on base that have been stickered to be towed and then to be junked. So there’s sailors that are going to come back and have no cars,” the spouse said. “They left in the winter months, and there’s some sailors that live off base and are single sailors and will have abandoned their entire house, their apartment, for over a year. And when they left in the winter months, when they left everything on heat mode, and then the summer came.” Sailors know “that they’re going to come home and all their stuff will be trashed.”
For families, it’s more than a year without a parent—without any of the planning for a long deployment.
“It’s been absolutely gut-wrenching to my kids,” the spouse said, and there is “next to no mental health support” available on base. The deployment length is “absolutely unheard-of for a destroyer,” she said.
The Finn’s story is extreme—but not unique among Yokosuka-based destroyers.
Photos posted on the Pentagon’s DVIDS media site show the Rafael Peralta in the Philippine Sea in November, in the South China Sea in December, and back in the Philippine Sea on Jan. 8. Then, instead of returning home, it headed for the Middle East in April, where it remains today. Families have been told not to expect the ship home until April 2027.
The Higgins, which lost power and propulsion for a few hours in the Indo-Pacific in April, continued its deployment after repairs and is currently operating in the Indian Ocean. The Milius left Japan in February and has been in the Middle East since March.
The Mustin left its old homeport of San Diego in February and arrived in Japan in March. Sailors are usually given 30 days to help their families move and settle in for a homeport shift, particularly when the move is to a foreign country, and the majority of the families had waited until the ship arrived to make the move. But “the moment they pulled in, my husband stepped off the ship, and he goes, ‘We have to be prepared to leave tomorrow,” a Mustin spouse told Defense One.

Kennedy Jr. and a chief advocate for the Make America Healthy Again movement, resigned from his position with the Trump administration Thursday. In a statement, Means did not say why he was leaving. His departure comes as leading voices in the MAHA movement have expressed discontent with what they say is the Trump administration's lack of progress on a variety of issues, including food security and regulating the weed killer glyphosate. WATCH: Some MAHA backers grow frustrated with Trump's health policies Means said he "leaves with tremendous respect" for President Donald Trump and Kennedy. "The past two years have seen historic policy and cultural change to confront the chronic disease crisis and healthcare incentives that profit from us being sick," Means said. "This movement is in the first inning and just getting started." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Means was hired as a White House adviser early in the second Trump administration. He used his perch at the Health and Human Services Department to attack the nation's leading physician groups, federal agencies and government scientists, claiming they only protect their own interests. READ MORE: RFK Jr. aide attacks U.S. health system as corrupt while running company that promotes alternatives White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the Trump administration is "grateful" for Means' time and "he has done a fantastic job for the MAHA movement." A representative from Health and Human Services did not respond to a request for comment. Health activist Kelly Ryerson, a leader of American Regeneration who is also known as Glyphosate Girl on social media, said she is "impressed that he completed over two years at HHS fighting the food battle, despite all of the obstacles presented by corporate interests." "At the heart of MAHA is a shared belief that the nation's health must not be sacrificed to corporate profit, and that a preventable slide into chronic disease is a threat to America itself," she said. Means is the brother of wellness influencer, author and entrepreneur Dr. Casey Means, who failed to be confirmed as surgeon general earlier this year after doubts were raised over her vaccine stance. Means, along with his sister, came to prominence within the MAHA movement by arguing that ultraprocessed foods, additives and pesticides could be blamed for many of the chronic health conditions facing Americans. Means brought those arguments into the Trump administration and frequently clashed with senior White House officials who worried about alienating the powerful food industry. At the same time, Means' emphasis on food was a source of frustration for other figures within the MAHA movement who wanted to see Kennedy focus on "medical freedom" issues. For many, that meant rolling back federal recommendations and approvals for vaccines. Despite Means' efforts, the administration's progress on food reforms has been slow going. Kennedy had promised the release of a first-ever government definition of ultraprocessed food in April. Instead, FDA's acting commissioner, Kyle Diamantas, told a conference that month that defining the class "is really hard." In August, Kennedy staffers again suggested a major announcement on the issue was imminent. Instead, the announcement focused on a proposal bringing greater scrutiny to food additives. It made only passing mention of ultraprocessed foods. Zen Honeycutt, founder of Moms Across America, said Means will be missed by her organization, which operates local and national campaigns warning against pollution, water use and electricity costs associated with data center construction. Honeycutt said Means "brought an energy and fearlessness to the Hill, fighting for our children to have healthy food in schools and for America's health."
